### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6s 事彙部類 (*Shìhuì bù lèi*) is the catch-all "subject-collected" division of the Kanripo edition of the Chinese Buddhist canon. It assembles the auxiliary, paratextual, encyclopaedic, and bibliographically-organized materials that the medieval and early-modern canon editors did not place in the doctrinal divisions (*sūtra*, *vinaya*, *abhidharma*) proper. In Taishō terms it spans large parts of vols 53–55 (T2121–T2184) plus selected items from T54's heterodox section (T2137–T2144) and T85's *gǔyì* / *yísì* 古逸／疑似 section (Dunhuang manuscripts and dubious texts), supplemented by Korean (高麗藏 → 嘉興藏 → 卍續藏) and Japanese imperial-era recensions for items that did not enter the Taishō main canon. The matching CANWWW divisions are `div22.xml` (事彙部, encyclopedic compendia and lexicographical works), `div24.xml` (外教部, non-Buddhist religions), `div18.xml` (目錄部, canon catalogs), `div25.xml` (悉曇部, Siddham studies), and `div09.xml` (古逸部全．疑似部, Dunhuang and dubious-text recoveries). The division covers chronologically from the early Liáng (the *Fān fányǔ* 翻梵語 [KR6s0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0018) and the 510s anthological projects) to the high Qīng (the Yōngzhèng 雍正 imperial Chán anthologies of the 1730s [KR6s0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0068)–[KR6s0071](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0071)).

Generically the division is the most heterogeneous in the canon: a single shelf brings together (1) topical Buddhist *lèi-shū* 類書 (encyclopedias arranged by subject), (2) numerical-categories *fǎshù* 法數 lexicons of doctrine, (3) the great *yīnyì* 音義 phonological-semantic glossaries that are the principal philological apparatus to the canon, (4) Sanskrit-script and Indo-Chinese translation aids (*Xītán* 悉曇 primers, Sanskrit thousand-character classics, bilingual word-lists), (5) the 古逸部 recoveries of Dūnhuáng ritual, popular, and *biànwén* 變文 literature, (6) imperial-author Buddhist literary collections — Sòng Tàizōng, Míng Tàizōng (the Yǒnglè 永樂 emperor), and Qīng Shìzōng (the Yōngzhèng emperor) — that the editors chose not to scatter into the doctrinal divisions of their original genres, (7) the 外教部 corpus of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Daoist apocrypha, Manichaean, and Nestorian-Christian texts that the Táng canon transmitted under the same shelf as Buddhist material, (8) the 目錄部 series of canon catalogs from the Liáng *Chū sānzàng jì jí* 出三藏記集 [KR6s0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0084) to the Míng *Yuèzàng zhījīn* 閱藏知津 [KR6s0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0104), and (9) the parallel record of Japanese pilgrim-importation catalogs (*qǐnglái mùlù* 請來目錄) running from Saichō (805) and Kūkai (806) through the *nittō hakke* 入唐八家. The principal scholarly traditions a reader must keep in view are accordingly four: (a) Buddhist encyclopedism modelled on the secular *lèi-shū* (Bǎochàng → Dào-shì → late-Míng compilers), (b) Sino-Indian philology — *yīnyì*, *Xītán*, *fānyì míngyì* — as a continuous Táng-Sòng project of preserving Sanskrit sound and translation equivalence, (c) the *jīnglù* 經錄 / canon-catalog tradition as the metadata-and-version-control layer of Chinese Buddhism (the *Kāiyuán shìjiào lù* 開元釋教錄 [KR6s0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0093) is the load-bearing center of the entire canonical organization), and (d) East-Asian transmission philology, where the Japanese 請來 catalogs and the Korean *Gāolìguó xīndiāo... biélù* 高麗國新雕大藏校正別錄 [KR6s0133](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0133) together document how the canon moved beyond the Chinese world.

### Important texts and text clusters

- **Topical Buddhist encyclopedias (*lèi-shū*).** *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* 經律異相 [KR6s0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0001) (Bǎochàng, 508–516) is the earliest substantial Chinese Buddhist *lèi-shū* and the direct prototype for *Fǎyuàn zhūlín* 法苑珠林 [KR6s0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0002) (Dào-shì, 668), the great hundred-juan Táng encyclopedia. *Zhūjīng yàojí* 諸經要集 [KR6s0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0003) (Dào-shì, 656–660) is its companion abridgement. *Shìshì yàolǎn* 釋氏要覽 [KR6s0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0005) (Dào-chéng, 1019–1020) is the standard Sòng one-volume reference for monastic life and terminology. *Dàzàng yīlǎn* 大藏一覽 [KR6s0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0006) (Chén Shí, late Wànlì) and *Yuèzàng zhījīn* 閱藏知津 [KR6s0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0104) (Ǒu-yì Zhì-xù 蕅益智旭, 1654) are the two great late-Míng readers' guides to the canon as a whole.
- **Numerical-categories lexicons (*fǎshù*).** *Dà Míng sānzàng fǎshù* 大明三藏法數 [KR6s0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0007) (Yīrú 一如, 1417–1419, by Yǒnglè edict) is the standard topically-arranged numerical lexicon, in 50 juan; *Jiàoshèng fǎshù* 教乘法數 [KR6s0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0008) (Yuán-jìng 圓瀞, c. 1426–1431) and its Qīng re-edition *Chóngdìng jiàoshèng fǎshù* [KR6s0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0009) (Chāo-hǎi 超海, 1734–1735) carry the same genre forward.
- **Phonological-semantic glossaries (*yīnyì*).** *Yīqiè jīng yīnyì* 一切經音義 [KR6s0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0010) (Xuán-yìng 玄應, 645–656) inaugurates the genre; *Xīnyì Dàfāngguǎng fó Huáyán jīng yīnyì* 新譯大方廣佛華嚴經音義 [KR6s0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0011) [KR6s0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0012) (Huì-yuàn 慧苑, c. 700–720) is the dedicated Huáyán companion; the magnum opus is Huì-lín's 慧琳 hundred-juan *Yīqiè jīng yīnyì* [KR6s0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0013) (783–807) — the single most important Táng philological work for the canon — extended by Xī-lín's 希麟 *Xù yīqiè jīng yīnyì* [KR6s0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0014) (980–990, Liáo); the Hòu-Jìn *Xīnjí zàngjīng yīnyì suíhán lù* 新集藏經音義隨函錄 [KR6s0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0015) (Kě-hóng 可洪, 932–940) is its principal alternative organized by canonical case-position. *Shàoxīng chóngdiāo dàzàng yīn* 紹興重雕大藏音 [KR6s0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0016) (Chǔ-guān 處觀, c. 1070s–1090s) and *Běijīng wǔ dà bù zhíyīn huìyùn* 北京五大部直音會韻 [KR6s0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0017) (Jiǔ-yǐn 久隱, 1522–1543) are the Sòng and Míng continuations.
- **Sanskrit script and translation aids.** *Fān fányǔ* 翻梵語 [KR6s0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0018) (anonymous Liáng) is the earliest Sanskrit-glossary in the canon. *Fānyì míngyì jí* 翻譯名義集 [KR6s0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0019) (Fǎ-yún 法雲, 1136–1143) is the standard Sòng dictionary of translated terms. *Xītán zìjì* 悉曇字記 [KR6s0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0020) (Zhì-guǎng 智廣, 780–806) is the foundational Chinese primer of Siddham. The Sanskrit-Chinese bilingual cluster — *Fànyǔ qiānzìwén* 梵語千字文 [KR6s0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0021) [KR6s0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0022) (Yì-jìng 義淨, 695–713), *Táng Fàn wénzì* 唐梵文字 [KR6s0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0023) (Quán-zhēn 全真), *Fànyǔ zámíng* 梵語雜名 [KR6s0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0024) (Lǐ-yán 禮言), *Táng Fàn liǎngyǔ shuāngduì jí* 唐梵兩語雙對集 [KR6s0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0025) (Sēng Dáduō-niè-duō 僧怛多蘖多 with Bōluó-jùnà-míshě-shā 波羅瞿那彌捨沙) — preserves the Táng working-vocabulary of the translation bureaus.
- **The Dūnhuáng cluster (T85 古逸部・疑似部).** [KR6s0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0026) through [KR6s0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0056) are the Dūnhuáng manuscript fragments that the Taishō editors classified as "ancient lost / dubious." They include doctrinal compendia (*Dàshèng jīng zuǎn yàoyì* [KR6s0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0026), *Dàshèng èrshíèr wèn běn* [KR6s0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0027)), liturgical and ritual texts (penitential liturgies [KR6s0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0033) [KR6s0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0046)–[KR6s0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0048), *upoṣadha* and bodhisattva-precept formulae [KR6s0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0043)–[KR6s0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0045), dedication and vow texts [KR6s0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0038)–[KR6s0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0040) [KR6s0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0049)), the *biànwén* 變文 transformation-text *Dà Mùjiānlián míngjiān jiùmǔ biànwén bìng tú* 大目乾連冥間救母變文并圖 [KR6s0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0050), the verse-encomium *Quánzhōu qiānfó xīnzhù zhū zǔshī sòng* 泉州千佛新著諸祖師頌 [KR6s0053](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0053), the Tibetan-period Shāzhōu inscription for Hé-shàng Hóng-biàn 洪辯 [KR6s0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0054) (850–869), and — separate from the Taishō recension but included here — the Wáng Fán-zhì poetry corpus [KR6s0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0055) [KR6s0134](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0134). Together this cluster is the principal canonical witness for the religious life of medieval Dūnhuáng.
- **Imperial-author Buddhist literary collections (御製).** Three layers: (i) Sòng Tàizōng 宋太宗 (Zhào Jiǒng 趙炅, r. 976–997) — six poetry / prose collections [KR6s0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0057) *Yùzhì liánhuá xīnlún huíwén jìsòng*, [KR6s0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0058) *Yùzhì mìzàng quán*, [KR6s0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0059) *Yùzhì xiāoyáo yǒng*, [KR6s0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0060) *Yùzhì yuánshí*, [KR6s0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0061) *Yùzhì fó fù*, [KR6s0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0062) *Yùzhì quányuán gē* — the foundational corpus of explicitly imperial Chinese Buddhist literature; (ii) Míng Tàizōng (Yǒnglè 永樂 emperor, Zhū Dì 朱棣, r. 1402–1424) — *Dà Míng Tàizōng yùzhì xùzàn wén* [KR6s0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0063), the Buddha-name liturgical works *Zhū fó shìzūn rúlái púsà zūnzhě shénsēng míng jīng* [KR6s0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0064) and *Zhū fó míngchēng gēqū* [KR6s0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0065), and the *Wénshū zàn* / *Shìjiā Móuní fó zàn* encomia [KR6s0066](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0066) [KR6s0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0067); (iii) Qīng Shìzōng (Yōngzhèng 雍正 emperor, r. 1722–1735) — the polemical *Yùzhì jiǎnmó biànyì lù* 御製揀魔辨異錄 [KR6s0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0068) against the Hànyuè 漢月 line of Línjì Chán, the *Yùxuǎn yǔlù* 御選語錄 anthology [KR6s0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0069), and the digest editions *Yùlù Zōngjìng dàgāng* [KR6s0070](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0070) and *Yùlù jīnghǎi yī dī* [KR6s0071](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0071) of the *Zōng-jìng-lù* and the canon — the most ambitious imperial intervention in Chán historiography in late imperial China.
- **The 外教部 (non-Buddhist religions in the canon).** *Jīn qīshí lùn* 金七十論 [KR6s0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0072) (Paramārtha 真諦, 557–569) is the Chinese translation of the Sāṃkhya *Suvarṇasaptati* / *Sāṃkhyakārikā* commentary, the principal Chinese-Buddhist source on Sāṃkhya. *Shèngzōng shí jùyì lùn* 勝宗十句義論 [KR6s0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0073) (Huì-yuè 慧月, tr. Xuán-zàng 玄奘, 645–664) is the parallel Vaiśeṣika treatise. *Lǎozǐ huàhú jīng* 老子化胡經 [KR6s0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0074) is the Dūnhuáng witness to the Daoist "conversion of the barbarians" polemic — the central textual irritant of the Buddho-Daoist controversy ([KR6r0149](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6r/KR6r0149)). *Zhuāngzǐ nèipiān zhù* 莊子內篇註 [KR6s0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0075) (Hānshān Dé-qīng 憨山德清, c. 1593–1623) is the late-Míng Chán commentary on Zhuāng-zǐ, included as a Buddhist work despite its subject. *Gāoshàng Yùhuáng běnxíng jí jīng suǐ* [KR6s0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0076) and *Wúshàng Yùhuáng xīnyìn jīng* [KR6s0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0077) are Daoist Jade-Emperor texts preserved in the *Fāngshān shíjīng* 房山石經 (here in the *Fāng-shān* recension, F29). The Manichaean cluster — *Móníjiào xiàbù zàn* 摩尼教下部讚 [KR6s0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0078), *Móní guāngfó jiàofǎ yí luè* 摩尼光佛教法儀略 [KR6s0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0079) (Fú-duō-dàn 拂多誕, presented to the Táng court 731), *Bōsījiào cánjīng* 波斯教殘經 [KR6s0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0080) — and the Nestorian-Christian (景教 *jǐngjiào*) cluster — *Xùtīng Míshīsuǒ jīng* 序聽迷詩所經 [KR6s0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0081) (the *Sūtra of Jesus the Messiah*), *Jǐngjiào sānwēi méngdù zàn* 景教三威蒙度讚 [KR6s0082](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0082) (the *Gloria*), and *Dà-Qín jǐngjiào liúxíng zhōngguó bēisòng* 大秦景教流行中國碑頌 [KR6s0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0083) (Jǐng-jìng 景淨, 781, the Xī'ān Nestorian stele) — together constitute the canon's principal record of medieval Chinese encounters with West-Asian religions.
- **Canon catalogs (目錄), Chinese sequence.** *Chū sānzàng jì jí* 出三藏記集 [KR6s0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0084) (Sēngyòu 僧祐, 510–518) is the earliest extant Chinese Buddhist *jīnglù* and the foundation of all later catalogs. The Suí-Táng sequence runs through the three *Zhòngjīng mùlù* 眾經目錄 [KR6s0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0085) (Fǎ-jīng 法經, 594), [KR6s0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0086) (Yàn-cōng 彥琮, 602), [KR6s0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0087) (Jìng-tài 靜泰, 663–666), Dào-xuān's *Dà-Táng nèidiǎn lù* 大唐內典錄 [KR6s0088](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0088) and *Xù...* [KR6s0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0089) (664–667), Jìng-mài's *Gǔjīn yìjīng tú jì* 古今譯經圖紀 [KR6s0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0090) and Zhì-shēng's *Xù...* [KR6s0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0091) (730), and Míng-quán's Wǔ-Zhōu-court *Dà-Zhōu kāndìng zhòngjīng mùlù* 大周刊定眾經目錄 [KR6s0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0092) (695). The 730 *Kāiyuán shìjiào lù* 開元釋教錄 [KR6s0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0093) (Zhì-shēng 智昇), with its abridgement *Lüèchū* [KR6s0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0094) and the working-document *Dà-Táng Kāiyuán shìjiào guǎngpǐn lìzhāng* [KR6s0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0095) (Xuán-yì 玄逸), is the load-bearing standard catalog for the Chinese canon thereafter. The *Zhēnyuán* 貞元 era continuations — Yuán-zhào's 圓照 *Dà-Táng Zhēnyuán xù Kāiyuán shìjiào lù* [KR6s0096](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0096) (794) and *Zhēnyuán xīndìng shìjiào mùlù* [KR6s0097](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0097) (800), and Héng-ān's *Xù Zhēnyuán shìjiào lù* [KR6s0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0098) (945, Southern Táng) — close the Táng sequence. The Sòng catalog series — *Tiānshèng shìjiào zǒnglù* [KR6s0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0099) (Wéi-jìng 惟淨, 1023–1031), *Dà-zhōng-xiángfú fǎbǎo lù* [KR6s0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0100) (Yáng Yì 楊億, 1011–1013), *Jǐng-yòu xīnxiū fǎbǎo lù* [KR6s0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0101) (Lǚ Yí-jiǎn 呂夷簡, 1034–1037) — documents the Northern-Sòng official translation bureau. *Dàzàng shèngjiào fǎbǎo biāomù* [KR6s0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0102) (Wáng Gǔ 王古, Yuán) and *Dà Míng chóngkān sānzàng shèngjiào mùlù* [KR6s0103](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0103) (Wànlì Jìng-shān recension) carry the genre into the Yuán-Míng. The genre culminates in *Yuèzàng zhījīn* 閱藏知津 [KR6s0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0104) (Ǒu-yì Zhì-xù, 1654), the late-Míng readers'-guide to the canon.
- **Japanese pilgrim-importation catalogs (*qǐnglái mùlù*).** The 805 catalogs of Saichō 最澄 — *Chuánjiào dàshī jiānglái Tāizhōu lù* [KR6s0105](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0105) and *... Yuèzhōu lù* [KR6s0106](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0106) — and the 806 *Yù qǐnglái mùlù* [KR6s0107](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0107) of Kūkai 空海 inaugurate a continuous Heian-era genre. The *nittō hakke* 入唐八家 ("eight Heian pilgrims to Táng") sequence runs through the Jōgyō 常曉 catalog [KR6s0109](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0109) (839), Engyō 圓行 [KR6s0110](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0110) (839), Ennin 圓仁 [KR6s0111](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0111)–[KR6s0113](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0113) (839–847), Eun 惠運 [KR6s0114](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0114) [KR6s0115](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0115) (847), Enchin 圓珍 [KR6s0116](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0116)–[KR6s0120](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0120) (858), Shūei 宗叡 [KR6s0121](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0121) [KR6s0122](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0122) (865), and the *Lùwài jīng děng mùlù* [KR6s0123](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0123) miscellany; the seventh of the eight, the foundational *Gēnběn dàhéshàng zhēnjì cèzǐ děng mùlù* [KR6s0108](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0108), records Kūkai-school manuscript apparatus. Annen's 安然 *Zhū āshélí zhēnyán mìjiào bùlèi zǒnglù* 諸阿闍梨真言密教部類總錄 [KR6s0124](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0124) (885–902) consolidates the esoteric portion. Together this corpus is the principal documentary source for what 9th-century Chinese Buddhism actually moved out of the empire.
- **Japanese sectarian (六宗) sub-catalogs.** Yuán-chāo's (Enchō 圓超) *Huāyán zōng zhāngshū bìng yīnmíng lù* [KR6s0125](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0125), Xuán-rì's (Gennichi 玄日) *Tiāntāi zōng zhāngshū* [KR6s0126](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0126), Ān-yuǎn's (An'on 安遠) *Sānlùn zōng zhāngshū* [KR6s0127](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0127), Píng-zuò's (Heiso 平祚) *Fǎxiàng zōng zhāngshū* [KR6s0128](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0128) (all c. 950–1100), Zōshun 藏俊's *Zhùjìn Fǎxiàng zōng zhāngshū* [KR6s0129](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0129) (12th c.), and Yǒng-wěn's (Eion 榮穩) *Lǜ zōng zhāngshū* [KR6s0130](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0130) are the school-by-school sub-catalogs of the commentarial literature held in Heian-era Japanese monastic libraries. Eichō 永超's *Dōngyù chuándēng mùlù* 東域傳燈目錄 [KR6s0131](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0131) (1094) is the consolidated successor.
- **Korean canon catalogs.** Ŭich'ŏn 義天's *Xīnbiān zhūzōng jiàozàng zǒnglù* 新編諸宗教藏總錄 [KR6s0132](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0132) (1090) is the canonical record of the Goryeo *Sok-jang* 續藏 supplementary canon project and the most important pre-modern East-Asian catalog of commentarial literature. Sugi 守其's *Gāolìguó xīndiāo dàzàng jiàozhèng biélù* 高麗國新雕大藏校正別錄 [KR6s0133](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0133) (1236–1248) is the critical-collation apparatus to the Goryeo *Tripiṭaka* (the *Koryŏ Taejanggyŏng* 高麗大藏經 second carving), and the foundation document of all modern critical editions of the Chinese canon (the Taishō uses the Goryeo as base text).

### Topics

- **Buddhist encyclopedism and the *lèi-shū* tradition.** The 6th-century *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* [KR6s0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0001) → 7th-century *Fǎyuàn zhūlín* [KR6s0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0002) → 11th-century *Shìshì yàolǎn* [KR6s0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0005) → 17th-century *Dàzàng yīlǎn* [KR6s0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0006) / *Yuèzàng zhījīn* [KR6s0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0104) sequence is a deliberate Buddhist appropriation of the secular *lèi-shū* form (Liú Xiàng, *Yìwén lèijù*, *Tàipíng yùlǎn*) for the management of canonical material; the canon, on this account, is something to be navigated by topic and synopsis as much as read straight through.
- **The *yīnyì* (sound-and-sense) tradition as canonical philology.** Xuán-yìng → Huì-lín → Xī-lín → Kě-hóng → Chǔ-guān → Jiǔ-yǐn ([KR6s0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0010)–[KR6s0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0017)) constitutes the most sustained pre-modern East Asian project of philological-lexicographical apparatus to a single textual corpus, and the principal source for the historical phonology of Middle Chinese as much as for canonical reading.
- **The *Xītán* / *fānyì míngyì* project.** The Sino-Indian translation aids ([KR6s0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0018)–[KR6s0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0025)) and *Fānyì míngyì jí* [KR6s0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0019) together attempt to keep the Sanskrit substrate of the canon visible in the Chinese reception — both as a script (Siddham as a memorized inventory of dharanis and seed-syllables) and as a translation-equivalence dictionary. Through Kūkai and the Heian Mikkyō transmission this project becomes load-bearing for Japanese esoteric Buddhism.
- **The 經錄 / canon catalog as version control.** From Sēngyòu (510s) through Zhì-shēng's 730 *Kāiyuán* standardization to Sugi's 1230s *Goryeo* collation and Zhì-xù's 1654 reader's guide, the catalog tradition is the metadata layer that makes the Chinese canon a canon at all — fixing what counts, what is dubious, what is lost, and what is duplicated. The *Kāiyuán shìjiào lù* [KR6s0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0093) is the load-bearing standard down to the Taishō.
- **East Asian transmission and the Japanese 請來 record.** The catalogs of Saichō, Kūkai, Ennin, Eun, Enchin, Shūei, and Annen ([KR6s0105](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0105)–[KR6s0124](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0124)) are the principal documentary record of which texts moved out of Táng China into Heian Japan, and at what pace. Together with the Korean *Sok-jang* catalog of Ŭich'ŏn [KR6s0132](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0132) and the Goryeo-canon collation of Sugi [KR6s0133](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0133), they constitute the East-Asian extension of the Chinese canon-catalog tradition.
- **Imperial patronage and imperial authorship of Buddhist texts.** Three discrete moments — Sòng Tàizōng's 980s–990s self-presentation as a Buddhist sovereign-author ([KR6s0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0057)–[KR6s0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0062)), the Yǒnglè-emperor's early-Míng commissioning programme ([KR6s0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0063)–[KR6s0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0067) plus [KR6s0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0007)), and the Yōngzhèng-emperor's 1730s polemical-anthological intervention into Chán historiography ([KR6s0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0068)–[KR6s0071](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0071)) — define the principal late-imperial axis of state engagement with the canon.
- **The "外教" question: religions of the West preserved in a Buddhist shelf.** The Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Daoist apocryphal, Manichaean, and Nestorian-Christian texts ([KR6s0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0072)–[KR6s0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0083)) — preserved in Táng-period canonical company because the editors classed them with translated Indo-Iranian doctrinal literature — make this division the canon's principal record of medieval Chinese encounter with non-Buddhist religious systems beyond Daoism and Confucianism. The Nestorian stele [KR6s0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0083) (781) and the Manichaean court-presentation [KR6s0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0079) (731) are the centrepiece documents.
- **Dūnhuáng popular Buddhism in the canon.** The T85 *gǔyì* / *yísì* cluster ([KR6s0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0026)–[KR6s0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0056)) opens the canon to a class of materials — penitential and *upoṣadha* liturgies, vow and merit-dedication formulae, *biànwén* transformation-texts, vernacular poetry, local hagiographies — that the doctrinal divisions systematically excluded. The cluster is the principal canonical witness for the religious life of medieval Dūnhuáng outside the elite monastic establishments.
- **Wáng Fán-zhì and vernacular Buddhist poetry.** The two recensions of the Wáng Fán-zhì poetry corpus [KR6s0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0055) [KR6s0134](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0134) are the canon's principal record of popular vernacular Buddhist verse, recovered almost entirely from Dūnhuáng witnesses and substantially recovered into modern editions only in the 20th century.

## Division note (scope only): [KR6u 疑似部 *Yísì bù* — Buddhist Canon — Apocrypha (Doubtful and Spurious Scriptures)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6u 疑似部 (*Yísì bù*) is the Kanripo division of **Chinese Buddhist apocrypha** — sūtras, śāstras, and ritual texts composed in China but presenting themselves as Indic translations or as canonical Buddha-discourses. In Taishō terms the division reproduces *Taishō shinshū daizōkyō* vol. 85 nos. 2865–2920 (T85N2865–T85N2920); the matching CANWWW classification (`div09`) is the unified Taishō section 古逸部全．疑似部 ("Ancient-Lost Section [complete] and Apocrypha Section"), of which KR6u inherits the *Yísì* (apocrypha) half. The fifty-seven texts now on disk are almost without exception Chinese-composed forgeries (偽 *wěi*) or doubtful works (疑 *yí*) preserved because copies entered the **Dūnhuáng** 敦煌 library cave and were exhumed in the early twentieth century — Pelliot chinois, Stein, Beijing, IDP, and Nakamura collection manuscripts — having never entered the regular *Dàzàngjīng* 大藏經. The chronological span runs from the early **Northern Dynasties** (5th–6th century — the *Yuèguāng* / Dharma-King messianic stratum: [KR6u0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0009), [KR6u0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0010), [KR6u0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0015)) through the **late Tang and Five Dynasties** (the *Quànshàn* / *Xīn púsà* "warning sūtra" cluster of c. 793–900: [KR6u0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0052), [KR6u0053](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0053), [KR6u0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0054), [KR6u0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0057)). The corpus is the single most important body of evidence for the popular, sectarian, and indigenously-recast Buddhism of medieval China.

The scholarly tradition for this division is largely a modern creation. Although the cataloguers — Fǎjīng 法經 (《眾經目錄》, 594), Yàncóng 彥琮, Zhīshēng 智昇 (《開元釋教錄》, 730) and their successors — registered most of these scriptures as *yí* or *wěi* and excluded them from the official canon, the texts themselves continued to circulate at the level of monastic ritual, Fángshān 房山 stone scripture, lay devotion, and miracle-tale collection. Modern study of the corpus begins with Makita Tairyō 牧田諦亮's *Gikyō kenkyū* 疑經研究 (Kyōto: Jinbun Kagaku Kenkyūsho, 1976) — the foundational monograph cited in nearly every per-text note — and continues through Robert E. Buswell, Jr.'s 1990 edited volume *Chinese Buddhist Apocrypha* (Honolulu: University of Hawaiʻi Press), Kyoko Tokuno's *Apocryphal Texts in Chinese Buddhism* (2003) and her 1994 critical study of [KR6u0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0006), Christine Mollier's *Buddhism and Taoism Face to Face* (2008), and Cao Ling 曹凌's *Zhōngguó fójiào yíwěijīng zōnglù* 中國佛教疑偽經綜錄 (Shànghǎi gǔjí, 2011), the standard contemporary bibliographical compendium in Chinese. A reader of KR6u must keep four overlapping frameworks in mind simultaneously: the Suí–Tang **bibliographic-rejection tradition** that classified these texts; the medieval **Dūnhuáng manuscript culture** that preserved them; the **East Asian transmission** that disseminated some of them (e.g. [KR6u0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0033), the *Tiāndì bāyáng shénzhòu jīng*, which survives in Chinese, Tibetan, Uyghur, Khotanese, and Mongol versions); and the **Taishō editorial decision** of the 1920s to gather every recovered non-canonical Dūnhuáng text under T85, which gives the division its peculiar mix of straightforward apocrypha alongside paracanonical items such as Yìjìng's authentic *Wúcháng sānqǐ jīng* [KR6u0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6u/KR6u0048).

## Division note: [KR6i 經集部 *Jīngjí bù* — Buddhist Canon — Sūtra Collection (Mahāyāna Sūtrasaṃgraha)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6i mirrors the Taishō Tripiṭaka's 經集部 (*Jīngjí bù*, "Sūtrasaṃgraha"), the catch-all division in which the Taishō editors gathered the Mahāyāna sūtras that did not belong to one of the canon's named text-cycles. The principal axis is Taishō nos. 425–847 across Vols. 14–17, corresponding to CANWWW `div11.xml`; the Kanripo arrangement supplements this with Xuzangjing (卍續) commentaries, a handful of Jiāxīng-zàng titles, and — at the tail end (KR6i0589–0596) — a small block of Yogācāra 論釋 that drifted into the *jīng* collection through their attachment to single-sūtra commentary. Texts in the other "named" divisions are explicitly excluded: Prajñāpāramitā (KR6a), Ratnakūṭa (KR6b), Mahāsannipāta (KR6c), Avataṃsaka (KR6d), Nirvāṇa (KR6e), Lotus (KR6f), Bhadrakalpika (KR6g) and the Āgamas (KR6h) are catalogued elsewhere.

Because *Jīngjí bù* is structurally residual, its scholarly profile is not generic. The "leftover" works concentrate, in fact, several of the most consequential sūtras in the entire Chinese Mahāyāna corpus — *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras*, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa*, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* corpus, the Maitreya cycle, and the major Sinitic apocrypha *Yuánjué jīng* 圓覺經, *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經, *Yúlánpén jīng* 盂蘭盆經, and the *Shíwáng jīng* 十王經. The transmissional pattern is therefore stratigraphic: an Eastern Hàn–Western Jin layer of single-fascicle sūtras translated by Ān Shìgāo, Zhī Qiān, and above all Dharmarakṣa; a Yáo Qín / Northern Liáng turning-point in which Kumārajīva, Buddhabhadra, and Dharmakṣema fix the literary canon; a sixth- and seventh-century Yogācāra wave (Bodhiruci, Paramārtha, Saṅghapāla, Divākara, Xuánzàng); a Tang aftermath that adds re-translations and the great commentarial schools (Zhìyǐ, Jízàng, Kuījī, Zōngmì); and a Sòng coda of Indian translations from Shīhù 施護, Fǎtiān 法天, and Fǎxián 法賢. The chronological depth is matched by a high commentarial density — the *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty exegetical works in this division.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The *Vimalakīrti* cluster.** *Wéimójié suǒshuō jīng* 維摩詰所說經 [KR6i0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0076) (Kumārajīva, 406) is the canonical Chinese *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the most influential single text in the division — it shaped Chinese Buddhist literary style and supplied the central image of the bodhisattva-householder. Zhī Qiān's earlier *Fóshuō wéimójié jīng* 佛說維摩詰經 [KR6i0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0075) (Wú, c. 223–253) and Xuánzàng's *Shuō wúgòuchēng jīng* 說無垢稱經 [KR6i0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0077) preserve the parallel recensions. The exegetical apparatus runs from Sui–Tang masters — Huìyuǎn 慧遠 [KR6i0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0079), Zhìyǐ 智顗 [KR6i0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0080)–[KR6i0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0081), Jízàng 吉藏 [KR6i0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0083)–[KR6i0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0084), Kuījī 窺基 [KR6i0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0085) — through Song Tiāntái revival and Ming–Qing commentary, ending with the Qīng *Wéimó jīng wúwǒ shū* [KR6i0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0095) tradition.

**The Maitreya cluster.** A tight block of six canonical sūtras (KR6i0030–0036) covers the lower-birth (*xiàshēng*) and upper-birth (*shàngshēng*) traditions, including *Fóshuō mílè lái shí jīng* 佛說彌勒來時經 [KR6i0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0036), the briefest and most archaic of the canonical Maitreya texts. Tang commentarial elaboration comes via Jízàng [KR6i0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0037), Kuījī [KR6i0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0038), the Korean exegete Wǒnhyo 元曉 [KR6i0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0039), and Gyeongheung 憬興 [KR6i0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0040) — a rare witness to Silla Buddhist scholarship inside the Chinese canon.

**The *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Medicine Buddha) cluster.** *Yàoshī liúlí guāng rúlái běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* 藥師琉璃光如來本願功德經 [KR6i0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0048) (Xuánzàng, 650) is the canonical East Asian standard, with the seven-Buddha expanded recension *Yàoshī liúlí guāng qī fó běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* [KR6i0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0049) (Yìjìng, 707) and a Tang ritual-manual lineage. Tang Dunhuang exegesis survives in two anonymous *Yàoshī jīng shū* [KR6i0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0054)–[KR6i0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0055) preserved in Taishō Vol. 85, and Ming–Qing devotional commentary revives the cluster with Língyào 靈耀's *Yàoshī jīng zhíjiě* [KR6i0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0056) and the Ming repentance-liturgy tradition (KR6i0057–0058).

**The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) cluster.** Dharmakṣema's *Jīnguāngmíng jīng* 金光明經 [KR6i0301](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0301) (Northern Liáng, c. 414–426) is the earliest complete Chinese witness; Yìjìng's *Jīnguāngmíng zuìshèng wáng jīng* 金光明最勝王經 [KR6i0303](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0303) (Táng, 703) renders the full Sanskrit recension and supplies the canonical "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter foundational to East Asian state-protective Buddhism. The commentarial chain includes Zhìyǐ–Guàndǐng 灌頂 [KR6i0304](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0304), Zhīlǐ 知禮 [KR6i0305](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0305), Jízàng [KR6i0308](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0308), and a Tang Esoteric layer.

**The *tathāgatagarbha* / Laṅkāvatāra cluster.** The doctrinal core of East Asian Buddha-nature thought sits inside KR6i: Buddhabhadra's *Dàfāngděng rúláizàng jīng* 大方等如來藏經 [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323) (c. 420), Bodhiruci's *Fóshuō bù zēng bù jiǎn jīng* 佛說不增不減經 [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325) (c. 525), the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* — Guṇabhadra's four-fascicle *Léngqié ābáduōluó bǎo jīng* 楞伽阿跋多羅寶經 [KR6i0327](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0327) (443), Bodhiruci's ten-fascicle *Rù léngqié jīng* 入楞伽經 [KR6i0328](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0328) (513), and Śikṣānanda's seven-fascicle *Dàshèng rù léngqié jīng* 大乘入楞伽經 [KR6i0329](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0329) (700–704) — and Divākara's *Dàshèng mìyán jīng* 大乘密嚴經 [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) (676–688). The Laṅkāvatāra triad is foundational both for East Asian Yogācāra and for early Chán self-identification as the "Laṅkāvatāra School" (楞伽宗).

**The samādhi cluster.** Three central Indian samādhi-sūtras stand together: Kumārajīva's *Shǒulèngyán sānmèi jīng* 佛說首楞嚴三昧經 [KR6i0279](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0279) (c. 402–409 — to be distinguished sharply from the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945), his *Sīyì fàntiān suǒwèn jīng* 思益梵天所問經 [KR6i0218](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0218) (c. 402–405), and Narendrayaśas's *Yuèdēng sānmèi jīng* 月燈三昧經 [KR6i0276](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0276) (Northern Qí, 557–559), the canonical Chinese witness to the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*.

**The Ullambana / filial-piety cluster.** *Fóshuō yúlán-pén jīng* 佛說盂蘭盆經 [KR6i0364](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0364) (attrib. Dharmarakṣa, but widely considered a Western Jin Chinese apocryphon) and its short twin *Fóshuō bào'ēn fèng-pén jīng* 佛說報恩奉盆經 [KR6i0376](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0376) together founded the East Asian *zhōngyuán* / Ghost Festival. Zōngmì's *Yúlán-pén jīng shū* [KR6i0365](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0365) and the ten or so subsequent Song–Qīng sub-commentaries make the cluster one of the densest commentarial bodies in the division. The related *Fùmǔ ēn nán bào jīng* 佛說父母恩難報經 [KR6i0363](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0363) (and the apocryphal *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng* tradition) carry the same filial-piety theme into popular Buddhism.

**The *Yuánjué jīng* (Perfect Enlightenment) cluster.** *Dàfāngguǎng yuánjué xiūduōluó liǎoyì jīng* 大方廣圓覺修多羅了義經 [KR6i0551](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0551) — attributed to Buddhatrāta but securely identified as a Tang Chinese apocryphon (c. 690–750) — together with Zōngmì's massive *Yuánjué jīng dàshū* [KR6i0555](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0555) and the long Sòng–Míng commentarial chain (KR6i0553–0574) constitute the textual base of the Huáyán–Chán synthesis Zōngmì engineered.

**The Sinitic apocrypha and divinatory / underworld cluster.** Alongside *Yuánjué jīng*, the division contains the *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經 [KR6i0545](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0545) (Sui-period Sinitic apocryphon, foundational to the Kṣitigarbha cult and the unique wooden-block divination liturgy), Zàngchuān 藏川's *Shíwáng jīng* 佛說地藏菩薩發心因緣十王經 [KR6i0583](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0583) and *Yùxiū shíwáng shēngqī jīng* [KR6i0584](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0584) (Late Tang, foundational to East Asian ten-kings underworld iconography), and the late *Huàzhū bǎomìng zhēn jīng* [KR6i0586](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0586) (Míng *zhēn-jīng*-genre fusion of Buddhist form, Daoist neidan imagery, and popular medicine).

**The Mañjuśrī cluster.** Dharmarakṣa's *Wénshū shīlì xiàn bǎozàng jīng* 佛說文殊師利現寶藏經 [KR6i0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0062) (c. 270–308), Saṅghapāla's *Wénshū shīlì wèn jīng* 文殊師利問經 [KR6i0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0069) (Liáng, 515–520 — a principal canonical source for the eighteen Indian sectarian schools), and a series of Tang–Sòng Mañjuśrī texts down to Fǎxián's late-Sòng *Fóshuō miàojíxiáng púsà suǒwèn dàshèng fǎluó jīng* 佛說妙吉祥菩薩所問大乘法螺經 [KR6i0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0074) (989–1000) trace the gradual standardization of Mañjuśrī's Chinese epithets — from older phonetic *Wénshūshīlì* to the standardized Sòng rendering *Miàojíxiáng*.

**The Yogācāra tail (KR6i0589–0596).** Bandhuprabha *et al.*'s *Fódì jīng lùn* 佛地經論 [KR6i0589](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0589) (Xuánzàng, 649), three Vasubandhu-style *upadeśa* commentaries translated by Bodhiruci [KR6i0590](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0590)–[KR6i0592](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0592) and Vimokṣaprajñā [KR6i0593](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0593), and a Dunhuang-derived *Dàshèng sìfǎ jīng* exegetical trio [KR6i0594](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0594)–[KR6i0596](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0596) sit at the catalog's end. They are structurally 釋經論 (commentaries on single sūtras), and in Taishō proper occupy Vol. 26; their inclusion here reflects the Kanripo principle of grouping sūtra commentaries with the parent sūtra division.

### Important persons

- [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) (Dharmarakṣa, c. 239–316) — the single most prolific translator in this division (43 catalogued titles): *Xiánjié jīng*, the early Mañjuśrī texts, the Maitreya core, and a substantial Western-Jin Mahāyāna sūtra corpus.
- [支謙](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%94%AF%E8%AC%99) (Zhī Qiān, fl. c. 222–253) — early Wu-period sūtra translator; 27 titles here, including the first Chinese *Vimalakīrti*.
- [安世高](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%89%E4%B8%96%E9%AB%98) (Ān Shìgāo, fl. 148–168) — Eastern Hàn pioneer; 26 short *jīng* of meditation and ethics surviving in this division.
- [鳩摩羅什](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%B3%A9%E6%91%A9%E7%BE%85%E4%BB%80) (Kumārajīva, 344–413) — fixed the canonical Chinese versions of *Vimalakīrti*, *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Viśeṣacintābrahma-paripṛcchā*, and a clutch of other doctrinally central sūtras.
- [曇無讖](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%87%E7%84%A1%E8%AE%96) (Dharmakṣema, 385–433) — Northern Liáng translator of the earliest complete *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
- [佛陀跋陀羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BD%9B%E9%99%80%E8%B7%8B%E9%99%80%E7%BE%85) (Buddhabhadra, 359–429) — translator of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, opening the textual base of East Asian Buddha-nature doctrine.
- [求那跋陀羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B1%82%E9%82%A3%E8%B7%8B%E9%99%80%E7%BE%85) (Guṇabhadra, 394–468) — translator of the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra*, the lineage text of early Chán.
- [菩提流支](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8F%A9%E6%8F%90%E6%B5%81%E6%94%AF) (Bodhiruci, fl. 508–537) — Northern Wei Yogācāra translator; ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva*, several Vasubandhu *upadeśa*.
- [僧伽婆羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%83%A7%E4%BC%BD%E5%A9%86%E7%BE%85) (Saṅghapāla, 460–524) — Liáng translator of the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*.
- [那連提耶舍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%82%A3%E9%80%A3%E6%8F%90%E8%80%B6%E8%88%8D) (Narendrayaśas, 517–589) — translator of the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*.
- [闍那崛多](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%97%8D%E9%82%A3%E5%B4%9B%E5%A4%9A) (Jñānagupta, 523–600) — Sui-period sūtra retranslator.
- [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98) (Xuánzàng, 602–664) — canonical *Bhaiṣajyaguru*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, and several authoritative re-translations.

### Topics

- **The residual category as doctrinal repository.** Because the Taishō editors used *Jīngjí bù* as the bin for sūtras lacking a named cycle, the division accumulated isolates of unusual doctrinal density — single-text founders of major traditions (*Vimalakīrti*, *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, *Yuánjué jīng*) sit beside short ritual texts. Reading the division requires constant attention to which texts are doctrinal pivots and which are devotional or apotropaic miniatures.
- **Tathāgatagarbha and the Laṅkāvatāra problem.** The three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* (KR6i0327–0329), the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323), the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa* [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325), and the *Ghanavyūha* [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) together form the textual base from which East Asian Buddha-nature theory was synthesized — including the question of whether *ālayavijñāna* and *tathāgatagarbha* are identical, the doctrine that became canonical for Huáyán and Chán.
- **Samādhi literature.** The trio of *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, and *Viśeṣacintā* offers a coherent Indian sūtra theory of the bodhisattva's contemplative attainments; this is distinct from — and historically prior to — the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945 with which the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi* is often confused.
- **Sinitic apocrypha and lay Buddhism.** *Yuánjué jīng*, *Zhànchá jīng*, *Yúlánpén jīng*, *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng*, and the *Shíwáng jīng* corpus are the clearest cases in the Mahāyāna canon of texts produced in China and re-presented as Indian sūtras. They are also the texts with the broadest social reach: filial piety, calendrical festival, divination, and post-mortem judgement.
- **State-protective Buddhism.** The two Chinese *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* recensions, particularly Yìjìng's "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter, supplied the dharmic ideology of East Asian Buddhist statecraft from Sui through Nara and beyond.
- **Filial piety as Buddhist genre.** The Ullambana cluster, the Tang *fùmǔ ēn* texts, the *Shíwáng jīng*, and the *Dìzàng púsà běnyuàn jīng* tradition (its earliest witnesses sit in this division) together constitute Buddhism's most successful response to Confucian objections about filial debt.
- **Translation history through multi-recension witnesses.** Several core texts survive in two or three Chinese versions spanning four to seven centuries — *Vimalakīrti* (Zhī Qiān, Kumārajīva, Xuánzàng), *Laṅkāvatāra* (Guṇabhadra, Bodhiruci, Śikṣānanda), *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Xuánzàng + Yìjìng + earlier witnesses), *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Dharmakṣema + Yìjìng + Bǎoguì compendium). This makes KR6i an unusually rich laboratory for translation-history research.
- **The Chinese exegetical density.** The *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty Chinese commentaries spanning Sui to Qīng, and the *Yuánjué jīng* almost as many. The exegetical superstructure here is comparable in scale to that built around the *Lotus*, even though no individual non-Lotus sūtra reaches the *Lotus*'s extreme commentarial density.

## Division note (scope only): [KR6p 淨土宗著述部 *Jìngtǔ zōng zhùshù bù* — Buddhist Canon — Compositions of the Pure Land School](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6p collects the Chinese-language compositions of the Pure Land school (*jìngtǔ zōng* 淨土宗) — the body of doctrinal treatises, sūtra-commentaries, liturgical *zàn* / *chàn* / *yí* texts, devotional anthologies, biographies, and devotional poetry that grew up around the three principal Pure Land sūtras: the *Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha* (*Wúliángshòu jīng* 無量壽經), the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha* (*Āmítuó jīng* 阿彌陀經), and the apocryphal *Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guān wúliángshòu jīng* 觀無量壽經). The 140 works gathered here are drawn from three regions of the Sino-Japanese canon: (i) the Taishō *Zhū-zōng bù* 諸宗部 (vol. 47, nos. 1957–1984) — the principal classical Pure Land treatises from Tánluán through Sòng-period Tiantai; (ii) the supplementary *Xùzàngjīng* 卍續藏 (vols. 1, 2, 22, 61, 62, 74) — the great bulk of Sòng–Qīng commentaries, ritual handbooks, and lay-Buddhist anthologies that the early-twentieth-century Japanese editors recovered from Chinese monastic libraries; and (iii) the Taishō *Gǔyì bù* 古逸部 (vol. 85, nos. 2826–2830), preserving Dunhuang-recovered Pure Land liturgies. The corresponding Taishō structural division — `div31.xml` 諸宗部 — is the formal canonical container, but the Kanripo arrangement extracts the Pure Land subset and supplements it heavily from the *Xùzàngjīng*.

Chronologically the division spans c. 530 CE (Tánluán 曇鸞's foundational tracts) through the very end of the Qīng (c. 1900). The internal centre of gravity is unusually late: roughly two-thirds of the entries date from the Míng-Qīng period, reflecting the fact that Pure Land devotion became the dominant lay-monastic practice of late imperial China and produced an immense vernacular literature absent from earlier canonical strata. Three transmissional issues run through the division: the inflation of the *Wúliángshòu* sūtra-corpus through apocryphal "translations" preserved only in the *Xùzàngjīng* (KR6p0031–0035); the Tiantai monopoly on the *Guān-jīng* commentarial tradition via the 觀經疏妙宗鈔 chain initiated by Zhīlǐ 知禮; and the steady migration of Pure Land authorship from the cloister to the lay literati class, culminating in the Péng Shàoshēng circle of the eighteenth century and Wèi Yuán's *Huìyì* recension of 1854.

## Division note: [KR6j 密教部 *Mìjiào bù* — Buddhist Canon — Esoteric (Tantric) Texts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6j 密教部 (*Mìjiào bù*, Jp. *Mikkyō-bu*) is the Esoteric (Tantric) section of the Buddhist canon as organised by the Taishō *Shinshū Daizōkyō* 大正新脩大藏經 — Taishō volumes 18–21 in their canonical sequence, plus an extensive Japanese commentarial corpus drawn from later Taishō volumes (notably T39, T58, T59, T60, T61, T75, T77, T78, T79). It corresponds to division *div17* 密教部 in the CANWWW digital catalogue, which is the principal scholarly mapping of the Taishō to which Kanripo here adheres. The 762 entries gathered in KR6j make it one of the largest sub-divisions of the entire Kanripo Buddhist canon, comparable in scale only to the dhāraṇī- and ritual-heavy sections such as the 經集部 and the late-Sòng translation corpus.

The texts in KR6j fall into three temporally and doctrinally distinct strata. (1) **Pre-Esoteric dhāraṇī sūtras** translated in the Eastern Hàn through Suí period (c. 25 CE – 600 CE), often single-fascicle scriptures centred on a specific *dhāraṇī* (mantra-formula) and a single deity (Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Bhaiṣajyaguru, etc.); these are the proto-Tantric substrate. (2) The **High-Tang Esoteric synthesis** (c. 716–774 CE) carried out at Cháng'ān and Luòyáng by the so-called "Three Tang Esoteric Patriarchs" — Śubhakarasiṃha 善無畏 ([善無畏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E7%84%A1%E7%95%8F), 637–735), Vajrabodhi 金剛智 ([金剛智](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%87%91%E5%89%9B%E6%99%BA), 671–741), and Amoghavajra 不空 ([不空](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%8D%E7%A9%BA), 705–774) — which gave East Asian Esoteric Buddhism its doctrinal core (the *Dàrì jīng* / *Vajraśekhara* / *Susiddhikara* triad) and its institutional shape under the *Kāiyuán* / *Tiānbǎo* / *Dàlì* reign-eras. (3) The **Sòng "new translation" bureau** (c. 982 – c. 1110), in which Dānapāla 施護 ([施護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%96%BD%E8%AD%B7)), Devaśāntika / Tiānxīzāi 天息災 ([天息災](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A4%A9%E6%81%AF%E7%81%BD)), Dharmadeva / Fǎtiān 法天 ([法天](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9)), and Fǎxián 法賢 ([法賢](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E8%B3%A2)) — operating from the Yìjīngyuàn 譯經院 founded in 982 — rendered a large body of Indian *yoga-* and *anuttarayoga*-tantra material into Chinese, though by then the East Asian institutional tradition of Esoteric practice was in decline. To these three strata Kanripo adds a fourth, paratextual layer: Japanese Heian–Kamakura sub-commentary in the *kāití* 開題, *shìjì* 私記 (Jp. *shiki*), and *kǒuchuán* 口傳 (Jp. *kuden*) genres — Kūkai's 開題 corpus and the medieval Shingon scholastic glosses on Yīxíng's *Dàrìjīng shū*.

The principal commentarial pivot of the division is Yīxíng's 一行 ([一行](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%80%E8%A1%8C)) twenty-fascicle *Dàrìjīng shū* 大日經疏 ([KR6j0662](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0662), T39n1796), composed at Luòyáng 724–727 under Śubhakarasiṃha's oral direction and the doctrinal foundation of every subsequent East Asian Esoteric exegesis. Kūkai 空海 ([空海](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%A9%BA%E6%B5%B7)) brought this commentary to Japan in 806 and built the entire Shingon 真言 scholastic edifice on it — a transmission whose secondary literature occupies a substantial portion of the latter half of KR6j (the *Miàoyìn chāo* 妙印鈔 cluster KR6j0663–0671 and adjacent items). For the Tendai 天台 *Taimitsu* 台密 transmission of the same body of material — through Saichō 最澄, Ennin 圓仁 ([圓仁](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%93%E4%BB%81)), Enchin 圓珍 ([圓珍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%93%E7%8F%8D)), and Annen 安然 ([安然](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%89%E7%84%B6)) — the principal exegetical apparatus is dispersed elsewhere in KR6 and in the Japanese non-canonical literature; only a small number of *Taimitsu*-authored items (the *kāití* and *zhǐguī* 指歸 of Enchin) sit inside KR6j proper.

### Important texts and text clusters

The division is anchored by the two foundational sūtras of East Asian Esoteric Buddhism, the *Dàrì jīng* and the *Jīngāngdǐng jīng*, which together define the two-mandala (*liǎngjiè* 兩界 / Jp. *ryōkai*) system of doctrine and practice:

- *Dà Pílúzhēnà chéngfó shénbiàn jiāchí jīng* 大毘盧遮那成佛神變加持經 (*Mahāvairocana-sūtra*; *Dàrì jīng* 大日經) — [KR6j0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0001) (T18n0848). Translated 724–725 by [善無畏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E7%84%A1%E7%95%8F) and [一行](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%80%E8%A1%8C). The basis of the **Garbhadhātu** (*Tāizàngjiè* 胎藏界) lineage; locus classicus for the doctrines of the Three Mysteries (三密), *dharmakāya*-preached scripture (法身說法), and the *bodhi-mind / great-compassion / expedient-means* triad.
- *Jīngāngdǐng yīqiè rúlái zhēnshí shè dàshèng xiànzhèng dàjiàowáng jīng* 金剛頂一切如來真實攝大乘現證大教王經 (*Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*; *Jīngāngdǐng jīng* 金剛頂經) — [KR6j0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0024) (T18n0865), Amoghavajra's three-fascicle rendering c. 753. The basis of the **Vajradhātu** (*Jīngāngjiè* 金剛界) lineage. The companion six-fascicle "short version" by Vajrabodhi is *Jīngāngdǐng yújiā zhōng lüèchū niànsòng jīng* 金剛頂瑜伽中略出念誦經 ([KR6j0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0030), T18n0866); the full thirty-fascicle Sòng rendering of the same *Tattvasaṃgraha* by Dānapāla is [KR6j0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0041); Amoghavajra's important meta-text *Eighteen Assemblies* (*Shíbāhuì zhǐguī* 金剛頂經瑜伽十八會指歸) — the only Chinese-language overview of the *Vajraśekhara* tantra-corpus as a literary system — is [KR6j0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0035) (T18n0869).
- *Sūxīdì jiéluó jīng* 蘇悉地羯羅經 (*Susiddhikara-sūtra*) — [KR6j0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0061) (T18n0893), translated 724–735 by [善無畏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E7%84%A1%E7%95%8F). The third pillar of the Tang Esoteric canon, principally a ritual-procedural scripture; the *Tendai* 台密 tradition gave it canonical status equal to the *Dàrì* and *Jīngāngdǐng*, generating a distinct three-sūtra (*sānbù* 三部) doctrinal framework as opposed to the Shingon two-mandala system. Its companion ritual manuals are [KR6j0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0063) and *Sūxīdì jiéluó gōngyǎng fǎ* 蘇悉地羯羅供養法 ([KR6j0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0064)).
- *Sūpóhū tóngzǐ qǐngwèn jīng* 蘇婆呼童子請問經 (*Subāhu-paripṛcchā*) — [KR6j0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0065) / [KR6j0066](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0066) (T18n0895a/b), again Śubhakarasiṃha. The principal *kriyā*-tantra ritual scripture; its concern with the *sādhana* failure-modes (*siddhi-vighna*) and ritual purification became the textual basis for the Esoteric handling of obstacles.

The principal exegetical apparatus of the *Dàrì jīng* is concentrated in a tight commentarial cluster:

- *Dà Pílúzhēnà chéngfó jīng shū* 大毘盧遮那成佛經疏 (*Dàrìjīng shū*) — [KR6j0662](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0662) (T39n1796) by [一行](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%80%E8%A1%8C), 724–727. Twenty fascicles recording Śubhakarasiṃha's oral exegesis; the most consequential single commentary in the Esoteric tradition.
- *Dà Pílúzhēnà jīng gōngyǎng cìdì fǎ shū* 大毘盧遮那經供養次第法疏 — [KR6j0670](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0670), Yīxíng's ritual companion.
- *Dàrì jīng yìshì* 大日經義釋 — [KR6j0734](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0734), the redacted recension of Yīxíng's commentary that became canonical in Tendai *Taimitsu*.
- *Dàrì jīng yìshì yǎnmì chāo* 大日經義釋演密鈔 — [KR6j0735](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0735), the principal Liáo gloss.
- The medieval Japanese Shingon sub-commentary cluster on Yīxíng's *shū*: [KR6j0663](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0663) *Miàoyìn chāo* 妙印鈔, [KR6j0664](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0664) *Miàoyìn chāo kǒuzhuàn* 妙印鈔口傳, [KR6j0665](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0665) / [KR6j0669](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0669) *Zhùxīn-pǐn shū sījì* 住心品疏私記, [KR6j0666](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0666) *Yǎn'ào chāo* 演奧鈔, [KR6j0667](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0667) *Zhǐxīn chāo* 指心鈔, [KR6j0668](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0668) *Dàrìjīng shū chāo* 大日經疏鈔, [KR6j0671](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0671) *Gōngyǎng cìdì fǎ shū sījì* 供養次第法疏私記.

Kūkai's own writings in KR6j are confined to four *kāití* 開題 (Jp. *kaidai*, "title-expositions"): [KR6j0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0002) *Dàrìjīng kāití* 大日經開題, [KR6j0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0025) *Jīngāngdǐngjīng kāití* 金剛頂經開題, [KR6j0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0026) *Jiàowángjīng kāití* 教王經開題, and [KR6j0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0119) *Dà-fódǐng jīng kāití* 大佛頂經開題. His doctrinal *Sandai-bu* — the *Jūjūshinron* 十住心論, *Hizō-hōyaku* 秘藏寶鑰, *Kenmitsu-nikyō-ron* 顯密二教論, *Sokushin-jōbutsu-gi* 即身成佛義 — sits in Taishō vol. 77 (諸宗部) and is **not** in KR6j.

The third major textual block of KR6j is the **dhāraṇī-sūtra and ritual-manual corpus**, organised in deity-clusters:

- The **Uṣṇīṣa / 大佛頂 / 尊勝** cluster: [KR6j0144](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0144) *Fódǐng zūnshèng tuóluóní jīng* 佛頂尊勝陀羅尼經 (*Uṣṇīṣavijaya*) and the satellite items [KR6j0148](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0148)–[KR6j0157](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0157); the *Yīzìdǐnglún* 一字頂輪 cluster (*Ekākṣaroṣṇīṣacakra*) at [KR6j0124](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0124) and [KR6j0129](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0129)–[KR6j0135](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0135).
- The **Avalokiteśvara dhāraṇī corpus** — the *Dàbēi zhòu* 大悲咒 / *Qiānshǒu jīng* 千手經 cluster [KR6j0258](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0258)–[KR6j0274](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0274) (anchor scripture [KR6j0260](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0260), Bhagavaddharma's 650s translation); the *Eleven-Faced* (*Ekādaśamukha*) cluster [KR6j0275](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0275)–[KR6j0277](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0277); the *Bùkōng juànsuǒ* 不空羂索 (*Amoghapāśa*) cluster [KR6j0300](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0300)–[KR6j0306](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0306).
- The **Mañjuśrī ritual corpus** [KR6j0395](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0395)–[KR6j0424](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0424), the densest single deity-cluster in the division.
- The **Bhaiṣajyaguru** (*Yàoshī*) ritual corpus [KR6j0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0093)–[KR6j0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0100).
- The Esoteric **Pure-Land overlap** (Amitābha / *Wúliángshòu* mantric scriptures): [KR6j0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0102), [KR6j0108](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0108), [KR6j0109](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0109), [KR6j0451](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0451), [KR6j0621](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0621).

A fourth, doctrinally pivotal text-cluster is the **Lǐqù** 理趣 (*Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā*) **corpus**: Amoghavajra's exegetical *Lǐqù shì* 理趣釋 — *Dàlè jīngāng bùkōng zhēnshí sānmèiyé jīng bōrě bōluómìduō lǐqù shì* ([KR6j0193](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0193), T1003), the locus classicus of the famous "passion as enlightenment" hermeneutic; with its sub-commentaries [KR6j0194](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0194) and *Lǐqù shì bìyào chāo* 理趣釋祕要鈔 ([KR6j0195](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0195), 1356, by [杲寶](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%B2%E5%AF%B6)), and the structural variant [KR6j0196](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0196). (The base scripture itself, *Bōrě bōluómìduō lǐqù jīng* 般若波羅蜜多理趣經 = T243, is canonically classified by Taishō under 般若部 and sits in [KR6c](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6c/), not here.)

### Important persons

- [善無畏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E7%84%A1%E7%95%8F) (Śubhakarasiṃha, 637–735) — Indian master, arrived Cháng'ān 716; translated the *Dàrìjīng* and *Susiddhikara* and inaugurated the Tang Esoteric transmission. **First** of the Three Tang Patriarchs; 23 texts in KR6j.
- [金剛智](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%87%91%E5%89%9B%E6%99%BA) (Vajrabodhi, 671–741) — South Indian master, arrived Cháng'ān c. 720; translated the "short *Vajraśekhara*" ([KR6j0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0030)) and the *Yúqí jīng* ([KR6j0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0031)). **Second** Tang Patriarch; 25 texts in KR6j.
- [不空](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%8D%E7%A9%BA) (Amoghavajra, 705–774) — Sogdian-born disciple of Vajrabodhi; the single most prolific translator-author in the division (165 texts, c. 22% of the entire corpus). **Third** Tang Patriarch; honoured by three emperors (Xuánzōng, Sùzōng, Dàizōng) and the dominant institutional figure of mid-Tang Buddhism. Author of the canonical *Jīngāngdǐngjīng* ([KR6j0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0024)), the *Eighteen Assemblies* ([KR6j0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0035)), the *Lǐqù shì* ([KR6j0193](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0193)), and the bulk of the Tang ritual-manual corpus.
- [一行](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%80%E8%A1%8C) (Yīxíng, 683–727) — Chinese disciple of Śubhakarasiṃha; calendrical astronomer and the principal Chinese exegete of the Tang Esoteric transmission. Author of the *Dàrìjīng shū* ([KR6j0662](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0662)) — the doctrinal foundation of every subsequent East Asian Esoteric commentary.
- [施護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%96%BD%E8%AD%B7) (Dānapāla, fl. 982 – c. 1018) — Uḍḍiyāna master; co-founding translator at the Sòng Yìjīngyuàn 譯經院 from 982. The largest Sòng-era contributor: 48 texts, including the full thirty-fascicle Sòng rendering of the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha* ([KR6j0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0041)).
- [法賢](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E8%B3%A2) (Fǎxián / Dharmadeva, fl. 982 – c. 1001) — second of the Sòng Yìjīngyuàn translators (43 texts); responsible for a substantial body of late-Indian dhāraṇī material.
- [法天](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9) (Fǎtiān / Dharmadeva-bis, fl. 973 – c. 1001) — Magadhan master; translated Indian *anuttarayoga* tantra-fragments into Chinese (23 texts).
- [天息災](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A4%A9%E6%81%AF%E7%81%BD) (Tiānxīzāi / Devaśāntika, fl. 980 – c. 1000) — head of the Yìjīngyuàn at its founding; 6 texts.
- [慈賢](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%85%88%E8%B3%A2) (Cíxián, fl. 11th c.) — Liáo-period Khitan master; 9 texts. Principal locus of post-Tang continental Esoteric transmission outside the Sòng bureau.
- [空海](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%A9%BA%E6%B5%B7) (Kūkai, 774–835) — Japanese student of Huìguǒ 惠果 at Qīnglóngsì 青龍寺 (804–806); founder of the Japanese Shingon 真言 school; brought the entire Tang Esoteric corpus to Japan in 806. Author of [KR6j0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0002), [KR6j0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0025), [KR6j0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0026), [KR6j0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0119) (the four *kāití*) within this division; his doctrinal *Sandai-bu* is preserved outside KR6j.
- [圓仁](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%93%E4%BB%81) (Ennin, 794–864) — Japanese Tendai monk, founder of Tendai-side *Taimitsu* 台密 transmission; in China 838–847. Contributor to the *kāití* / *zhǐguī* literature.
- [圓珍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%93%E7%8F%8D) (Enchin, 814–891) — Japanese Tendai monk, in China 853–858; deepened the *Taimitsu* synthesis. Author of *Dà-Pílúzhēnà jīng zhǐguī* 大毘盧遮那經指歸 ([KR6j0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0003)).
- [安然](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%89%E7%84%B6) (Annen, c. 841 – c. 915) — *Taimitsu* doctrinal systematiser; principal author of the Heian Tendai esoteric synthesis (largely outside KR6j proper).
- [杲寶](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%B2%E5%AF%B6) (Gōhō, 1306–1362) — Kamakura-Nanbokuchō Shingon scholastic at Tō-ji 東寺; principal author of the *Lǐqù-shì bìyào chāo* and other late-medieval Shingon sub-commentaries.
- [宥範](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%A5%E7%AF%84) (Yūhan, 1270–1352) — contemporary of Gōhō; Shingon scholastic, contributed the *Yǎn'ào chāo* 演奧鈔 ([KR6j0666](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0666)) and adjacent gloss-texts.
- [菩提流志](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8F%A9%E6%8F%90%E6%B5%81%E5%BF%97) (Bodhiruci, d. 727) — Indian translator at Cháng'ān under Wǔ Zétiān and Xuánzōng; 15 dhāraṇī-sūtra translations in KR6j, bridging the pre-Tang dhāraṇī corpus and the High-Tang Esoteric synthesis.
- [義淨](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%BE%A9%E6%B7%A8) (Yìjìng, 635–713), [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98) (Xuánzàng, 602–664), [實叉難陀](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AF%A6%E5%8F%89%E9%9B%A3%E9%99%80) (Śikṣānanda, 652–710), [菩提流支](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8F%A9%E6%8F%90%E6%B5%81%E6%94%AF) (Bodhiruci-the-earlier, fl. 508–537) — major Tang-and-earlier translators whose dhāraṇī-related output is collected in KR6j alongside their main Mahāyāna corpora (collected elsewhere in KR6).

### Topics

The principal interpretive and doctrinal issues running through KR6j are:

- **The two-mandala system** (*liǎngjiè* 兩界 / Jp. *ryōkai*): the doctrinal organisation of the Esoteric canon around the polar pair *Garbhadhātu* 胎藏界 (the *Dàrìjīng*'s mandala of compassion-as-cause) and *Vajradhātu* 金剛界 (the *Jīngāngdǐngjīng*'s mandala of wisdom-as-fruit). The Shingon school treats them as a non-dual pair; the Tendai *Taimitsu* tradition adds the *Susiddhikara* as a third co-equal element (*sānbù* 三部).
- **Dharmakāya-preached scripture** (法身說法): the doctrinal claim — first articulated systematically in Yīxíng's *Dàrìjīng shū* and developed in Kūkai's *kāití* — that the speaker of the Esoteric sūtras is not the historical Śākyamuni in *nirmāṇakāya* but the cosmic *dharmakāya* Mahāvairocana itself. The basis of the entire tradition's claim to supersede the exoteric Mahāyāna.
- **The Three Mysteries** (三密 *sānmì*): the practical-soteriological doctrine of body-, speech-, and mind-correspondence between the practitioner and the Buddha, mediated by *mudrā*, *mantra*, and *samādhi*. Locus classicus the *Dàrìjīng*'s first chapter.
- **The Eighteen Assemblies** (十八會) of the *Vajraśekhara*-corpus: Amoghavajra's *Shíbāhuì zhǐguī* ([KR6j0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0035)) is the only Chinese-language schematic of the *Vajraśekhara* tantra-cycle as a literary system, identifying the Chinese-translated *Tattvasaṃgraha* as the first of an eighteen-text tantra-cycle of which the bulk circulated in India / Tibet but not in Chinese.
- ***Abhiṣeka* and lineage transmission**: the consecration ritual that confers Esoteric authority. The institutional spine of the tradition from Vajrabodhi's transmission of *abhiṣeka* to Amoghavajra, through Huìguǒ to Kūkai, and through the Saichō / Ennin / Enchin lineage in Tendai *Taimitsu*.
- **Mantra and dhāraṇī efficacy**: the broad doctrinal question — present already in the pre-Tang dhāraṇī sūtras and refined in the *Lǐqù shì* — of how mantric sound, considered as the resonance of the *dharmakāya*, accomplishes soteriological work. The basis of the entire ritual-manual corpus.
- **"Passion as enlightenment"** (the *Lǐqù shì* hermeneutic): Amoghavajra's claim in [KR6j0193](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0193) that the human passions, when read at the Esoteric semantic level, are themselves enlightenment; the doctrinal hinge between the exoteric *Prajñāpāramitā* literature and the developed Esoteric tradition. The most controversial single text in the division.
- **Garbhadhātu mandala iconography and the *taizōkai* 胎藏界 visual programme**: the ritual layout of the Garbhadhātu mandala, codified in the *Dàrìjīng*'s middle chapters, became the basis for the entire East Asian Esoteric iconographic tradition — paintings, sculptural programmes, ritual diagrams, and the *abhiṣeka* hall layouts of Tō-ji and Mt. Kōya.
- **Tang-to-Japan transmission**: the institutional history of the transmission from Huìguǒ's *abhiṣeka* of Kūkai (805) and Saichō (804) onward — the single most consequential transfer of a Buddhist textual-ritual tradition between two East Asian polities, and the reason for the heavy Japanese commentarial layer in KR6j.
- **Sòng "new translations" and the decline of Chinese institutional Esotericism**: the Sòng Yìjīngyuàn (982–1082) rendered substantial new tantra-material into Chinese (the Dānapāla / Fǎxián / Fǎtiān corpus, 100+ texts in KR6j), but by then the Tang Esoteric institutional infrastructure had collapsed and these texts had no significant ritual reception in China itself. They became principally a Japanese scholastic resource.
- **The Heian–Kamakura *kāití* / *shìjì* genre**: the Japanese Shingon and Tendai scholastic apparatus on the Esoteric scriptures, codified in the *kāití* (title-exegesis), *shìjì* (sub-commentarial note), and *kǒuchuán* (oral-transmission record) genres. KR6j's largest paratextual layer.

### Timeline

- c. 25–600 — Pre-Esoteric dhāraṇī sūtras (Eastern Hàn through Suí). Approximately 90 texts in KR6j; representative items include *Qiānshǒu qiānyǎn dàbēi xīn tuóluóní jīng* 千手千眼陀羅尼經 ([KR6j0260](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6j/KR6j0260), Bhagavaddharma, 650–661) at the late end of the bracket, and the Hàn–Suí 文殊 / 觀音 dhāraṇī corpus at the early end.
