### Topics

- **The residual category as doctrinal repository.** Because the Taishō editors used *Jīngjí bù* as the bin for sūtras lacking a named cycle, the division accumulated isolates of unusual doctrinal density — single-text founders of major traditions (*Vimalakīrti*, *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, *Yuánjué jīng*) sit beside short ritual texts. Reading the division requires constant attention to which texts are doctrinal pivots and which are devotional or apotropaic miniatures.
- **Tathāgatagarbha and the Laṅkāvatāra problem.** The three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* (KR6i0327–0329), the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323), the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa* [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325), and the *Ghanavyūha* [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) together form the textual base from which East Asian Buddha-nature theory was synthesized — including the question of whether *ālayavijñāna* and *tathāgatagarbha* are identical, the doctrine that became canonical for Huáyán and Chán.
- **Samādhi literature.** The trio of *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, and *Viśeṣacintā* offers a coherent Indian sūtra theory of the bodhisattva's contemplative attainments; this is distinct from — and historically prior to — the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945 with which the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi* is often confused.
- **Sinitic apocrypha and lay Buddhism.** *Yuánjué jīng*, *Zhànchá jīng*, *Yúlánpén jīng*, *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng*, and the *Shíwáng jīng* corpus are the clearest cases in the Mahāyāna canon of texts produced in China and re-presented as Indian sūtras. They are also the texts with the broadest social reach: filial piety, calendrical festival, divination, and post-mortem judgement.
- **State-protective Buddhism.** The two Chinese *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* recensions, particularly Yìjìng's "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter, supplied the dharmic ideology of East Asian Buddhist statecraft from Sui through Nara and beyond.
- **Filial piety as Buddhist genre.** The Ullambana cluster, the Tang *fùmǔ ēn* texts, the *Shíwáng jīng*, and the *Dìzàng púsà běnyuàn jīng* tradition (its earliest witnesses sit in this division) together constitute Buddhism's most successful response to Confucian objections about filial debt.
- **Translation history through multi-recension witnesses.** Several core texts survive in two or three Chinese versions spanning four to seven centuries — *Vimalakīrti* (Zhī Qiān, Kumārajīva, Xuánzàng), *Laṅkāvatāra* (Guṇabhadra, Bodhiruci, Śikṣānanda), *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Xuánzàng + Yìjìng + earlier witnesses), *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Dharmakṣema + Yìjìng + Bǎoguì compendium). This makes KR6i an unusually rich laboratory for translation-history research.
- **The Chinese exegetical density.** The *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty Chinese commentaries spanning Sui to Qīng, and the *Yuánjué jīng* almost as many. The exegetical superstructure here is comparable in scale to that built around the *Lotus*, even though no individual non-Lotus sūtra reaches the *Lotus*'s extreme commentarial density.

## Division note (scope only): [KR6f 寶積部 *Bǎojī bù* — Buddhist Canon — Ratnakūṭa Section](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

`KR6f` is the Kanripo mirror of the Taishō *Bǎojī bù* 寶積部 — the canonical Buddhist division that gathers the *Mahā-ratnakūṭa* "Heap of Jewels" compendium together with the parallel and independent Chinese translations of the sūtras absorbed into it, plus the Sukhāvatī / Pure-Land sūtra corpus that the Taishō editors classed in the same volume-pair, plus the entire East-Asian commentarial superstructure that grew out of both. In CANWWW the division is `div03` (`div03.xml`, `寶積部`); it runs from `T11N0310` Bodhiruci's 120-fascicle compendium through `T12N0373` and is followed in the Taishō architecture by the *Nièpán bù* 涅槃部 (div19, T374–T396, which is grouped in Kanripo as `KR6g`). `KR6f` extends the Taishō *Bǎojī bù* by absorbing the related *śāstra* and *upadeśa* corpus from Taishō volumes 26 (T1523–T1525) and 40 (T1819), the entire *jīngshūbù* commentarial cluster on the Sukhāvatī and Śrīmālā sūtras from Taishō volume 37 (T1744–T1762), the Japanese Pure-Land sub-commentaries from volume 57 (T2208), the Dūnhuáng fragments from volume 85 (T2759–T2763), and a small *Xùzàngjīng* 卍續藏經 tail (X264, X351–X353) — 104 works in total.

The chronological span runs from the late-second-century translations of Lokakṣema 支婁迦讖 ([KR6f0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0004) *Akṣobhyatathāgatasya-vyūha* of c. 178–189, [KR6f0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0042) *Kāśyapa-parivarta* of c. 178–189) and An Shigao 安世高 ([KR6f0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0040), [KR6f0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0048), c. 148–170) through to the mid-seventeenth-century Ming Pure-Land synthesis of Zhìxù 智旭 ([KR6f0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0093) *Ēmítuójīng yàojiě* of c. 1620–1655), with a thin late tail of Kamakura-period Japanese sub-commentaries on the *Guānjīngshū* extending the run to the early fourteenth century. The textual core of the division is Indic and the principal transmissional traditions a reader must keep in mind are four: (i) the Hàn–Wú southern lineage of Lokakṣema, Zhī Qiān 支謙 and Saṅghavarman 康僧鎧 that produced the earliest Chinese renderings of the *Akṣobhya-vyūha*, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* and the *Larger Sukhāvatī*; (ii) the Western-Jìn Cháng'ān lineage of Dharmarakṣa 竺法護, by some margin the most productive single translator in the division (twelve attributed works, from [KR6f0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0006) and [KR6f0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0009) through [KR6f0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6f/KR6f0041)); (iii) the Yáo-Qín / Liú-Sòng lineage of Kumārajīva 鳩摩羅什, Guṇabhadra 求那跋陀羅 and Kālayaśas 畺良耶舍, which gave the canonical Chinese forms of the *Smaller Sukhāvatī*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the *Visualisation-of-Amitāyus*; and (iv) the Northern-Sòng *Yìjīngyuàn* 譯經院 of Shīhù 施護, Fǎhù 法護 (the Northern-Sòng Dharmapāla, distinct from the Western-Jìn Dharmarakṣa), Fǎxián 法賢 and Rìchēng 日稱, which produced a long final stratum of retranslations of *Ratnakūṭa* assemblies (T310 assemblies 6, 35, 36, 39, 47 all retranslated 980–1058). Around this Indic core grew the East-Asian commentarial layers: the Suí *Dìlùn*-school readings of Jìngyǐng Huìyuǎn 淨影慧遠 and the early Sānlùn readings of Jízàng 吉藏; the foundational Tiāntái Pure-Land works of Zhìyǐ 智顗; the great Táng Pure-Land patriarchal corpus of Shàndǎo 善導, Huìjìng 慧淨, Kuījī 窺基 and Cí'ēn 慈恩; the Sillan tradition of Wǒnhyo 元曉 and Jǐngxīng 璟興; the Northern-Sòng Tiāntái synthesis of Zhīlǐ 知禮 and Yuánzhào 元照; and a Kamakura Japanese sub-commentarial tradition centred on Shàndǎo's *Four-Fascicle Commentary* (源信, 良忠, 顯意, 證忍). The division is thus the principal canonical arena for the constitution of East-Asian Pure-Land Buddhism as a doctrinal and ritual tradition, while simultaneously housing the *tathāgatagarbha*-class *Śrīmālā* literature and the most ambitious editorial-translational project of the Táng — Bodhiruci II's 120-fascicle assembly of the *Mahā-ratnakūṭa*.

## Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君 divisions

This volume holds 12 texts. In the Ask Bunkankun catalog, which follows CBETA's subject classes rather than Taishō/Zokuzōkyō volumes, they belong to:

- [KR6i 經集部 *Jīngjí bù* — Buddhist Canon — Sūtra Collection (Mahāyāna Sūtrasaṃgraha)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/): 9 texts (75%)
- [KR6b 本緣部 *Běnyuán bù* — Buddhist Canon — Past-Life Narratives (Jātaka, Avadāna, Buddha-Biography, Parable, Dharmapada)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/): 3 texts (25%)

## Division note: [KR6i 經集部 *Jīngjí bù* — Buddhist Canon — Sūtra Collection (Mahāyāna Sūtrasaṃgraha)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6i mirrors the Taishō Tripiṭaka's 經集部 (*Jīngjí bù*, "Sūtrasaṃgraha"), the catch-all division in which the Taishō editors gathered the Mahāyāna sūtras that did not belong to one of the canon's named text-cycles. The principal axis is Taishō nos. 425–847 across Vols. 14–17, corresponding to CANWWW `div11.xml`; the Kanripo arrangement supplements this with Xuzangjing (卍續) commentaries, a handful of Jiāxīng-zàng titles, and — at the tail end (KR6i0589–0596) — a small block of Yogācāra 論釋 that drifted into the *jīng* collection through their attachment to single-sūtra commentary. Texts in the other "named" divisions are explicitly excluded: Prajñāpāramitā (KR6a), Ratnakūṭa (KR6b), Mahāsannipāta (KR6c), Avataṃsaka (KR6d), Nirvāṇa (KR6e), Lotus (KR6f), Bhadrakalpika (KR6g) and the Āgamas (KR6h) are catalogued elsewhere.

Because *Jīngjí bù* is structurally residual, its scholarly profile is not generic. The "leftover" works concentrate, in fact, several of the most consequential sūtras in the entire Chinese Mahāyāna corpus — *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras*, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa*, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* corpus, the Maitreya cycle, and the major Sinitic apocrypha *Yuánjué jīng* 圓覺經, *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經, *Yúlánpén jīng* 盂蘭盆經, and the *Shíwáng jīng* 十王經. The transmissional pattern is therefore stratigraphic: an Eastern Hàn–Western Jin layer of single-fascicle sūtras translated by Ān Shìgāo, Zhī Qiān, and above all Dharmarakṣa; a Yáo Qín / Northern Liáng turning-point in which Kumārajīva, Buddhabhadra, and Dharmakṣema fix the literary canon; a sixth- and seventh-century Yogācāra wave (Bodhiruci, Paramārtha, Saṅghapāla, Divākara, Xuánzàng); a Tang aftermath that adds re-translations and the great commentarial schools (Zhìyǐ, Jízàng, Kuījī, Zōngmì); and a Sòng coda of Indian translations from Shīhù 施護, Fǎtiān 法天, and Fǎxián 法賢. The chronological depth is matched by a high commentarial density — the *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty exegetical works in this division.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The *Vimalakīrti* cluster.** *Wéimójié suǒshuō jīng* 維摩詰所說經 [KR6i0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0076) (Kumārajīva, 406) is the canonical Chinese *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the most influential single text in the division — it shaped Chinese Buddhist literary style and supplied the central image of the bodhisattva-householder. Zhī Qiān's earlier *Fóshuō wéimójié jīng* 佛說維摩詰經 [KR6i0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0075) (Wú, c. 223–253) and Xuánzàng's *Shuō wúgòuchēng jīng* 說無垢稱經 [KR6i0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0077) preserve the parallel recensions. The exegetical apparatus runs from Sui–Tang masters — Huìyuǎn 慧遠 [KR6i0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0079), Zhìyǐ 智顗 [KR6i0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0080)–[KR6i0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0081), Jízàng 吉藏 [KR6i0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0083)–[KR6i0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0084), Kuījī 窺基 [KR6i0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0085) — through Song Tiāntái revival and Ming–Qing commentary, ending with the Qīng *Wéimó jīng wúwǒ shū* [KR6i0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0095) tradition.

**The Maitreya cluster.** A tight block of six canonical sūtras (KR6i0030–0036) covers the lower-birth (*xiàshēng*) and upper-birth (*shàngshēng*) traditions, including *Fóshuō mílè lái shí jīng* 佛說彌勒來時經 [KR6i0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0036), the briefest and most archaic of the canonical Maitreya texts. Tang commentarial elaboration comes via Jízàng [KR6i0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0037), Kuījī [KR6i0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0038), the Korean exegete Wǒnhyo 元曉 [KR6i0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0039), and Gyeongheung 憬興 [KR6i0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0040) — a rare witness to Silla Buddhist scholarship inside the Chinese canon.

**The *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Medicine Buddha) cluster.** *Yàoshī liúlí guāng rúlái běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* 藥師琉璃光如來本願功德經 [KR6i0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0048) (Xuánzàng, 650) is the canonical East Asian standard, with the seven-Buddha expanded recension *Yàoshī liúlí guāng qī fó běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* [KR6i0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0049) (Yìjìng, 707) and a Tang ritual-manual lineage. Tang Dunhuang exegesis survives in two anonymous *Yàoshī jīng shū* [KR6i0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0054)–[KR6i0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0055) preserved in Taishō Vol. 85, and Ming–Qing devotional commentary revives the cluster with Língyào 靈耀's *Yàoshī jīng zhíjiě* [KR6i0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0056) and the Ming repentance-liturgy tradition (KR6i0057–0058).

**The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) cluster.** Dharmakṣema's *Jīnguāngmíng jīng* 金光明經 [KR6i0301](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0301) (Northern Liáng, c. 414–426) is the earliest complete Chinese witness; Yìjìng's *Jīnguāngmíng zuìshèng wáng jīng* 金光明最勝王經 [KR6i0303](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0303) (Táng, 703) renders the full Sanskrit recension and supplies the canonical "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter foundational to East Asian state-protective Buddhism. The commentarial chain includes Zhìyǐ–Guàndǐng 灌頂 [KR6i0304](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0304), Zhīlǐ 知禮 [KR6i0305](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0305), Jízàng [KR6i0308](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0308), and a Tang Esoteric layer.

**The *tathāgatagarbha* / Laṅkāvatāra cluster.** The doctrinal core of East Asian Buddha-nature thought sits inside KR6i: Buddhabhadra's *Dàfāngděng rúláizàng jīng* 大方等如來藏經 [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323) (c. 420), Bodhiruci's *Fóshuō bù zēng bù jiǎn jīng* 佛說不增不減經 [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325) (c. 525), the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* — Guṇabhadra's four-fascicle *Léngqié ābáduōluó bǎo jīng* 楞伽阿跋多羅寶經 [KR6i0327](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0327) (443), Bodhiruci's ten-fascicle *Rù léngqié jīng* 入楞伽經 [KR6i0328](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0328) (513), and Śikṣānanda's seven-fascicle *Dàshèng rù léngqié jīng* 大乘入楞伽經 [KR6i0329](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0329) (700–704) — and Divākara's *Dàshèng mìyán jīng* 大乘密嚴經 [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) (676–688). The Laṅkāvatāra triad is foundational both for East Asian Yogācāra and for early Chán self-identification as the "Laṅkāvatāra School" (楞伽宗).

**The samādhi cluster.** Three central Indian samādhi-sūtras stand together: Kumārajīva's *Shǒulèngyán sānmèi jīng* 佛說首楞嚴三昧經 [KR6i0279](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0279) (c. 402–409 — to be distinguished sharply from the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945), his *Sīyì fàntiān suǒwèn jīng* 思益梵天所問經 [KR6i0218](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0218) (c. 402–405), and Narendrayaśas's *Yuèdēng sānmèi jīng* 月燈三昧經 [KR6i0276](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0276) (Northern Qí, 557–559), the canonical Chinese witness to the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*.

**The Ullambana / filial-piety cluster.** *Fóshuō yúlán-pén jīng* 佛說盂蘭盆經 [KR6i0364](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0364) (attrib. Dharmarakṣa, but widely considered a Western Jin Chinese apocryphon) and its short twin *Fóshuō bào'ēn fèng-pén jīng* 佛說報恩奉盆經 [KR6i0376](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0376) together founded the East Asian *zhōngyuán* / Ghost Festival. Zōngmì's *Yúlán-pén jīng shū* [KR6i0365](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0365) and the ten or so subsequent Song–Qīng sub-commentaries make the cluster one of the densest commentarial bodies in the division. The related *Fùmǔ ēn nán bào jīng* 佛說父母恩難報經 [KR6i0363](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0363) (and the apocryphal *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng* tradition) carry the same filial-piety theme into popular Buddhism.

**The *Yuánjué jīng* (Perfect Enlightenment) cluster.** *Dàfāngguǎng yuánjué xiūduōluó liǎoyì jīng* 大方廣圓覺修多羅了義經 [KR6i0551](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0551) — attributed to Buddhatrāta but securely identified as a Tang Chinese apocryphon (c. 690–750) — together with Zōngmì's massive *Yuánjué jīng dàshū* [KR6i0555](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0555) and the long Sòng–Míng commentarial chain (KR6i0553–0574) constitute the textual base of the Huáyán–Chán synthesis Zōngmì engineered.

**The Sinitic apocrypha and divinatory / underworld cluster.** Alongside *Yuánjué jīng*, the division contains the *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經 [KR6i0545](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0545) (Sui-period Sinitic apocryphon, foundational to the Kṣitigarbha cult and the unique wooden-block divination liturgy), Zàngchuān 藏川's *Shíwáng jīng* 佛說地藏菩薩發心因緣十王經 [KR6i0583](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0583) and *Yùxiū shíwáng shēngqī jīng* [KR6i0584](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0584) (Late Tang, foundational to East Asian ten-kings underworld iconography), and the late *Huàzhū bǎomìng zhēn jīng* [KR6i0586](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0586) (Míng *zhēn-jīng*-genre fusion of Buddhist form, Daoist neidan imagery, and popular medicine).

**The Mañjuśrī cluster.** Dharmarakṣa's *Wénshū shīlì xiàn bǎozàng jīng* 佛說文殊師利現寶藏經 [KR6i0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0062) (c. 270–308), Saṅghapāla's *Wénshū shīlì wèn jīng* 文殊師利問經 [KR6i0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0069) (Liáng, 515–520 — a principal canonical source for the eighteen Indian sectarian schools), and a series of Tang–Sòng Mañjuśrī texts down to Fǎxián's late-Sòng *Fóshuō miàojíxiáng púsà suǒwèn dàshèng fǎluó jīng* 佛說妙吉祥菩薩所問大乘法螺經 [KR6i0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0074) (989–1000) trace the gradual standardization of Mañjuśrī's Chinese epithets — from older phonetic *Wénshūshīlì* to the standardized Sòng rendering *Miàojíxiáng*.

**The Yogācāra tail (KR6i0589–0596).** Bandhuprabha *et al.*'s *Fódì jīng lùn* 佛地經論 [KR6i0589](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0589) (Xuánzàng, 649), three Vasubandhu-style *upadeśa* commentaries translated by Bodhiruci [KR6i0590](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0590)–[KR6i0592](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0592) and Vimokṣaprajñā [KR6i0593](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0593), and a Dunhuang-derived *Dàshèng sìfǎ jīng* exegetical trio [KR6i0594](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0594)–[KR6i0596](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0596) sit at the catalog's end. They are structurally 釋經論 (commentaries on single sūtras), and in Taishō proper occupy Vol. 26; their inclusion here reflects the Kanripo principle of grouping sūtra commentaries with the parent sūtra division.

### Important persons

- [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) (Dharmarakṣa, c. 239–316) — the single most prolific translator in this division (43 catalogued titles): *Xiánjié jīng*, the early Mañjuśrī texts, the Maitreya core, and a substantial Western-Jin Mahāyāna sūtra corpus.
- [支謙](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%94%AF%E8%AC%99) (Zhī Qiān, fl. c. 222–253) — early Wu-period sūtra translator; 27 titles here, including the first Chinese *Vimalakīrti*.
- [安世高](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%89%E4%B8%96%E9%AB%98) (Ān Shìgāo, fl. 148–168) — Eastern Hàn pioneer; 26 short *jīng* of meditation and ethics surviving in this division.
- [鳩摩羅什](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%B3%A9%E6%91%A9%E7%BE%85%E4%BB%80) (Kumārajīva, 344–413) — fixed the canonical Chinese versions of *Vimalakīrti*, *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Viśeṣacintābrahma-paripṛcchā*, and a clutch of other doctrinally central sūtras.
- [曇無讖](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%87%E7%84%A1%E8%AE%96) (Dharmakṣema, 385–433) — Northern Liáng translator of the earliest complete *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
- [佛陀跋陀羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BD%9B%E9%99%80%E8%B7%8B%E9%99%80%E7%BE%85) (Buddhabhadra, 359–429) — translator of the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, opening the textual base of East Asian Buddha-nature doctrine.
- [求那跋陀羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B1%82%E9%82%A3%E8%B7%8B%E9%99%80%E7%BE%85) (Guṇabhadra, 394–468) — translator of the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra*, the lineage text of early Chán.
- [菩提流支](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8F%A9%E6%8F%90%E6%B5%81%E6%94%AF) (Bodhiruci, fl. 508–537) — Northern Wei Yogācāra translator; ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva*, several Vasubandhu *upadeśa*.
- [僧伽婆羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%83%A7%E4%BC%BD%E5%A9%86%E7%BE%85) (Saṅghapāla, 460–524) — Liáng translator of the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*.
- [那連提耶舍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%82%A3%E9%80%A3%E6%8F%90%E8%80%B6%E8%88%8D) (Narendrayaśas, 517–589) — translator of the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*.

### Topics

- **The residual category as doctrinal repository.** Because the Taishō editors used *Jīngjí bù* as the bin for sūtras lacking a named cycle, the division accumulated isolates of unusual doctrinal density — single-text founders of major traditions (*Vimalakīrti*, *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, *Yuánjué jīng*) sit beside short ritual texts. Reading the division requires constant attention to which texts are doctrinal pivots and which are devotional or apotropaic miniatures.
- **Tathāgatagarbha and the Laṅkāvatāra problem.** The three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* (KR6i0327–0329), the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323), the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa* [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325), and the *Ghanavyūha* [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) together form the textual base from which East Asian Buddha-nature theory was synthesized — including the question of whether *ālayavijñāna* and *tathāgatagarbha* are identical, the doctrine that became canonical for Huáyán and Chán.
- **Samādhi literature.** The trio of *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, and *Viśeṣacintā* offers a coherent Indian sūtra theory of the bodhisattva's contemplative attainments; this is distinct from — and historically prior to — the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945 with which the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi* is often confused.
- **Sinitic apocrypha and lay Buddhism.** *Yuánjué jīng*, *Zhànchá jīng*, *Yúlánpén jīng*, *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng*, and the *Shíwáng jīng* corpus are the clearest cases in the Mahāyāna canon of texts produced in China and re-presented as Indian sūtras. They are also the texts with the broadest social reach: filial piety, calendrical festival, divination, and post-mortem judgement.
- **State-protective Buddhism.** The two Chinese *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* recensions, particularly Yìjìng's "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter, supplied the dharmic ideology of East Asian Buddhist statecraft from Sui through Nara and beyond.
- **Filial piety as Buddhist genre.** The Ullambana cluster, the Tang *fùmǔ ēn* texts, the *Shíwáng jīng*, and the *Dìzàng púsà běnyuàn jīng* tradition (its earliest witnesses sit in this division) together constitute Buddhism's most successful response to Confucian objections about filial debt.
- **Translation history through multi-recension witnesses.** Several core texts survive in two or three Chinese versions spanning four to seven centuries — *Vimalakīrti* (Zhī Qiān, Kumārajīva, Xuánzàng), *Laṅkāvatāra* (Guṇabhadra, Bodhiruci, Śikṣānanda), *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Xuánzàng + Yìjìng + earlier witnesses), *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Dharmakṣema + Yìjìng + Bǎoguì compendium). This makes KR6i an unusually rich laboratory for translation-history research.
- **The Chinese exegetical density.** The *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty Chinese commentaries spanning Sui to Qīng, and the *Yuánjué jīng* almost as many. The exegetical superstructure here is comparable in scale to that built around the *Lotus*, even though no individual non-Lotus sūtra reaches the *Lotus*'s extreme commentarial density.

## Division note (scope only): [KR6b 本緣部 *Běnyuán bù* — Buddhist Canon — Past-Life Narratives (Jātaka, Avadāna, Buddha-Biography, Parable, Dharmapada)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6b corresponds to the 本緣部 *Běnyuán bù* ("Section on Original Conditions") of the Taishō canon, occupying Taishō volumes 3 and 4 (T152–T219). In the CANWWW structural division  this is the fourth division of the canon, sitting between the 寶積部 *Ratnakūṭa* collections (div03) and the 般若部 *Prajñāpāramitā* section (div05). The unifying generic category is **narrative scripture about prior lives or originary events** — *jātaka* tales of the *bodhisattva*'s past births, *avadāna* anthologies of edifying karmic biographies, full Buddha-biographies (*Buddhacarita* / *Lalitavistara*-class works and their Chinese variants), the *Dharmapada* / *Udānavarga* gnomic-verse traditions, and the various *pìyù* 譬喻 (parable) compilations. The Chinese title literally means "section on origins and conditioned causes," capturing the karmic-narrative logic that ties this generically heterogeneous material together.

Chronologically the division spans roughly thirteen centuries of Chinese translation and compilation, from Ān Shìgāo's mid-second-century *Tàizǐ Mùpò jīng* 太子慕魄經 ([KR6b0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0019), c. 148–170) through the great Northern-Sòng *Yìjīng yuàn* 譯經院 translation programme of c. 980–1001 (the [Shīhù](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0017) / [Fǎxián](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0048) / [Tiānxīzāi](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0070) cluster). A single late-imperial commentarial extension — Lái Zhōu's 來舟 Yōngzhèng-era *Qiǎnzhù* on the *Xīndì-guān jīng* ([KR6b0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0009), [KR6b0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0010), [KR6b0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0011)) — carries the division into the eighteenth century. The principal transmissional traditions a reader must keep in mind are: (i) the Hàn–Wú southern translation lineage (Ān Shìgāo → Zhī Qiān → Kāng Sēnghuì), which produced the foundational Chinese *jātaka*-anthologies and the canonical *Dharmapada*; (ii) the Western-Jìn Dūnhuáng/Cháng'ān lineage of Zhú Fǎhù (Dharmarakṣa), responsible for an unusually large fraction of the division (at least seven works); (iii) the early-fifth-century Northern-Liáng (Dharmakṣema), Latter-Qín (Kumārajīva, Zhú Fóniàn), and Liú-Sòng (Guṇabhadra, Bǎoyún) translation programmes, which gave Chinese readers the *Buddhacarita*, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, and the *Udānavarga* with auto-commentary; and (iv) the Northern Sòng *Yìjīng yuàn*, which produced systematic re-translations of jātaka and parable material (T165, T173, T191, T213, T218, T219). One unusual feature of this division is the prominence of **Chinese editorial compilation** alongside translation: several of the most-influential works — *[Liù-dù jí jīng (T152)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0001)*, *[Xiányú jīng (T202)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0059)*, the four *[Zá pìyù jīng](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0061)* anthologies — are sinophone editorial assemblages of Indic narrative material rather than translations of single Indic recensions.

## Division note: [KR6i 經集部 *Jīngjí bù* — Buddhist Canon — Sūtra Collection (Mahāyāna Sūtrasaṃgraha)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6i mirrors the Taishō Tripiṭaka's 經集部 (*Jīngjí bù*, "Sūtrasaṃgraha"), the catch-all division in which the Taishō editors gathered the Mahāyāna sūtras that did not belong to one of the canon's named text-cycles. The principal axis is Taishō nos. 425–847 across Vols. 14–17, corresponding to CANWWW `div11.xml`; the Kanripo arrangement supplements this with Xuzangjing (卍續) commentaries, a handful of Jiāxīng-zàng titles, and — at the tail end (KR6i0589–0596) — a small block of Yogācāra 論釋 that drifted into the *jīng* collection through their attachment to single-sūtra commentary. Texts in the other "named" divisions are explicitly excluded: Prajñāpāramitā (KR6a), Ratnakūṭa (KR6b), Mahāsannipāta (KR6c), Avataṃsaka (KR6d), Nirvāṇa (KR6e), Lotus (KR6f), Bhadrakalpika (KR6g) and the Āgamas (KR6h) are catalogued elsewhere.

Because *Jīngjí bù* is structurally residual, its scholarly profile is not generic. The "leftover" works concentrate, in fact, several of the most consequential sūtras in the entire Chinese Mahāyāna corpus — *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras*, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa*, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* corpus, the Maitreya cycle, and the major Sinitic apocrypha *Yuánjué jīng* 圓覺經, *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經, *Yúlánpén jīng* 盂蘭盆經, and the *Shíwáng jīng* 十王經. The transmissional pattern is therefore stratigraphic: an Eastern Hàn–Western Jin layer of single-fascicle sūtras translated by Ān Shìgāo, Zhī Qiān, and above all Dharmarakṣa; a Yáo Qín / Northern Liáng turning-point in which Kumārajīva, Buddhabhadra, and Dharmakṣema fix the literary canon; a sixth- and seventh-century Yogācāra wave (Bodhiruci, Paramārtha, Saṅghapāla, Divākara, Xuánzàng); a Tang aftermath that adds re-translations and the great commentarial schools (Zhìyǐ, Jízàng, Kuījī, Zōngmì); and a Sòng coda of Indian translations from Shīhù 施護, Fǎtiān 法天, and Fǎxián 法賢. The chronological depth is matched by a high commentarial density — the *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty exegetical works in this division.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The *Vimalakīrti* cluster.** *Wéimójié suǒshuō jīng* 維摩詰所說經 [KR6i0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0076) (Kumārajīva, 406) is the canonical Chinese *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the most influential single text in the division — it shaped Chinese Buddhist literary style and supplied the central image of the bodhisattva-householder. Zhī Qiān's earlier *Fóshuō wéimójié jīng* 佛說維摩詰經 [KR6i0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0075) (Wú, c. 223–253) and Xuánzàng's *Shuō wúgòuchēng jīng* 說無垢稱經 [KR6i0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0077) preserve the parallel recensions. The exegetical apparatus runs from Sui–Tang masters — Huìyuǎn 慧遠 [KR6i0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0079), Zhìyǐ 智顗 [KR6i0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0080)–[KR6i0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0081), Jízàng 吉藏 [KR6i0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0083)–[KR6i0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0084), Kuījī 窺基 [KR6i0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0085) — through Song Tiāntái revival and Ming–Qing commentary, ending with the Qīng *Wéimó jīng wúwǒ shū* [KR6i0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0095) tradition.

**The Maitreya cluster.** A tight block of six canonical sūtras (KR6i0030–0036) covers the lower-birth (*xiàshēng*) and upper-birth (*shàngshēng*) traditions, including *Fóshuō mílè lái shí jīng* 佛說彌勒來時經 [KR6i0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0036), the briefest and most archaic of the canonical Maitreya texts. Tang commentarial elaboration comes via Jízàng [KR6i0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0037), Kuījī [KR6i0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0038), the Korean exegete Wǒnhyo 元曉 [KR6i0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0039), and Gyeongheung 憬興 [KR6i0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0040) — a rare witness to Silla Buddhist scholarship inside the Chinese canon.

**The *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Medicine Buddha) cluster.** *Yàoshī liúlí guāng rúlái běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* 藥師琉璃光如來本願功德經 [KR6i0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0048) (Xuánzàng, 650) is the canonical East Asian standard, with the seven-Buddha expanded recension *Yàoshī liúlí guāng qī fó běnyuàn gōngdé jīng* [KR6i0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0049) (Yìjìng, 707) and a Tang ritual-manual lineage. Tang Dunhuang exegesis survives in two anonymous *Yàoshī jīng shū* [KR6i0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0054)–[KR6i0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0055) preserved in Taishō Vol. 85, and Ming–Qing devotional commentary revives the cluster with Língyào 靈耀's *Yàoshī jīng zhíjiě* [KR6i0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0056) and the Ming repentance-liturgy tradition (KR6i0057–0058).

**The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) cluster.** Dharmakṣema's *Jīnguāngmíng jīng* 金光明經 [KR6i0301](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0301) (Northern Liáng, c. 414–426) is the earliest complete Chinese witness; Yìjìng's *Jīnguāngmíng zuìshèng wáng jīng* 金光明最勝王經 [KR6i0303](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0303) (Táng, 703) renders the full Sanskrit recension and supplies the canonical "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter foundational to East Asian state-protective Buddhism. The commentarial chain includes Zhìyǐ–Guàndǐng 灌頂 [KR6i0304](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0304), Zhīlǐ 知禮 [KR6i0305](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0305), Jízàng [KR6i0308](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0308), and a Tang Esoteric layer.

**The *tathāgatagarbha* / Laṅkāvatāra cluster.** The doctrinal core of East Asian Buddha-nature thought sits inside KR6i: Buddhabhadra's *Dàfāngděng rúláizàng jīng* 大方等如來藏經 [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323) (c. 420), Bodhiruci's *Fóshuō bù zēng bù jiǎn jīng* 佛說不增不減經 [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325) (c. 525), the three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* — Guṇabhadra's four-fascicle *Léngqié ābáduōluó bǎo jīng* 楞伽阿跋多羅寶經 [KR6i0327](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0327) (443), Bodhiruci's ten-fascicle *Rù léngqié jīng* 入楞伽經 [KR6i0328](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0328) (513), and Śikṣānanda's seven-fascicle *Dàshèng rù léngqié jīng* 大乘入楞伽經 [KR6i0329](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0329) (700–704) — and Divākara's *Dàshèng mìyán jīng* 大乘密嚴經 [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) (676–688). The Laṅkāvatāra triad is foundational both for East Asian Yogācāra and for early Chán self-identification as the "Laṅkāvatāra School" (楞伽宗).

**The samādhi cluster.** Three central Indian samādhi-sūtras stand together: Kumārajīva's *Shǒulèngyán sānmèi jīng* 佛說首楞嚴三昧經 [KR6i0279](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0279) (c. 402–409 — to be distinguished sharply from the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945), his *Sīyì fàntiān suǒwèn jīng* 思益梵天所問經 [KR6i0218](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0218) (c. 402–405), and Narendrayaśas's *Yuèdēng sānmèi jīng* 月燈三昧經 [KR6i0276](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0276) (Northern Qí, 557–559), the canonical Chinese witness to the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*.

**The Ullambana / filial-piety cluster.** *Fóshuō yúlán-pén jīng* 佛說盂蘭盆經 [KR6i0364](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0364) (attrib. Dharmarakṣa, but widely considered a Western Jin Chinese apocryphon) and its short twin *Fóshuō bào'ēn fèng-pén jīng* 佛說報恩奉盆經 [KR6i0376](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0376) together founded the East Asian *zhōngyuán* / Ghost Festival. Zōngmì's *Yúlán-pén jīng shū* [KR6i0365](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0365) and the ten or so subsequent Song–Qīng sub-commentaries make the cluster one of the densest commentarial bodies in the division. The related *Fùmǔ ēn nán bào jīng* 佛說父母恩難報經 [KR6i0363](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0363) (and the apocryphal *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng* tradition) carry the same filial-piety theme into popular Buddhism.

**The *Yuánjué jīng* (Perfect Enlightenment) cluster.** *Dàfāngguǎng yuánjué xiūduōluó liǎoyì jīng* 大方廣圓覺修多羅了義經 [KR6i0551](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0551) — attributed to Buddhatrāta but securely identified as a Tang Chinese apocryphon (c. 690–750) — together with Zōngmì's massive *Yuánjué jīng dàshū* [KR6i0555](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0555) and the long Sòng–Míng commentarial chain (KR6i0553–0574) constitute the textual base of the Huáyán–Chán synthesis Zōngmì engineered.

**The Sinitic apocrypha and divinatory / underworld cluster.** Alongside *Yuánjué jīng*, the division contains the *Zhànchá shàn'è yèbào jīng* 占察善惡業報經 [KR6i0545](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0545) (Sui-period Sinitic apocryphon, foundational to the Kṣitigarbha cult and the unique wooden-block divination liturgy), Zàngchuān 藏川's *Shíwáng jīng* 佛說地藏菩薩發心因緣十王經 [KR6i0583](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0583) and *Yùxiū shíwáng shēngqī jīng* [KR6i0584](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0584) (Late Tang, foundational to East Asian ten-kings underworld iconography), and the late *Huàzhū bǎomìng zhēn jīng* [KR6i0586](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0586) (Míng *zhēn-jīng*-genre fusion of Buddhist form, Daoist neidan imagery, and popular medicine).

**The Mañjuśrī cluster.** Dharmarakṣa's *Wénshū shīlì xiàn bǎozàng jīng* 佛說文殊師利現寶藏經 [KR6i0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0062) (c. 270–308), Saṅghapāla's *Wénshū shīlì wèn jīng* 文殊師利問經 [KR6i0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0069) (Liáng, 515–520 — a principal canonical source for the eighteen Indian sectarian schools), and a series of Tang–Sòng Mañjuśrī texts down to Fǎxián's late-Sòng *Fóshuō miàojíxiáng púsà suǒwèn dàshèng fǎluó jīng* 佛說妙吉祥菩薩所問大乘法螺經 [KR6i0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0074) (989–1000) trace the gradual standardization of Mañjuśrī's Chinese epithets — from older phonetic *Wénshūshīlì* to the standardized Sòng rendering *Miàojíxiáng*.

**The Yogācāra tail (KR6i0589–0596).** Bandhuprabha *et al.*'s *Fódì jīng lùn* 佛地經論 [KR6i0589](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0589) (Xuánzàng, 649), three Vasubandhu-style *upadeśa* commentaries translated by Bodhiruci [KR6i0590](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0590)–[KR6i0592](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0592) and Vimokṣaprajñā [KR6i0593](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0593), and a Dunhuang-derived *Dàshèng sìfǎ jīng* exegetical trio [KR6i0594](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0594)–[KR6i0596](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0596) sit at the catalog's end. They are structurally 釋經論 (commentaries on single sūtras), and in Taishō proper occupy Vol. 26; their inclusion here reflects the Kanripo principle of grouping sūtra commentaries with the parent sūtra division.

### Topics

- **The residual category as doctrinal repository.** Because the Taishō editors used *Jīngjí bù* as the bin for sūtras lacking a named cycle, the division accumulated isolates of unusual doctrinal density — single-text founders of major traditions (*Vimalakīrti*, *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, *Yuánjué jīng*) sit beside short ritual texts. Reading the division requires constant attention to which texts are doctrinal pivots and which are devotional or apotropaic miniatures.
- **Tathāgatagarbha and the Laṅkāvatāra problem.** The three Chinese *Laṅkāvatāras* (KR6i0327–0329), the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* [KR6i0323](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0323), the *Anūnatva-apūrṇatva-nirdeśa* [KR6i0325](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0325), and the *Ghanavyūha* [KR6i0359](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0359) together form the textual base from which East Asian Buddha-nature theory was synthesized — including the question of whether *ālayavijñāna* and *tathāgatagarbha* are identical, the doctrine that became canonical for Huáyán and Chán.
- **Samādhi literature.** The trio of *Śūraṅgamasamādhi*, *Samādhirāja*, and *Viśeṣacintā* offers a coherent Indian sūtra theory of the bodhisattva's contemplative attainments; this is distinct from — and historically prior to — the apocryphal *Lèngyán jīng* T945 with which the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi* is often confused.
- **Sinitic apocrypha and lay Buddhism.** *Yuánjué jīng*, *Zhànchá jīng*, *Yúlánpén jīng*, *Fùmǔ ēnzhòng jīng*, and the *Shíwáng jīng* corpus are the clearest cases in the Mahāyāna canon of texts produced in China and re-presented as Indian sūtras. They are also the texts with the broadest social reach: filial piety, calendrical festival, divination, and post-mortem judgement.
- **State-protective Buddhism.** The two Chinese *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* recensions, particularly Yìjìng's "Right Discourse on the Dharma of Kings" chapter, supplied the dharmic ideology of East Asian Buddhist statecraft from Sui through Nara and beyond.
- **Filial piety as Buddhist genre.** The Ullambana cluster, the Tang *fùmǔ ēn* texts, the *Shíwáng jīng*, and the *Dìzàng púsà běnyuàn jīng* tradition (its earliest witnesses sit in this division) together constitute Buddhism's most successful response to Confucian objections about filial debt.
- **Translation history through multi-recension witnesses.** Several core texts survive in two or three Chinese versions spanning four to seven centuries — *Vimalakīrti* (Zhī Qiān, Kumārajīva, Xuánzàng), *Laṅkāvatāra* (Guṇabhadra, Bodhiruci, Śikṣānanda), *Bhaiṣajyaguru* (Xuánzàng + Yìjìng + earlier witnesses), *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Dharmakṣema + Yìjìng + Bǎoguì compendium). This makes KR6i an unusually rich laboratory for translation-history research.
- **The Chinese exegetical density.** The *Vimalakīrti* alone carries some twenty Chinese commentaries spanning Sui to Qīng, and the *Yuánjué jīng* almost as many. The exegetical superstructure here is comparable in scale to that built around the *Lotus*, even though no individual non-Lotus sūtra reaches the *Lotus*'s extreme commentarial density.

### Timeline

- 148–168 — *Eastern Hàn short-sūtra layer* attributed to Ān Shìgāo (e.g. *Ānbān shǒuyì jīng* and related ethics / meditation miniatures): the oldest stratum of the division.
- 222–253 — Zhī Qiān's *Fóshuō wéimójié jīng* 佛說維摩詰經 [KR6i0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0075) — the first Chinese *Vimalakīrti*.
- 265–311 — *Fóshuō yúlán-pén jīng* 佛說盂蘭盆經 [KR6i0364](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0364), traditionally Dharmarakṣa, more likely Western Jin Sinitic apocryphon: founder of the East Asian Ghost Festival.
- 266–308 — *Fóshuō wénshū shīlì xiàn bǎozàng jīng* 佛說文殊師利現寶藏經 [KR6i0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0062) (Dharmarakṣa).

## Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君 divisions

## Division note: [KR6p 淨土宗著述部 *Jìngtǔ zōng zhùshù bù* — Buddhist Canon — Compositions of the Pure Land School](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR6p collects the Chinese-language compositions of the Pure Land school (*jìngtǔ zōng* 淨土宗) — the body of doctrinal treatises, sūtra-commentaries, liturgical *zàn* / *chàn* / *yí* texts, devotional anthologies, biographies, and devotional poetry that grew up around the three principal Pure Land sūtras: the *Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha* (*Wúliángshòu jīng* 無量壽經), the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha* (*Āmítuó jīng* 阿彌陀經), and the apocryphal *Contemplation Sūtra* (*Guān wúliángshòu jīng* 觀無量壽經). The 140 works gathered here are drawn from three regions of the Sino-Japanese canon: (i) the Taishō *Zhū-zōng bù* 諸宗部 (vol. 47, nos. 1957–1984) — the principal classical Pure Land treatises from Tánluán through Sòng-period Tiantai; (ii) the supplementary *Xùzàngjīng* 卍續藏 (vols. 1, 2, 22, 61, 62, 74) — the great bulk of Sòng–Qīng commentaries, ritual handbooks, and lay-Buddhist anthologies that the early-twentieth-century Japanese editors recovered from Chinese monastic libraries; and (iii) the Taishō *Gǔyì bù* 古逸部 (vol. 85, nos. 2826–2830), preserving Dunhuang-recovered Pure Land liturgies. The corresponding Taishō structural division — `div31.xml` 諸宗部 — is the formal canonical container, but the Kanripo arrangement extracts the Pure Land subset and supplements it heavily from the *Xùzàngjīng*.

Chronologically the division spans c. 530 CE (Tánluán 曇鸞's foundational tracts) through the very end of the Qīng (c. 1900). The internal centre of gravity is unusually late: roughly two-thirds of the entries date from the Míng-Qīng period, reflecting the fact that Pure Land devotion became the dominant lay-monastic practice of late imperial China and produced an immense vernacular literature absent from earlier canonical strata. Three transmissional issues run through the division: the inflation of the *Wúliángshòu* sūtra-corpus through apocryphal "translations" preserved only in the *Xùzàngjīng* (KR6p0031–0035); the Tiantai monopoly on the *Guān-jīng* commentarial tradition via the 觀經疏妙宗鈔 chain initiated by Zhīlǐ 知禮; and the steady migration of Pure Land authorship from the cloister to the lay literati class, culminating in the Péng Shàoshēng circle of the eighteenth century and Wèi Yuán's *Huìyì* recension of 1854.

### Important texts and text clusters

- **Wúliángshòu jīng 無量壽經 (Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha) corpus** — *Wúliángshòu jīng huìyì* 無量壽經會譯 [KR6p0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0001) (Wèi Yuán 魏源, 1854), *Wúliángshòu jīng jì* 無量壽經記 [KR6p0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0002) (Xuányī 玄一, Táng), *Wúliángshòu jīng qǐxìn lùn* 無量壽經起信論 [KR6p0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0003) (Péng Jìqīng 彭際清, late 18th c.), and Wáng Gēngxīn 王耕心's *Móhē Āmítuó jīng zhōnglùn* 摩訶阿彌陀經衷論 [KR6p0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0004); together they constitute the most sustained East-Asian commentarial engagement with the *larger* Pure Land sūtra.
- **Guān wúliángshòu jīng 觀無量壽經 (Contemplation Sūtra) commentarial chain** — the apex is Zhìyǐ 智顗 (attr.) and Zhīlǐ 知禮's *Guān wúliángshòu fó jīng shū miàozōng chāo* 觀無量壽佛經疏妙宗鈔 [KR6p0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0007) (preface 1021), the canonical Tiantai reading of the sūtra, around which a dense Sòng-period sub-cluster forms — Zhīlǐ's own *Róngxīn jiě* 融心解 [KR6p0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0008), Jièdù 戒度's *Fúxīn lùn* 扶新論 [KR6p0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0009) and *Zhèngguān jì* 正觀記 [KR6p0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0010), Chuándēng 傳燈's *Túsòng* 圖頌 [KR6p0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0011), Xùfǎ 續法's *Zhízhǐ shū* 直指疏 [KR6p0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0012), and Péng Jìqīng's *Yuē lùn* 約論 [KR6p0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0013); the *Kē* 妙宗鈔科 [KR6p0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0006) supplies the structural outline. Earlier strata are Fǎcōng 法聰's *Jì* 釋觀無量壽佛經記 [KR6p0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0005) (Táng).

- **Sòng-Tiantai systematization** — *Wǎngshēng jìngtǔ juéyí xíngyuàn èrmén* 往生淨土決疑行願二門 [KR6p0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0047) and *Wǎngshēng jìngtǔ chànyuàn yí* 往生淨土懺願儀 [KR6p0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0079) of Cíyún Zūnshì 慈雲遵式 (1000–1032); Zōngxiǎo 宗曉's two great anthologies *Lèbāng wénlèi* 樂邦文類 [KR6p0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0048) and *Lèbāng yígǎo* 樂邦遺稿 [KR6p0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0049) (1200–1214), the principal Sòng-period repositories of Pure Land prefaces, epigraphy, and hagiography; Chéngyù 澄彧's *Zhù shíyí lùn* 注十疑論 [KR6p0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0051); and Wáng Rìxiū 王日休's vastly influential lay manual *Lóngshū zēngguǎng jìngtǔ wén* 龍舒增廣淨土文 [KR6p0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0050) (c. 1160–1173).

- **Late-Míng lay-monastic revival cluster** — Yúnqī Zhūhóng 雲棲袾宏's prolific oeuvre, including the *Shūchāo* (above), *Jìngtǔ yíbiàn* 淨土疑辨 [KR6p0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0058), *Dá sìshíbā wèn* 答四十八問 [KR6p0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0063), *Xīfāng yuànwén* 西方願文 [KR6p0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0064), and the encyclopaedic *Jìngtǔ zīliáng quánjí* 淨土資糧全集 [KR6p0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0065); Chuándēng 傳燈's Tiantai-school *Jìngtǔ shēng-wúshēng lùn* 淨土生無生論 [KR6p0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0056) with its commentaries [KR6p0070](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0070)/[KR6p0071](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0071); Yuán Hóngdào 袁宏道's Gōng'ān-school *Xīfāng hé lùn* 西方合論 [KR6p0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0057) (1599) and the Míng-Qīng commentary on it [KR6p0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0068); Lǐ Zhì 李贄's *Jìngtǔ jué* 淨土決 [KR6p0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0062); the *Jìngtǔ zhǐguī jí* 淨土指歸集 of Dàyòu 大佑 [KR6p0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0059); Dàoyǎn 道衍's *Jìngtǔ jiǎnyào lù* 淨土簡要錄 [KR6p0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0060); Zōngběn 宗本's *Guīyuán zhízhǐ jí* 歸元直指集 [KR6p0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0061); and the apex anthology of late-Míng / early-Qīng Pure Land, Chéngshí 成時's *Jìngtǔ shíyào* 淨土十要 [KR6p0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0067) (1655–1678).
- **Qīng lay-Buddhist Pure Land movement** — built around Péng Shàoshēng / Péng Jìqīng 彭紹升 / 彭際清 (1740–1796), who is here represented by no fewer than nine works: doctrinal treatises *Wúliángshòu jīng qǐxìn lùn* [KR6p0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0003), *Guān-jīng yuē lùn* [KR6p0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0013), *Āmítuó jīng yuē lùn* [KR6p0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0028); anthologies *Chóngdìng xīfāng gōngjù* 重訂西方公據 [KR6p0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0099) and *Niànfó jǐngcè* 念佛警策 [KR6p0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0100); the *Shěng'ān fǎshī yǔlù* 省菴法師語錄 [KR6p0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0098); and the poetic collections *Èrlín chànghé shī* 二林唱和詩 [KR6p0128](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0128), *Guānhé jí jiéchāo* 觀河集節鈔 [KR6p0129](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0129), *Cèhǎi jí jiéchāo* 測海集節鈔 [KR6p0130](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0130). Around Péng cluster Shíxián 實賢 (Xǐng'ān 省菴), Xíngcè 行策 (*Jìngtǔ jǐngyǔ* [KR6p0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0093), *Qǐyī xīn jīngjìn niànfó qīqī guīshì* [KR6p0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0094)), Chèwù 徹悟 (*Chèwù chánshī yǔlù* [KR6p0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0101)), Zhōu Mèngyán 周夢顏's *Xīguī zhízhǐ* 西歸直指 [KR6p0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0092), Sōng Shàndēng 沈善登's *Bàoēn lùn* 報恩論 [KR6p0124](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0124), and Wèi Yuán's *Huìyì*. The late-Qīng strand of Hangzhou-area devotional anthologies by Gǔkūn 古崑 ([KR6p0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0085), [KR6p0106](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0106), [KR6p0107](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0107), [KR6p0116](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0116), [KR6p0117](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0117)) forms the closing wave of the division.
- **Liturgical / praise (zàn 讚 / chàn 懺 / yí 儀) corpus** — beyond Shàndǎo's three liturgies and Zūnshì's *Chànyuàn yí* above: Tánluán's *Zàn Āmítuó fó jié* [KR6p0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0073); the Nāgārjuna *Shíèr lǐ* 十二禮 (tr. Jñānagupta 禪那崛多) [KR6p0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0080); Zhìshēng 智昇's *Jí zhū jīng lǐchàn yí* 集諸經禮懺儀 [KR6p0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0077); Fǎzhào 法照's *Jìngtǔ wǔhuì niànfó lüè fǎshì yízàn* 淨土五會念佛略法事儀讚 [KR6p0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0078) and *Wǔhuì niànfó sòngjīng guānxíng yí (juǎn zhōng, xià)* [KR6p0136](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0136); Yuánzhào and Jièdù's *Wúliángshòu fó zàn zhù* 無量壽佛讚註 [KR6p0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0083); and the Dunhuang stratum [KR6p0137](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0137)–[KR6p0140](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0140).
- **Dunhuang stratum (Taishō vol. 85)** — Huìrì 慧日's *Lüè zhū jīnglùn niànfó fǎmén wǎngshēng jìngtǔ jí (juǎn shàng)* 略諸經論念佛法門往生淨土集 [KR6p0135](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0135), the only surviving juǎn of Huìrì's three-juǎn defence of "*niànfó* by sūtra and treatise" composed before 748; Fǎzhào's *Wǔhuì* middle and lower fascicles [KR6p0136](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0136) (the upper juǎn survives independently as KR6p0078); and the anonymous *Dàshèng jìngtǔ zàn* 大乘淨土讚 [KR6p0137](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0137), *Chízhāi niànfó chànhuǐ lǐwén* 持齋念佛懺悔禮文 [KR6p0138](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0138), *Dào'ān fǎshī niànfó zàn* 道安法師念佛讚 [KR6p0139](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0139) / *zànwén* 道安法師念佛讚文 [KR6p0140](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0140) — the principal Northwest-Chinese witnesses to Pure-Land devotional practice independent of the central-Táng exegetical traditions.
- **Devotional poetry (jìngtǔ shī 淨土詩) cluster** — Guǎngguì 廣貴's *Liánbāng shīxuǎn* 蓮邦詩選 [KR6p0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0072) (late Míng); Péng Shàoshēng's *Èrlín chànghé shī* and the *Jiéchāo* pair (above); Táo Shàn 陶善's *Qiónglóu yíngǎo jiéchāo* 瓊樓吟稿節鈔 [KR6p0131](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0131); Děrǔn 德潤's *Pǔnéng Sōng chánshī jìngtǔ shī* 普能嵩禪師淨土詩 [KR6p0133](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0133); and Kuānliàng 寬量's *Jìngtǔ jiùshēngchuán shī* 淨土救生船詩 [KR6p0134](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0134) — a distinctive Qīng vernacular genre giving the division much of its mid-late character.

### Important persons

- [曇鸞](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%87%E9%B8%9E) (Tánluán, c. 476–542) — the earliest Chinese Pure Land author preserved in the canon; the *Lüèlùn ānlè jìngtǔ yì* [KR6p0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0036) and the *Zàn Āmítuó fó jié* [KR6p0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0073) are the foundational texts of the *zìlì / tālì* (self-power / other-power) distinction.
- [道綽](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%81%93%E7%B6%BD) (Dàochuò, 562–645) — second of the "three masters of Xuánzhōng-sì 玄中寺"; the *Ānlè jí* [KR6p0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0037) is the principal Sui-Táng systematization of *niànfó* doctrine.
- [善導](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E5%B0%8E) (Shàndǎo, 613–681) — the central figure of classical Pure Land; four works in the division ([KR6p0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0038), [KR6p0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0074)–[KR6p0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0076)) establishing both doctrinal and liturgical practice.
- [智顗](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%BA%E9%A1%97) (Tiāntái Zhìyǐ, 538–597) — Sui Tiantai patriarch; *Jìngtǔ shíyí lùn* [KR6p0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0040) and *Wǔ fāngbiàn niànfó mén* [KR6p0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0041) traditionally attributed to him; the actual composition almost certainly Sòng-period under his name.
- [懷感](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%87%B7%E6%84%9F) (Huáigǎn, fl. 690–705) — Xuánzàng's disciple turned Pure-Land apologist; *Shì jìngtǔ qúnyí lùn* [KR6p0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0039) is the most rigorous early scholastic defence of Pure-Land practice within Yogācāra doctrine.
- [迦才](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%BF%A6%E6%89%8D) (Jiācái, fl. 645–670) — author of the early-Táng *Jìngtǔ lùn* [KR6p0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0042), an alternative scholastic systematization parallel to Dàochuò.
- [飛錫](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A3%9B%E9%8C%AB) (Fēixī, fl. 742–779) — late-Táng author of *Niànfó sānmèi bǎowáng lùn* [KR6p0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0046), a key statement of the universal-scope reading of *niànfó*.
- [元曉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%85%83%E6%9B%89) (Wǒnhyo, 617–686) — Silla scholar; the *Yóuxīn ānlè dào* [KR6p0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0044) is the Korean voice in the Táng Pure Land canon.
- [慧日](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%85%A7%E6%97%A5) (Címǐn Huìrì, 680–748) — author of the Dunhuang *Lüè zhū jīnglùn niànfó fǎmén* [KR6p0135](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0135); an opponent of Chán quietism who insisted on textual-scholastic foundations for Pure Land.
- [法照](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B3%95%E7%85%A7) (Fǎzhào, c. 745–805) — Wǔtáishān-based liturgist; creator of the *wǔhuì niànfó* 五會念佛 chanting system represented by KR6p0078 and KR6p0136.
- [知禮](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%9F%A5%E7%A6%AE) (Sìmíng Zhīlǐ, 960–1028) — the architect of Sòng-Tiantai Pure-Land thought; the *Miàozōng chāo* [KR6p0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0007), *Róngxīn jiě* [KR6p0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0008), and *Kē* [KR6p0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0006) together define the Tiantai reading of the *Guān-jīng* down to the present.
- [遵式](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%81%B5%E5%BC%8F) (Cíyún Zūnshì, 964–1032) — Zhīlǐ's contemporary; the *Juéyí xíngyuàn èrmén* [KR6p0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0047) and *Chànyuàn yí* [KR6p0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0079) codified Pure Land ritual for the Hángzhōu-area Tiantai network.
- [元照](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%85%83%E7%85%A7) (Língzhī Yuánzhào, 1048–1116) — Vinaya master who turned to Pure Land; *Āmítuó jīng yìshū* and *Wúliángshòu fó zàn zhù* together with the Jièdù sub-commentaries form a distinct Sòng-Vinaya reading of Pure Land texts.
- [戒度](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%88%92%E5%BA%A6) (Jièdù, fl. 1180–1240) — Yuánzhào's principal commentator; three works in the division ([KR6p0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0009), [KR6p0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0010), [KR6p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0015)).
- [宗曉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AE%97%E6%9B%89) (Zōngxiǎo, 1151–1214) — Sòng-period anthologist whose *Lèbāng wénlèi* / *Lèbāng yígǎo* preserve the bulk of the Sòng prefatory and hagiographic corpus.
- [王日休](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%97%A5%E4%BC%91) (Wáng Rìxiū, d. 1173) — Sòng lay literatus; the *Lóngshū jìngtǔ wén* [KR6p0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0050) is the most widely circulated lay Pure-Land manual in pre-modern China.
- [懷則](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%87%B7%E5%89%87) (Huáizé, fl. 1290–1340) and [天如則](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A4%A9%E5%A6%82%E5%89%87) (Tiānrú Wéizé, c. 1286–1354) — Yuán Tiantai authors of, respectively, the *Jìngguān yàomén* and the *Jìngtǔ huòwèn*.
- [普度](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%AE%E5%BA%A6) (Yōután Pǔdù, d. 1330) — Yuán reformer of the White Lotus society; the *Lúshān liánzōng bǎojiàn* [KR6p0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0054) is the canonical lineage-history of the "Lotus society" tradition.
- [袾宏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A2%BE%E5%AE%8F) (Yúnqī Zhūhóng, 1535–1615) — late-Míng master at Yúnqī-sì 雲棲寺; the dominant authorial presence in the division (eight works including the *Āmítuó jīng shūchāo*) and the architect of late-Míng Pure Land revival.
- [傳燈](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%82%B3%E7%87%88) (Yōuxī Chuándēng, 1554–1627) — Míng Tiantai exegete; commentator on both the *Guān-jīng* and the *Āmítuó jīng* tradition, author of the *Jìngtǔ shēng-wúshēng lùn*.
- [大佑](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A4%A7%E4%BD%91) (Dàyòu, 1334–1407) — Yuán-Míng compiler bridging the two dynasties; three works in the division.
- [袁宏道](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A2%81%E5%AE%8F%E9%81%93) (Yuán Hóngdào, 1568–1610) — Gōng'ān-school literatus; *Xīfāng hé lùn* [KR6p0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0057) is the principal late-Míng literati statement of Pure Land doctrine.
- [李贄](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E8%B4%84) (Lǐ Zhì, 1527–1602) — heterodox Míng literatus; *Jìngtǔ jué* [KR6p0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0062) places him in the Pure Land tradition.
- [智旭](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%BA%E6%97%AD) (Ǒuyì Zhìxù, 1599–1655) — last of the "four great Míng masters"; his *Āmítuó jīng yàojiě* (transmitted here in [KR6p0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0025)) is the standard Tiantai reading of the smaller sūtra.
- [成時](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%88%90%E6%99%82) (Chéngshí, 1618–1678) — Zhìxù's disciple; compiler of the *Jìngtǔ shíyào* [KR6p0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0067), the canonical late-Míng / early-Qīng Pure-Land anthology.
- [彭際清](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BD%AD%E9%9A%9B%E6%B8%85) (Péng Shàoshēng / Jìqīng, 1740–1796) — leading Qīng lay-Buddhist scholar; nine works represent his doctrinal, anthological, and poetic output and define eighteenth-century lay Pure Land literature.
- [實賢](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AF%A6%E8%B3%A2) (Xǐng'ān Shíxián, 1686–1734) — Qīng patriarch of the Pure Land lineage; subject of [KR6p0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0098) and annotator of [KR6p0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0087) and [KR6p0097](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0097).

### Topics

- **The five Chinese versions of the *Wúliángshòu jīng* and the problem of a unified Larger Pure Land Sūtra** — running from the medieval translator-attributions through Yúnqī Zhūhóng's preference for the smaller sūtra to Wèi Yuán's nineteenth-century *huìyì* solution and Xià Liánjū's twentieth-century continuation; the principal philological problem of the division.
- **The status of the *Guān wúliángshòu jīng* as a Central-Asian / Chinese composition** — debate, beginning with Mochizuki Shinkō's mid-twentieth-century work and continuing into Fujita Kōtatsu and Stevenson's studies, over whether the sūtra is an Indian translation or a Sino-Central-Asian composition; the entire commentarial chain [KR6p0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0005)–[KR6p0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0013) presupposes it as canonical.
- **The Tiantai monopolization of *Guān-jīng* exegesis** — how Zhīlǐ's *Miàozōng chāo* established a doctrinal grid (*xìng-shàn xìng-è* 性善性惡, *yīniàn sānqiān* 一念三千) on top of the sūtra's contemplative scheme, and how this Tiantai reading survived as the only living *Guān-jīng* commentarial tradition through the Sòng, Yuán, and Míng periods.
- **The *niànfó sānmèi* debate** — whether *niànfó* is a propaedeutic ritual practice, a meditative *samādhi*, or an actualization of *zìxìng Mítuó wéixīn jìngtǔ* 自性彌陀唯心淨土 (the Amitābha-of-one's-own-nature, the Pure Land of mind-only); a debate that runs from Fēixī's *Bǎowáng lùn* [KR6p0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0046) through Yánshòu and Yuán Hóngdào to the late-Míng "*chán-jìng yī-zhì* 禪淨一致" (Chán–Pure-Land synthesis) of Yúnqī and Zhìxù.
- **Chán–Pure-Land synthesis (chán-jìng shuāngxiū 禪淨雙修)** — the Sòng-Míng-Qīng convergence of Chán practice and Pure Land devotion, most clearly thematized in Tiānrú Wéizé's *Huòwèn* [KR6p0053](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0053), Yuán Hóngdào's *Hé lùn* [KR6p0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0057), Jīhúng 濟能's *Jiǎohǔ jí* 角虎集 [KR6p0096](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0096), and Chèwù's *Yǔlù* [KR6p0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0101); defined the dominant late-imperial monastic style.
- **Pure Land hagiography and the "Lotus society" lineage** — the construction of an unbroken lineage from Lúshān Huìyuǎn 廬山慧遠's 4th-c. society through the Táng masters to the present, codified by Pǔdù's *Liánzōng bǎojiàn* [KR6p0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0054) and Zōngxiǎo's anthologies, and disseminated as the model of Pure Land religious community.
- **The migration of authorship from cloister to lay literati** — most visible in the eighteenth-century Péng Shàoshēng circle (his nine works represent the apex), but already prepared in the Sòng with Wáng Rìxiū, in the Míng with Yuán Hóngdào and Lǐ Zhì, and continuing into the late-Qīng with Wèi Yuán, Shěn Shàndēng, and Wáng Gēngxīn.
- **Pure Land devotional poetry as canonical literature** — the unusual fact, distinctive to this division within the Kanripo Buddhist canon, that *jìngtǔ shī* 淨土詩 collections are treated as canonical religious texts and admitted to the *Xùzàngjīng*; a Qīng phenomenon documented in [KR6p0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0072), [KR6p0128](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0128)–[KR6p0134](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0134).
- **The *fó-qī* 佛七 (seven-day intensive *niànfó*) and Pure Land monastic regulation** — the standardization of ritual recitation regimes traceable from Zhìshēng's *Lǐchàn yí* [KR6p0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0077) and Fǎzhào's *Wǔhuì* [KR6p0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0078) through Xíngcè's *Qīqī guīshì* [KR6p0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0094) to nineteenth-century Hangzhou practice in Gǔkūn's manuals; the operational practice underlying the doctrinal literature.
- **The Dunhuang independent witness** — the *Gǔyì bù* texts [KR6p0135](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0135)–[KR6p0140](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6p/KR6p0140) preserve a Pure-Land devotional tradition (Címǐn Huìrì, Fǎzhào, anonymous liturgies) at least partly independent of the Chang'an-Luòyáng centres, and their survival only at Dunhuang shows how much medieval Chinese Pure Land literature has been lost in central transmission.

## Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君 divisions
