### Topics

- **The *fāngzhì* as instrument of governance.** The *Sìkù* editors retained the inherited classification of geography under *shǐbù* because, as Wilkinson §16.4.1 emphasizes, the gazetteer was first and foremost an administrator's handbook — the rules of avoidance forbade officials from serving in their own home region, so every new magistrate or prefect had to learn the locality from its gazetteer. Almost every text in [KR2k0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0010)–0056 was either commissioned by, or actively used by, the local administration. The 1672 and 1728 imperial edicts mandating provincial *tōngzhì* are the proximate cause of the dominance of Qīng *fāngzhì* in the division.
- **The empire-wide *yītǒng zhì* programme.** From the *Tàipíng huányǔ jì* through the *Da-Yuán da-yītǒng zhì* (lost in part) and the *Dà Míng yītǒng zhì* [KR2k0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0008) to the *Dà Qīng yītǒng zhì* [KR2k0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0009), each unifying dynasty signaled its claim to *tiānxià* by commissioning a single empire-wide gazetteer (Wilkinson §16.3.3). The Sìkù sub-cluster preserves the standard recension of every surviving member of the sequence except the Yuán entry.
- **Historical hydrology and the *Shuǐjīng zhù* tradition.** The 23-text 河渠 cluster ([KR2k0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0058)–0080) preserves the entire long arc from Lì Dàoyuán to the late-Qiánlóng imperial Yellow-River programmes. The *kǎojù* reconstruction of the *Shuǐjīng zhù* in the 18th century (Quán Zǔwàng, Zhào Yīqīng, Shěn Bǐngxùn, Dài Zhèn) and the Dài–Zhào plagiarism controversy is one of the most documented affairs in early-modern Chinese textual scholarship.
- **The Sòng prefectural-gazetteer renaissance.** Of the 1,000+ known Southern-Sòng *fāngzhì*, fewer than 30 survive; the Sòng cluster of [KR2k0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0010)–0022 contains the bulk of them, including the two great Línān gazetteers ([KR2k0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0011), [KR2k0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0022)) and the canonical Sūzhōu set ([KR2k0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0010), [KR2k0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0013)). These works embody the Southern-Sòng shift Wilkinson describes (§16.4.1) — from military-administrative reportage to gentry biography, literary citation, and cultural display.
- **Late-Sòng urban nostalgia.** The cluster [KR2k0111](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0111), [KR2k0117](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0117), [KR2k0118](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0118), [KR2k0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0119) preserves the most concentrated body of urban-cultural-historical writing in the pre-modern Chinese tradition, all four works composed retrospectively after the loss of their respective capitals (Kāifēng to the Jīn; Línān to the Mongols). They are the documentary basis of almost every modern study of Sòng urban culture, popular entertainment, ritual calendar, and material life.
- **Foreign-records and the boundary of *tiānxià*.** The 外紀 cluster [KR2k0136](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0136)–[KR2k0152](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0152) traces the genealogy of Chinese knowledge of the outer world — Buddhist pilgrim accounts of South and Central Asia (Fǎxiǎn, Xuánzàng), Sòng–Yuán maritime ethnography (*Zhūfān zhì*, *Dǎoyí zhìlüè*, *Zhēnlà fēngtǔ jì*), Míng tributary embassies (*Cháoxiǎn fù* [KR2k0143](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0143), *Cháoxiǎn zhì* [KR2k0148](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0148)), Jesuit world geographies ([KR2k0146](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0146), [KR2k0150](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0150)), and the high-Qīng visual-ethnographic synthesis ([KR2k0149](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0149)). It registers, within a single Sìkù sub-cluster, the entire pre-modern Chinese geographical imagination of what lay beyond the *zhífāng* world.
- **The Ming-loyalist historiographical legacy.** That Gù Yánwǔ's *Tiānxià jùnguó lìbìng shū* [KR2k0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0037) was admitted to the Sìkù but his *Zhàoyù zhì* and Gù Zǔyǔ's *Dúshǐ fāngyú jìyào* (the third great Qīng work of historical geography) were excluded — Wilkinson §16.3.4 makes the political-bibliographical point sharp — illustrates the Qiánlóng court's selective accommodation of *kǎojù* historical geography. The Qing imperial gazetteer programme inherited the methods of the Ming loyalists while editing out the politically resistant works.
- **The Jesuit world-geographies in the Sìkù.** The admission of [KR2k0146](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0146) (Aleni 1623) and [KR2k0150](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0150) (Verbiest 1672) to the *Sìkù* — alongside the rejection of most early-Qīng Christian writings — reflects the editors' technical regard for Jesuit cartography and astronomy even as they kept doctrinal Christianity outside the canon. The two works are the principal Sìkù-canonized European-language-derived geographies.
- **Encyclopedism and the imperial gazetteer.** The flowering of the *qīndìng* genre ([KR2k0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0035)–[KR2k0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0040), [KR2k0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0072), [KR2k0088](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0088), [KR2k0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0089), [KR2k0149](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/KR2k0149)) under Qiánlóng converted the *fāngzhì* from a working administrative reference into a state-ideological monument; many were produced in the same Hànlín / Wǔyīngdiàn editorial pipeline that produced the imperial *yùdìng* literary and *yuèlìng* anthologies (see [KR2j](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2j/) for the cognate *Shílìng* category).

# 職官類 (KR2l)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR2l 職官類 *Zhíguān lèi* — Histories — Official Posts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition
KR2l 職官類 (*Zhíguān lèi*, "Official Posts") is the twelfth sub-class of the Sìkù *Histories* division (KR2, 史部). It collects two distinct but adjacent textual traditions that the Sìkù editors treated together: (a) institutional monographs and gazetteers of particular central-government bureaus — most prominently the Hànlín Academy 翰林院, the Imperial Library *Mìshū shěng* 秘書省 / *Mìshū jiàn* 秘書監, the Ministry of Rites 禮部, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices 太常寺, and the Directorate of Education 國子監 — and (b) the *guānzhēn* 官箴 corpus, manuals of magistracy addressed to county-level officials. The first cluster is the source-base for the institutional history of Chinese imperial central government; the second is the principal premodern documentation of local-level administrative practice. Wilkinson treats the Sìkù *zhíguān* category and its successors at §19.5 (local government), §19.6 (ranks and prestige titles), and §19.7 (official posts), and the *guānzhēn* genre specifically at §19.5.3.2 — where he identifies *Guānzhēnshū jíchéng* 官箴書集成 (Huángshān, 1997, 101 titles) and Pierre-Étienne Will's *Handbooks and anthologies for officials in imperial China* (Brill, 2020, 1,165 titles) as the standard modern references.

Chronologically, the division begins with the Táng 唐 (the *Táng liùdiǎn* of 738 and Lǐ Zhào's *Hànlín zhì* of 819 — Wilkinson notes the *Táng liùdiǎn* at §25.4.1 as "the earliest extant collection of administrative law" to survive intact) and runs through to mid-Qīng (the *Cílín diǎngù* of 1747 and the *Qīndìng lìdài zhíguān biǎo* of 1780, the closing imperial syntheses). The bulk of the corpus is Sòng and Míng, reflecting the maturation of the central bureaucracy and the rise of professionalized magistracy after the Yuánfēng reorganization of 1078–1080 and the Southern Sòng intensification of local administration. The transmission picture is also distinctive: a number of the major Sòng monographs (*Líntái gùshì*, *Nán Sòng guǎngé lù*, *Zhōuxiàn tígāng*) were lost in standalone form by the late Míng and recovered by the Sìkù editors from the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn* 永樂大典 — one of the more visible cases of *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn*-mediated restoration in the entire Sìkù enterprise.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The Hànlín cluster** — successive monographs on the Hànlín Academy, the imperial drafting bureau, in a continuous Tang–Sòng–Míng–Qīng lineage:
- *Hànlín zhì* 翰林志 [KR2l0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0002) by Lǐ Zhào (819) — the founding monograph and the model for all that followed.
- *Hànyuàn qúnshū* 翰苑羣書 [KR2l0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0004) edited by Hóng Zūn (1173) — a Southern Sòng collectanea that preserves nine Tang and Northern Sòng treatises on the Academy that survive nowhere else in standalone form.
- *Yùtáng zájì* 玉堂雜記 [KR2l0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0006) by Zhōu Bìdà (1182) — the principal Southern Sòng documentary source, in a strongly first-person texture.
- *Hànlín jì* 翰林記 [KR2l0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0009) by Huáng Zuǒ (c. 1530s) — the comprehensive Míng-period monograph, with prosopographical name-lists by reign.
- *Cílín diǎngù* 詞林典故 [KR2l0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0013) by Èěrtài and Zhāng Tíngyù (1747) — the imperial Qīng counterpart, framed by Qiánlóng's own preface as the closure of a millennium-long genre.

**The Imperial Library cluster** — institutional self-portraits of the *Mìshū shěng* / *Mìshū jiàn*, in chronological succession:
- *Líntái gùshì* 麟臺故事 [KR2l0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0003) by Chéng Jù (1131) — composed at the moment of the Library's reconstitution in the south after the Jìn invasion.
- *Nán Sòng guǎngé lù* 南宋館閣錄 [KR2l0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0005) by Chén Kuí (1177, with anonymous continuation to 1269) — the principal Southern Sòng record.
- *Mìshū jiàn zhì* 祕書監志 [KR2l0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0008) by Wáng Shìdiǎn and Shāng Qǐwēng (c. 1340–1352) — the Yuán-period monograph, distinctive for incorporating the Astronomical Directorate and preserving Yuán chancery *zhíyì* 直譯 (literal-translation) prose.

**Comparative tables and prosopography**:
- *Táng liùdiǎn* 唐六典 [KR2l0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0001) (738) — the foundational comprehensive treatment of Tang central government, modelled on the *Zhōulǐ*.
- *Sòng zǎifǔ biānnián lù* 宋宰輔編年錄 [KR2l0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0007) by Xú Zìmíng (1215) — chronological prosopography of every Sòng Grand Councillor and Vice Grand Councillor, embedding full *zhì* 制 texts of investiture and dismissal.
- *Qīndìng lìdài zhíguān biǎo* 欽定歷代職官表 [KR2l0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0015) (1780) — the great Qiánlóng comparative tabulation of every imperial office from antiquity to the Qīng, organized retrospectively from the Qīng establishment. Wilkinson treats it at §19.6 as the foundation of all modern reference work on Chinese historical nomenclature.

**Specialized bureau and frontier monographs**:
- *Lǐbù zhìgǎo* 禮部志稿 [KR2l0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0010) by Lín Yáoyú and Yú Rǔjí (1620) — the 100-*juǎn* gazetteer of the late-Míng Ministry of Rites, supplementing the *Míng huìdiǎn* on court ritual and ceremonial.

- *Tǔguān dǐbù* 土官底簿 [KR2l0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0012) (anon., c. 1500–1521) — the principal early-Míng roster of 363 *tǔsī* (native chieftain) lineages in Yúnnán, Guǎngxī, Sìchuān, Guìzhōu, Húguǎng, and Guǎngdōng; a major source for the institutional history of southwest China.

**The *guānzhēn* cluster** — manuals of magistracy, the principal premodern documentation of local-level administrative practice:
- *Zuòyì zìzhēn* 作邑自箴 [KR2l0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0019) by Lǐ Yuánbì (1117) — the earliest dated *guānzhēn*, anchoring the genre in Northern Sòng oral magistracy tradition.

- *Zhōuxiàn tígāng* 州縣提綱 [KR2l0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0016) (anon., late twelfth or thirteenth century) — Southern Sòng manual whose false attribution to Chén Xiāng the Sìkù editors definitively debunked.
- *Bǎiguān zhēn* 百官箴 [KR2l0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0018) by Xǔ Yuèqīng (1260–1285) — rhymed admonitions for every Sòng central-government office, in the style of Yáng Xióng's lost *Guān zhēn*; a Sòng-loyalist 遺民 composition.
- *Zhòulián xùlùn* 晝簾緒論 [KR2l0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0020) by Hú Tàichū (1235) — a tightly organized fifteen-chapter manual that became influential on Yuán-Míng successors.
- *Sān shì zhōnggào* 三事忠告 [KR2l0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0021) by Zhāng Yǎnghào (c. 1308–1329) — the most important Yuán contribution to the genre, addressed in turn to the county magistrate, the Censor, and the Grand Councillor.

### Topics

- **The Tang–Qīng Hànlín lineage.** The five Hànlín monographs ([KR2l0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0002), [KR2l0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0004), [KR2l0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0006), [KR2l0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0009), [KR2l0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0013)) form one of the most continuous single-institution documentary chains in the Chinese historical literature, from the office's mature consolidation under Xuánzōng (early eighth century) to its closing Qīng codification (mid-eighteenth century). Each work is consciously written as a continuation of its predecessors; Hóng Zūn's *Hànyuàn qúnshū* is the principal vehicle by which the Tang and Northern Sòng strata are preserved at all.

- **The Imperial Library as a literary self-subject.** The three central Library monographs ([KR2l0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0003), [KR2l0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0005), [KR2l0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0008)) document successive stages of the *Mìshū shěng* / *Mìshū jiàn*: Northern-Sòng-into-Southern-Sòng reconstitution after 1127, mature Southern Sòng practice down to 1269, and the Yuán reorganization under Mongol rule (with the Astronomical Directorate folded in). Together they are the only continuous source on imperial book-collection, copying, and editorial practice across the Sòng–Yuán divide.

- **Administrative restoration and the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn*.** Several major Sòng monographs in this division (*Líntái gùshì*, *Nán Sòng guǎngé lù*, *Zhōuxiàn tígāng*) had been lost in standalone form by the late Míng and were recovered from the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn* by the Sìkù editors — a clearly visible Sìkù-era restoration enterprise.

- **The *guānzhēn* genre and the ethics of office.** The seven-text *guānzhēn* cluster ([KR2l0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0016)–[KR2l0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0022)) traces the evolution of a distinctive Chinese genre: practical-moral handbooks addressed to magistrates and other officials, fusing personal-cultivation maxims (*qīngshènqín*) with practical-administrative advice on lawsuits, taxation, clerk-management, and corvée. The genre takes shape in the Northern Sòng (Lǐ Yuánbì, 1117), develops the Confucian moralizing register in the Sòng-Yuán transition (Lǚ Běnzhōng, Xǔ Yuèqīng, Hú Tàichū, Zhāng Yǎnghào), and is appropriated as an instrument of imperial discipline in the early Qīng (Shùnzhì's *Jǐngxīn lù*).

- **Comparative cross-dynastic nomenclature.** The trajectory from Sūn Féngjí's Sòng *Zhíguān fēn jì* through to Qiánlóng's *Qīndìng lìdài zhíguān biǎo* (1780, [KR2l0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0015)) exemplifies the late-imperial impulse to map every office onto every predecessor system, with the Qīng establishment as the organizing baseline — a retrospective and Qīng-centric reading of all imperial institutional history.

- **Prosopography as institutional history.** Three works in this division ([KR2l0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0007), [KR2l0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0008), [KR2l0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0010)) anchor their institutional accounts in name-lists of office-holders down to surprisingly low levels (junior directors, clerical sub-officials), making the division an unexpectedly rich biographical resource. Xú Zìmíng's chronicle, in particular, sometimes corrects the *Sòngshǐ* "Year-table of Grand Councillors."

- **Frontier administration and *gǎitǔ guīliú*.** The anomalous *Tǔguān dǐbù* ([KR2l0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2l/KR2l0012)) is the principal pre-conquest source for the Míng *tǔsī* system in southwestern China and is therefore the single most important documentary basis for modern ethnohistorical study of Yi, Bai, Zhuang, Miao, and Yao political organization in the Yuán-Míng-Qīng transition.

# 政書類 (KR2m)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR2m 政書類 *Zhèngshū lèi* — Histories — Works relating to government administration](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2m/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

`KR2m` 政書類 is the *zhèngshū* (works relating to government administration) subdivision of the History branch (`KR2` 史部) of the *Sìkù quánshū* 四庫全書. As Wilkinson observes in his Chapter 51, the *Sìkù* category — credited by the editors to Qián Pǔ 錢溥 (*jìnshì* 1439) in his *Mìgé shūmù* 秘閣書目, and previously called *jiùshì* 舊事 in the *Qīlù* 七錄 and *Suízhì* 隋志, or *gùshì* 故事 in Táng-Sòng catalogs — gathers the topical-encyclopedic, administrative, and regulatory texts that lay outside the annals-biography (*jìzhuàn* 紀傳) and chronicle (*biānnián* 編年) genres but were nevertheless central to the practical operation of imperial government. The 57 works collected here — the same 57 listed by Wilkinson in his Table 73 — comprise the comprehensive institutional histories (the *Sāntōng* 三通 / *Shítōng* 十通), the dynasty-by-dynasty *huìyào* 會要 and *huìdiǎn* 會典 compendia, the ritual codes (*wǔlǐ* / *lǐqì túshì*), the famine-relief literature (*huāngzhèng* 荒政), the military-administration treatises, the major imperial law codes, and a small but historically pivotal group of works on construction, printing, and dynastic ceremonial.

The scholarly tradition is unusually long-running and self-conscious. Dù Yòu's 杜佑 *Tōngdiǎn* (801) established a nine-fold topical taxonomy — *shíhuò* 食貨, *xuǎnjǔ* 選舉, *zhíguān* 職官, *lǐ* 禮, *yuè* 樂, *bīng* 兵, *xíng* 刑, *zhōujùn* 州郡, *biānfáng* 邊防 — that every later *zhèngshū* author had to engage with, whether by extension (Mǎ Duānlín's 馬端臨 *Wénxiàn tōngkǎo*, which added five new *kǎo*), continuation (the eighteenth-century Qiánlóng commissions), or polemical critique (Zhèng Qiáo 鄭樵 in the *Tōngzhì*, whose own twenty *lüè* were classified by the *Sìkù* editors not here but as a *biéshǐ* 別史). The chronological span runs from a Late-Hàn institutional handbook (the *Hàn guān jiùyí* 漢官舊儀) at one end to Qiánlóng-era court compilations (the *Bāxún wànshòu shèngdiǎn* of 1792) at the other; the densest concentration is in the Sòng (*huìyào*, ritual codes, *Tōngkǎo*) and the Qīng (the imperially-commissioned continuations and the *Dà Qīng huìdiǎn* / *Dà Qīng lǜlì* / *Bāqí tōngzhì* state-machinery compendia).

### Important texts and text clusters

**The *Sāntōng* 三通 and their Qīng continuations (the *Jiǔtōng* 九通 backbone).** The three canonical encyclopedic institutional histories and the imperially-commissioned eighteenth-century extensions that, taken together, were eventually packaged as the *Shítōng* 十通.

- *Tōngdiǎn* 通典 [KR2m0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2m/KR2m0001) — Dù Yòu's 801 foundation of the genre, in 200 *juǎn*; the canonical framework on which the entire *Shítōng* series rests.
- *Wénxiàn tōngkǎo* 文獻通考 [KR2m0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2m/KR2m0009) — Mǎ Duānlín's 1307/1319 extension of the *Tōngdiǎn* through 1224, in 348 *juǎn* and 24 *kǎo*; the longest and most-used of the three.
- *Qīndìng xù wénxiàn tōngkǎo* 欽定續文獻通考 [KR2m0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2m/KR2m0014) — Qiánlóng-era continuation covering 1224–1644.

- *Qīndìng xù tōngdiǎn* 欽定續通典 [KR2m0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2m/KR2m0016) — Qiánlóng continuation of the *Tōngdiǎn* through 1644.

### Topics

The division's principal interpretive problems run along several axes.

**The structure of comprehensive coverage.** The fundamental methodological problem of *zhèngshū* is how to organize the institutions of imperial government across the entire historical span. Dù Yòu's nine-topic *Tōngdiǎn* taxonomy (food/finance, selection, office, ritual, music, military, punishments, local administration, border defense) became the default; Mǎ Duānlín added five new *kǎo*; the *huìyào* and *huìdiǎn* formats abandoned cross-dynastic synthesis for one-dynasty agency-by-agency comprehensiveness. The choice of structure was itself an argument about which aspects of governance were primary and how institutions developed historically.

**Ritual versus administration.** The *Sìkù* placement of imperial ritual codes (*Kāiyuán lǐ*, *Zhènghé wǔlǐ xīnyí*, *Míng jí lǐ*, *Dà Qīng tōnglǐ*) alongside law codes and fiscal compendia is itself a substantive claim — that imperial ritual is a branch of governance, not a separate "religious" domain. The same logic puts *Mǎnzhōu jìshén jìtiān diǎnlǐ* (Manchu shamanic ritual) and *Shàoxī zhōuxiàn shìdiàn yítú* (Confucian school sacrifice) in the same subdivision.

**The standing-army problem and military-institutional decline.** From Chén Fùliáng's *Lìdài bīngzhì* through the Qīng *Bāqí tōngzhì*, *zhèngshū* authors return repeatedly to the question of how military institutions degrade — the swollen post-*Huángyòu* Sòng armies, the Míng *wèisuǒ* system's collapse, the eighteenth-century Banner's loss of effectiveness — and what historical models of compact, militia-rooted armies might be recovered.

**Famine relief as administrative philosophy.** The *huāngzhèng* cluster, beginning with Dǒng Wěi and canonized in Yú Sēn's *Huāngzhèng cóngshū* and the Qīng *Kāngjì lù*, treats famine response not as ad-hoc emergency action but as a discipline with its own historical canon, institutional vocabulary (granaries, tax-remission, work-relief, locust extermination), and ethical foundation in classical "nourishing the people" doctrine.

**Legal codification and East-Asian transmission.** The *Táng lǜ shūyì* — *Sìkù*-classified here under *zhèngshū* rather than separately — is the source from which the *Sòng xíngtǒng*, the Korean and Japanese *ritsuryō*, the Vietnamese Lê code, and ultimately the *Dà Qīng lǜlì* all descend. Within this division the law-code cluster is small (two titles) but disproportionately consequential for comparative East-Asian legal history.

**Technical knowledge as state knowledge.** The presence of *Yíngzào fǎshì*, *Áobō tú*, and *Wǔyīng Diàn chéngshì* in the History branch (not in *zǐbù* / Masters) reflects a *Sìkù* judgment that engineering and craft regulation, when promulgated by the throne, become part of the institutional record proper rather than artisanal *zǐ* literature.

**Antiquarian recovery of lost institutions.** Wáng Yīnglín's *Hàn zhì kǎo*, Xú Tiānlín's *Liǎng Hàn huìyào* pair, Sūn Chéngzé's Yuán-institutions study, and Wàn Sītóng's temple-regulation diagram all belong to a long-running project of using textual evidence to reconstruct institutional configurations no longer documented in extant codes.

# 目錄類 (KR2n)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR2n 目錄類 *Mùlù lèi* — Histories — Bibliographic and Epigraphic Catalogues](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

*Mùlù* 目錄 — literally "tables and entries" — is the bibliographic-catalogue branch of the *shǐbù* 史部 (History division) in the Sìkù taxonomy. In Wilkinson's *Chinese History: A New Manual* it occupies §73.3 ("Catalogs of books & epigraphy"), and the *Sìkù quánshū* admits exactly 47 titles into the category — precisely the count of works collected in KR2n. The division splits into two internal *zhǔ* 屬 (sub-classes), reflected in the catalogue itself: the *jīngjí zhī shǔ* 經籍之屬 (catalogues of books, [KR2n0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0001)–[KR2n0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0011)) and the *jīnshí zhī shǔ* 金石之屬 (catalogues of inscriptions in bronze and stone, [KR2n0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0012)–[KR2n0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0047)). Both grew out of activities that flourished from the eleventh century onward: the systematic cataloguing of large book collections (imperial and private), and the antiquarian science of *jīnshí* 金石, born in the Northern Sòng with [歐陽修](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%AD%90%E9%99%BD%E4%BF%AE) (Ōuyáng Xiū) and made canonical by [趙明誠](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E6%98%8E%E8%AA%A0) (Zhào Míngchéng).

The book-catalogue strand within KR2n is the descendant of two earlier traditions discussed by Wilkinson at §73.2 — the *yìwén zhì* 藝文志 / *jīngjí zhì* 經籍志 chapters of the standard *Histories* (Wilkinson §73.3.1) — and the late-Liù-cháo / Suí *qìlù* 七錄-style classified catalogues. By the Sòng the Sìbù 四部 fourfold scheme (*jīngshǐzǐjí* 經史子集; Wilkinson §73.3.2) had become normative, and the imperial palace catalogues collected here (Wilkinson §73.3.4) and the great private *jiětí* 解題 catalogues of the Southern Sòng (Wilkinson §73.3.5) are the most important examples of its operation outside the standard Histories. The epigraphic strand begins with two Northern-Sòng pioneers (the *Jígǔ lù* and *Jīnshí lù*; Wilkinson §55.1, §73.3 introduction) and develops, through Yuán and Míng compilation, into the mature *jīnshí* scholarship of late-Míng and early-Qīng Sūzhōu, Wàn Sītóng's circle, and the *kǎozhèng* 考證 evidential current that culminates in [顧炎武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A1%A7%E7%82%8E%E6%AD%A6)'s three works on inscriptions and the stone classics.

### Important texts and text clusters

The 47 works fall into recognized clusters; entries are grouped accordingly.

**Sòng imperial and palace book catalogues.** [KR2n0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0001) *Chóngwén zǒngmù* 崇文總目 — the surviving fragment of the great Northern-Sòng imperial palace catalogue (originally 66 *juàn*, here 12), is the earliest catalogue of the imperial book collection of the period and the model for everything that follows.

**Sòng private *jiětí* catalogues.** Three Southern-Sòng works define the genre of the privately-compiled, annotated book catalogue:
- [KR2n0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0002) *Jùnzhāi dúshū zhì* 郡齋讀書志 by [晁公武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%81%E5%85%AC%E6%AD%A6) — the first major Chinese book catalogue to carry substantial *jiětí* 解題 notes on each title, with [趙希弁](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E5%B8%8C%E5%BC%81)'s continuation.
- [KR2n0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0003) *Suìchūtáng shūmù* 遂初堂書目 by [尤袤](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%B0%A4%E8%A2%A4) — a slim list, but the first to record multiple editions and printing locations as a routine feature.
- [KR2n0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0005) *Zhízhāi shūlù jiětí* 直齋書錄解題 by [陳振孫](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%8C%AF%E5%AD%AB) — the most ambitious annotated catalogue of the Southern Sòng, exhaustively cited by the Sìkù editors and the principal source for thousands of lost works.

**Sòng specialised bibliographies.** Two works treat one branch of literature in depth: [KR2n0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0004) *Zǐlüè* 子略 by [高似孫](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%AB%98%E4%BC%BC%E5%AD%AB) (the *zǐbù* / philosophical Masters) and [KR2n0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0006) *Hàn Yìwénzhì kǎozhèng* 漢藝文志考證 by [王應麟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%87%89%E9%BA%9F) (a critical commentary on the *Hànshū* 藝文志 — Wilkinson §73.2.1).

**Míng imperial and palace book catalogues.** [KR2n0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0007) *Wényuàngé shūmù* 文淵閣書目 by [楊士奇](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%A5%8A%E5%A3%AB%E5%A5%87) — the inventory of the early-Míng palace library at the Wényuàn Pavilion, and the chief source for what survived (and what was lost) of the Yuán-Míng book collections.

**Míng specialised bibliographies.** [KR2n0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0008) *Shòujīngtú yìlì* 授經圖義例 by [朱睦㮮](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E7%9D%A6%E3%AE%AE) — an unusual visual-genealogical catalogue diagramming the transmission of the Five Classics.

**Qīng palace book catalogues.** [KR2n0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0009) *Qīndìng Tiānlù línláng shūmù* 欽定天祿琳琅書目 — the imperially commissioned catalogue of the Qiánlóng emperor's collection of rare Sòng-Yuán-Míng imprints, compiled by [于敏中](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BA%8E%E6%95%8F%E4%B8%AD), [王際華](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E9%9A%9B%E8%8F%AF), and [梁國治](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%A2%81%E5%9C%8B%E6%B2%BB): the model imperial-collector catalogue of the eighteenth century.

**Qīng private bibliographies of earlier scholarship.** Two great early-Qīng works recover the bibliographic history of the preceding dynasties:
- [KR2n0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0010) *Qiānqǐngtáng shūmù* 千頃堂書目 by [黃虞稷](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%BB%83%E8%99%9E%E7%A8%B7) — the most complete bibliography of Míng publications, and the principal source for the *yìwén zhì* 藝文志 of the *Míngshǐ* 明史.
- [KR2n0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0011) *Jīngyì kǎo* 經義考 by [朱彝尊](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E5%BD%9D%E5%B0%8A) — an exhaustive bibliography (297 *juàn* surviving) of all classical-studies scholarship from antiquity through the seventeenth century, and the standard reference for the Classics-commentary tradition.

**Northern-Sòng founders of *jīnshí***. [KR2n0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0012) *Jígǔ lù* 集古錄 by [歐陽修](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%AD%90%E9%99%BD%E4%BF%AE) and [KR2n0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0013) *Jīnshí lù* 金石錄 by [趙明誠](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E6%98%8E%E8%AA%A0) (with [李清照](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E6%B8%85%E7%85%A7)) — the two foundational works that establish the rubbing-based, antiquarian study of inscriptions on bronze and stone as a discipline in its own right (Wilkinson §55.1).

**Sòng calligraphy-anthology scholarship.** A cluster centred on the famous *Chúnhuàgé tiè* 淳化閣帖 of 992 and its successors: [KR2n0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0014) *Fǎtiè kānwù* 法帖刋誤 by [黃伯思](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%BB%83%E4%BC%AF%E6%80%9D), [KR2n0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0015) *Fǎtiè shìwén* 法帖釋文 by [劉次莊](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E6%AC%A1%E8%8E%8A), [KR2n0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0019) *Jiàngtiè píng* 絳帖平 by [姜夔](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A7%9C%E5%A4%94), [KR2n0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0021) *Fǎtiè pǔxì* 法帖譜系 by [曹士冕](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%B9%E5%A3%AB%E5%86%95), plus the two *Lántíng* monographs [KR2n0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0022) *Lántíng kǎo* 蘭亭考 and [KR2n0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0023) *Lántíng xùkǎo* 蘭亭續考 — the principal Sòng efforts at textual and genealogical criticism of engraved calligraphy.

**Sòng *jīnshí* scholarship after the founders.** [KR2n0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0016) *Zhòushǐ* 籀史 by [翟耆年](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%BF%9F%E8%80%86%E5%B9%B4) (antique-script inscriptions), and the great Hàn-clerical-script project of [洪适](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B4%AA%E9%80%82) in two parts ([KR2n0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0017) *Lìshì* 隸釋 and [KR2n0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0018) *Lìxù* 隸續), which remained the standard reference for Hàn stelae until the Qīng. With them, [KR2n0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0020) *Shíkè pūxù* 石刻鋪敍 by [曾宏父](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%BE%E5%AE%8F%E7%88%B6), [KR2n0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0024) *Bǎokè cóngbiān* 寶刻叢編 by [陳思](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%80%9D), the geographical [KR2n0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0025) *Yúdì bēijì mù* 輿地碑記目 by [王象之](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E8%B1%A1%E4%B9%8B), and the anonymous [KR2n0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0026) *Bǎokè lèibiān* 寶刻類編.

**Yuán–Míng *jīnshí* and calligraphy.** [KR2n0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0027) *Gǔkè cóngchāo* 古刻叢鈔 by [陶宗儀](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B6%E5%AE%97%E5%84%80) preserves stone-inscription transcriptions otherwise lost. [KR2n0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0028) *Míngjì lù* 名蹟錄 by [朱珪](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E7%8F%AA) documents the famous early-Míng Sūzhōu collection. The Sūzhōu/Wú regional and antiquarian tradition continues in [KR2n0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0029) *Wúzhōng jīnshí xīnbiān* 吳中金石新編 by [陳暐](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%9A%90) and [KR2n0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0030) *Jīnxiè línláng* 金薤琳琅 by [都穆](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%83%BD%E7%A9%86). Late-Míng additions include [KR2n0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0031) *Fǎtiè shìwén kǎoyì* 法帖釋文考異 by [顧從義](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A1%A7%E5%BE%9E%E7%BE%A9), [KR2n0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0032) *Jīnshílín shídì kǎo* 金石林時地考 by [趙均](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E5%9D%87), [KR2n0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0033) *Shímò juānhuā* 石墨鐫華 by [趙崡](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E5%B4%A1), and [KR2n0034](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0034) *Jīnshí shǐ* 金石史 by [郭宗昌](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%83%AD%E5%AE%97%E6%98%8C).

**Qīng imperial calligraphy-anthology scholarship.** [KR2n0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0035) *Qīndìng chóngkè Chúnhuàgé tiè shìwén* 欽定重刻淳化閣帖釋文 — the imperially sponsored re-cutting and re-edition of the *Chúnhuàgé tiè* under Qiánlóng, supervised by [于敏中](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BA%8E%E6%95%8F%E4%B8%AD), [王際華](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E9%9A%9B%E8%8F%AF), and [裘日修](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A3%98%E6%97%A5%E4%BF%AE).

**Gù Yánwǔ's *jīnshí* trilogy.** [KR2n0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0036) *Qiúgǔ lù* 求古錄, [KR2n0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0037) *Jīnshí wénzì jì* 金石文字記, and [KR2n0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0038) *Shíjīng kǎo* 石經考 — three works by [顧炎武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A1%A7%E7%82%8E%E6%AD%A6) that decisively introduced *kǎozhèng* 考證 evidential method into the inscription disciplines. Together they fix the empirical, rubbing-comparing, autopsy-required practice that defines the early-Qīng tradition.

**Early-Qīng *jīnshí* after Gù Yánwǔ.** [KR2n0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0039) *Wànshì Shíjīng kǎo* 萬氏石經考 by [萬斯同](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%90%AC%E6%96%AF%E5%90%8C) (an immediate rival to Gù on the Stone Classics); regional and personal compilations [KR2n0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0040) *Láizhāi jīnshí kè kǎolüè* 來齋金石刻考略 by [林侗](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9E%97%E4%BE%97) and [KR2n0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0041) *Sōngyáng shíkè jíjì* 嵩陽石刻集記 by [葉封](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%91%89%E5%B0%81); the broad gazetteer-like [KR2n0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0042) *Jīnshí wén kǎolüè* 金石文考略 by [李光暎](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E5%85%89%E6%9A%8E); and the clerical-script paleography of [KR2n0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0043) *Fēnlì ǒucún* 分隸偶存 by [萬經](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%90%AC%E7%B6%93).

**Wáng Shù and the eighteenth-century calligraphic-textual-criticism school.** [KR2n0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0044) *Chúnhuà mìgé fǎtiè kǎozhèng* 淳化祕閣法帖考正 and [KR2n0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0045) *Zhúyún tíbá* 竹雲題跋 by [王澍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%BE%8D) together set the standard for *kǎozhèng* applied to engraved calligraphic anthologies in the high Qing.

**Mid-Qīng inscription connoisseurship and the Stone Classics revisited.** [KR2n0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0046) *Jīnshí jīngyǎn lù* 金石經眼錄 — diagrams by [褚峻](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A4%9A%E5%B3%BB) with supplementary explanations by [牛運震](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%89%9B%E9%81%8B%E9%9C%87) — and [KR2n0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0047) *Shíjīng kǎoyì* 石經考異 by [杭世駿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%AD%E4%B8%96%E9%A7%BF) (a critical follow-up to both Gù and Wàn on the Stone Classics) close out the division.

### Important persons

- [歐陽修](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%AD%90%E9%99%BD%E4%BF%AE) (Ōuyáng Xiū, 1007–1072) — co-compiler of the *Chóngwén zǒngmù* and author of the *Jígǔ lù*; presides over both founding moments of the division (book-catalogue and *jīnshí*).
- [王應麟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%87%89%E9%BA%9F) (Wáng Yīnglín, 1223–1296) — author of the *Hàn Yìwénzhì kǎozhèng*; the great Southern-Sòng critic of the bibliographic tradition.
- [晁公武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%99%81%E5%85%AC%E6%AD%A6) (Cháo Gōngwǔ, ca. 1105–1180) — author of the first major Chinese annotated private book catalogue, the *Jùnzhāi dúshū zhì*.
- [陳振孫](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%8C%AF%E5%AD%AB) (Chén Zhènsūn, ca. 1183 – after 1249) — author of the *Zhízhāi shūlù jiětí*, the most ambitious private book catalogue of the Southern Sòng.
- [尤袤](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%B0%A4%E8%A2%A4) (Yóu Mào, 1127–1194) — author of the *Suìchūtáng shūmù*, the first private catalogue to track editions.
- [楊士奇](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%A5%8A%E5%A3%AB%E5%A5%87) (Yáng Shìqí, 1365–1444) — chief compiler of the *Wényuàngé shūmù*, the inventory of the early-Míng palace library.
- [黃虞稷](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%BB%83%E8%99%9E%E7%A8%B7) (Huáng Yújī, 1629–1691) — author of the *Qiānqǐngtáng shūmù*, the principal bibliography of Míng publishing.
- [朱彝尊](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E5%BD%9D%E5%B0%8A) (Zhū Yízūn, 1629–1709) — author of the *Jīngyì kǎo*, the most extensive bibliography of classical-studies scholarship ever compiled.
- [趙明誠](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E6%98%8E%E8%AA%A0) (Zhào Míngchéng, 1081–1129) and [李清照](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E6%B8%85%E7%85%A7) (Lǐ Qīngzhào, 1084–ca. 1155) — joint compilers of the *Jīnshí lù*, the defining early *jīnshí* monograph.
- [洪适](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B4%AA%E9%80%82) (Hóng Kuò, 1117–1184) — author of the *Lìshì* and *Lìxù*, the canonical Sòng treatments of Hàn clerical-script stelae.
- [姜夔](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%A7%9C%E5%A4%94) (Jiāng Kuí, ca. 1155–1221) and [黃伯思](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%BB%83%E4%BC%AF%E6%80%9D) (Huáng Bósī, 1079–1118) — leading Sòng critics of the *Chúnhuàgé tiè* calligraphic anthology.
- [陶宗儀](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B6%E5%AE%97%E5%84%80) (Táo Zōngyí, ca. 1329–ca. 1409) — Yuán-Míng transition figure whose *Gǔkè cóngchāo* preserves otherwise-lost inscriptions.
- [顧炎武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A1%A7%E7%82%8E%E6%AD%A6) (Gù Yánwǔ, 1613–1682) — author of three of the most important early-Qīng *jīnshí* works (*Qiúgǔ lù*, *Jīnshí wénzì jì*, *Shíjīng kǎo*); decisive in introducing *kǎozhèng* method into the discipline.
- [萬斯同](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%90%AC%E6%96%AF%E5%90%8C) (Wàn Sītóng, 1638–1702) — author of the rival *Wànshì Shíjīng kǎo*; a major figure of the Zhèjiāng historical school.
- [王澍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%BE%8D) (Wáng Shù, 1668–1743) — leading high-Qīng calligrapher-philologist; author of two works in this division (*Chúnhuà mìgé fǎtiè kǎozhèng* and *Zhúyún tíbá*).
- [于敏中](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BA%8E%E6%95%8F%E4%B8%AD) (Yú Mǐnzhōng, 1714–1779) and [王際華](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E9%9A%9B%E8%8F%AF) (Wáng Jìhuá, 1717–1776) — repeat imperial-commission editors who appear at the head of both the *Tiānlù línláng shūmù* and the re-cut *Chúnhuàgé tiè* — the institutional spine of Qiánlóng-era palace cataloguing.
- [杭世駿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%AD%E4%B8%96%E9%A7%BF) (Háng Shìjùn, 1696–1773) — author of the *Shíjīng kǎoyì*, summing up early-Qīng scholarship on the Stone Classics.

### Topics

- **The architecture of the Sìbù (四部 *jīngshǐzǐjí*) scheme** and the recurring negotiation, visible across these catalogues, of how to classify works that straddle its boundaries (Wilkinson §73.3.2).
- ***Jiětí* 解題 / *tíyào* 提要 annotation** — the development, from the Sòng onward, of the descriptive catalogue note as a tool of textual criticism: who wrote it, when, in how many *juǎn*, in what editions, with what defects. The high point in this division is [KR2n0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0005) *Zhízhāi shūlù jiětí*, prefiguring the Sìkù *tíyào* themselves.
- **Imperial vs. private cataloguing.** Imperial catalogues (Chóngwén, Wényuàngé, Tiānlù línláng; Wilkinson §73.3.4) record holdings; private catalogues (Jùnzhāi, Suìchūtáng, Zhízhāi, Qiānqǐngtáng; Wilkinson §73.3.5) record judgements. The complementarity is constant throughout the division.
- **Loss and recovery.** A great many works in KR2n exist only because they cite, in passing, books whose texts are otherwise lost. The category therefore functions as a meta-archive: [KR2n0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0006) *Hàn Yìwénzhì kǎozhèng* recovers the *yìwén zhì* of the *Hànshū*; [KR2n0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0010) *Qiānqǐngtáng shūmù* recovers Míng publishing; [KR2n0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0011) *Jīngyì kǎo* recovers the entire classical-commentary tradition.
- **The birth of *jīnshí***. The systematic, rubbing-based study of inscriptions on bronze and stone is a Northern-Sòng invention (Wilkinson §55.1, §73.3 introduction); [KR2n0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0012) *Jígǔ lù* and [KR2n0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0013) *Jīnshí lù* are the foundational documents.
- **Calligraphic anthologies (*fǎtiè* 法帖) as a textual problem.** The repeated re-cutting of the *Chúnhuàgé tiè* (992) and its rivals produced a critical literature concerned with attribution, ordering, and the corruption of individual characters across recensions: [KR2n0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0014), [KR2n0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0015), [KR2n0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0019), [KR2n0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0021), [KR2n0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0031), [KR2n0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0035), [KR2n0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0044), [KR2n0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0045).
- **The *Lántíng* problem.** The reception-history of the *Lántíng xù* 蘭亭序 by Wáng Xīzhī 王羲之 became a self-contained scholarly genre, represented here by [KR2n0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0022) and [KR2n0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0023).
- **Stone Classics scholarship.** The successive cuttings of the Confucian Classics in stone (Xī-Píng, Zhèng-Shǐ, Kāichéng, etc.) produced a tightly-connected sub-literature: [KR2n0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0038), [KR2n0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0039), [KR2n0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0047).
- **Regionalism.** Several Míng–Qīng catalogues are explicitly local: Sūzhōu ([KR2n0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0029), [KR2n0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0030)), Mount Sōng ([KR2n0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2n/KR2n0041)). They prefigure the Qīng *jīnshí zhì* 金石志 chapters of provincial gazetteers.
- ***Kǎozhèng* applied to inscriptions.** The decisive shift from connoisseurial appreciation to philological evidential argument, traceable from [顧炎武](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%A1%A7%E7%82%8E%E6%AD%A6) through [萬斯同](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%90%AC%E6%96%AF%E5%90%8C), [王澍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%BE%8D), and [杭世駿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%AD%E4%B8%96%E9%A7%BF).

# 史評類 (KR2o)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR2o 史評類 *Shǐpíng lèi* — Histories — Historical Criticism](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

The *Shǐpíng* 史評 (literally "appreciation/evaluation of historical writing") category sits at the end of the History branch (*Shǐbù* 史部) of the *Sìkù quánshū* classification, where it gathers two distinct but adjacent kinds of work: critical assessments of past events (lessons drawn from a particular dynasty or episode in the form of a "mirror," *jiàn* 鑑) and critical assessments of historical writing itself — what a modern reader would call historiography. As Wilkinson notes (Wilkinson, *Chinese History: A New Manual*, § 46.6.4), the category as a catalog rubric was introduced in the twelfth century by Cháo Gōngwǔ 晁公武 (ca. 1105–80) in his *Jùnzhāi dúshū zhì* 郡齋讀書志 and retained ever after in the *Sìkù* and in the *Shūmù dáwèn* 書目答問. The unifying thread is that none of these works is itself a *history* in the annalistic, annals-biography, or topical forms collected in `KR2a` 正史類 through `KR2n` 史鈔類; rather, every work here stands at one remove from the historical record and judges it.

Chronologically `KR2o` spans almost twelve hundred years, from the foundational *Shǐtōng* 史通 of [劉知幾](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E7%9F%A5%E5%B9%BE) (Liú Zhījǐ, 661–721, completed 710 / extended posthumously 722) to the *Wénshǐ tōngyì* 文史通義 of [章學誠](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%A0%E5%AD%B8%E8%AA%A0) (Zhāng Xuéchéng, 1738–1801). Between these two methodological landmarks the bulk of the division consists of Sòng and Yuán "lessons-from-the-past" works built around the *Zīzhì tōngjiàn* 資治通鑑 ([KR2b0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2b/KR2b0010)) and Zhū Xī's *Gāngmù* 綱目 reduction of it. As Wilkinson observes (§ 48.5), it was the *Gāngmù* — not the *Zīzhì tōngjiàn* itself and certainly not the *Twenty-Four Histories* — that most educated people from the Sòng through the Qīng actually read; the works in `KR2o` are the upstream and downstream sediment of that fact. The Qīng additions to the category are dominated by imperial historiography: the Kāngxī emperor's *yùpī* 御批 (imperial top-of-page comments) appended to Zhū Xī's *Gāngmù* and its continuations, and the Qiánlóng emperor's own selected comments and didactic mirrors. Historical criticism, in other words, in late-imperial form became another vehicle for sovereign self-articulation.

### Important texts and text clusters

The division's twenty-five works fall into recognisable clusters.

**Foundational treatises on the writing of history.** [KR2o0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0001) *Shǐtōng* 史通 (*Comprehensive Treatise on Historiography*) of [劉知幾](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E7%9F%A5%E5%B9%BE) is the first sustained Chinese theory of historical writing, the work in which the analytical pairs Six Schools (*Liù jiā* 六家) and Two Forms (*Èr tǐ* 二體, i.e. *biānnián* 編年 vs. *jìzhuàn* 紀傳) were articulated and in which the demand for *zhí bǐ* 直筆 (straight-brushed recording, free of moral or political interference) was first programmatically defended. [KR2o0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0002) *Shǐtōng tōngshì* 史通通釋 (1750) by [浦起龍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B5%A6%E8%B5%B7%E9%BE%8D) (Pǔ Qǐlóng, 1679–c. 1762) is the standard annotated edition that has framed every subsequent reading of the *Shǐtōng*. [KR2o0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0025) *Wénshǐ tōngyì* 文史通義 of [章學誠](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%A0%E5%AD%B8%E8%AA%A0) (drafts 1771–96, posthumous editing to 1832) is the second great Chinese theoretical work on history, organised around the principle *liù jīng jiē shǐ yě* 六經皆史也 ("the Six Classics are all history"), and is conventionally paired with the *Shǐtōng* as the two poles of pre-modern Chinese historiography (Wilkinson § 46.6.4.1–2).

**Sòng "mirror" works on individual dynasties.** [KR2o0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0003) *Tángjiàn* 唐鑑 (1086) of [范祖禹](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8C%83%E7%A5%96%E7%A6%B9) (Fàn Zǔyǔ, 1041–98) — a participant in the *Zīzhì tōngjiàn* project — is the model exemplar of the genre, drawing systematic lessons from the Táng for the present court; it was the work Sīmǎ Guāng singled out as his deputy's masterpiece. [KR2o0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0004) *Tángshǐ lùnduàn* 唐史論斷 of [孫甫](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AD%AB%E7%94%AB) (Sūn Fǔ, 998–1057) is the earlier and more polemical equivalent; [KR2o0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0010) *Liùcháo tōngjiàn bóyì* 六朝通鑑博議 of [李燾](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E7%87%BE) (Lǐ Tāo, 1115–84) extends the same exercise to the period of disunion; [KR2o0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0007) *Sānguó záshì* 三國雜事 of [唐庚](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%94%90%E5%BA%9A) (Táng Gēng, 1071–1121) does the same for the Three Kingdoms; [KR2o0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0012) *Liǎng Hàn bǐjì* 兩漢筆記 of [錢時](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%8C%A2%E6%99%82) (Qián Shí, fl. 1230s) for the two Hàn. [KR2o0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0011) *Sòng dàshìjì jiǎngyì* 宋大事記講義 of [呂中](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%91%82%E4%B8%AD) (Lǚ Zhōng, fl. 1247–52) is the rare contemporaneous self-mirror — a Southern Sòng critique of the Sòng's own history, in *jiǎngyì* 講義 (lecture) form for imperial instruction.

**Works centred on the *Zīzhì tōngjiàn*.** [KR2o0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0005) *Tángshū zhíbǐ* 唐書直筆 of [呂夏卿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%91%82%E5%A4%8F%E5%8D%BF) (Lǚ Xiàqīng, 1015–70), although nominally a working notebook for the *Xīn Tángshū* drafting, became canonised as a critical-historical text. [KR2o0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0006) *Tōngjiàn wènyí* 通鑑問疑 of [劉羲仲](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E7%BE%B2%E4%BB%B2) (Liú Xīzhòng, son of Liú Shù 劉恕) preserves the questions Liú put to Sīmǎ Guāng during the *Tōngjiàn*'s compilation and Sīmǎ's replies — a unique window into the workshop. [KR2o0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0014) *Tōngjiàn dáwèn* 通鑑答問 of [王應麟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E6%87%89%E9%BA%9F) (Wáng Yīnglín, 1223–96) is the late-Sòng pedagogical companion that codifies the questions a serious reader of the *Tōngjiàn* must be able to answer.

**Sòng evidential-corrective notes.** [KR2o0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0013) *Jiùwén zhèngwù* 舊聞證誤 of [李心傳](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E5%BF%83%E5%82%B3) (Lǐ Xīnchuán, 1167–1244), the historian of the Southern Sòng restoration, applies evidential method to received Sòng anecdote and is singled out by Wilkinson (§ 46.6.4) alongside [洪邁](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B4%AA%E9%82%81)'s *Róngzhāi suíbǐ* 容齋隨筆 (in `KR3l`) as one of the great pre-Liú Zhījǐ Sòng contributions to historical criticism. [KR2o0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0009) *Shèshǐ suíbǐ* 涉史隨筆 of [葛洪](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%91%9B%E6%B4%AA) (Gě Hóng, jìnshì 1184, not to be confused with the Jìn-dynasty Daoist) is the looser, more belletristic *suíbǐ* cousin.

**The *jīngyán* 經筵 lecture genre as historical criticism.** [KR2o0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0008) *Jīngwò guǎnjiàn* 經幄管見 of [曹彥約](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%B9%E5%BD%A5%E7%B4%84) (Cáo Yànyuē, 1157–1228) preserves an imperial-lecturer's running commentary on history; alongside [KR2o0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0011) it documents how, by the late Southern Sòng, historical criticism had become a tool of *jīngyán* pedagogy at the court.

**Compilations of historical judgments.** [KR2o0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0015) *Lìdài míngxián quèlùn* 歷代名賢確論, an anonymous Sòng compilation of one hundred *juǎn*, gathers the considered judgments (*quèlùn* 確論) on past worthies from earlier writers and is the largest reference work of historical opinion in the division.

**Yuán synthetic-outline criticism.** [KR2o0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0016) *Lìdài tōnglüè* 歷代通略 of [陳櫟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%AB%9F) (Chén Lì, 1252–1334) and [KR2o0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0017) *Shíqī shǐ zuǎn gǔjīn tōngyào* 十七史纂古今通要 of [胡一桂](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%83%A1%E4%B8%80%E6%A1%82) (Hú Yīguì, fl. early 14th c.) abridge and judge the *Seventeen Histories* in a single critical synthesis — the Yuán face of the Sòng's *Gāngmù* impulse, oriented to private tutors and provincial examination candidates.

**Míng historical criticism.** [KR2o0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0018) *Xuéshǐ* 學史 of [邵寶](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%82%B5%E5%AF%B6) (Shào Bǎo, 1460–1527) is a methodical Míng student's handbook on how to read the *Histories*; [KR2o0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0019) *Shǐjiū* 史糾 of [朱明鎬](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E6%98%8E%E9%8E%AC) (Zhū Mínghào, 1607–52) is the late-Míng evidential-corrective work in the line of Lǐ Xīnchuán.

**The imperially-annotated *Gāngmù* cluster.** [KR2o0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0020) *Yùpī Zīzhì tōngjiàn gāngmù* 御批資治通鑑綱目 collects Zhū Xī's 1172 outline-history of pre-Sòng times with over one hundred *yùpī* added by the Kāngxī emperor (printed 1708); [KR2o0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0021) *Yùpī Zīzhì tōngjiàn gāngmù qián biān* 御批資治通鑑綱目前編 attaches the same imperial *yùpī* apparatus to [金履祥](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%87%91%E5%B1%A5%E7%A5%A5)'s 1273 pre-Yáo extension of the *Gāngmù*; [KR2o0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0022) *Yùpī Xù Zīzhì tōngjiàn gāngmù* 御批續資治通鑑綱目 does the same for [商輅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%95%86%E8%BC%85) (Shāng Lù, 1414–86) and his collaborators' Sòng-Yuán continuation. Together these three works are the embodiment of the *Gāngmù* tradition as it stood at the high tide of Qīng imperial appropriation. Wilkinson (§ 48.5–8) treats them as the principal vehicle by which historical knowledge actually reached the late-imperial reading public.

**The Qiánlóng emperor's own historical criticism.** [KR2o0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0023) *Píngjiàn chǎnyào* 評鑑闡要 (1768–71) is the 798 *yùpī* the Qiánlóng emperor selected from his own commentary on the *Yùpī lìdài tōngjiàn jílǎn* 御批歷代通鑑輯覽 (1767) and reissued separately as a free-standing historical criticism. [KR2o0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0024) *Qīndìng gǔjīn chǔ'èr jīnjiàn* 欽定古今儲貳金鑑 (1783) is the same emperor's didactic mirror specifically on crown-prince succession — a topic of acute personal interest in the wake of his 1735–73 succession crises.

### Important persons

- [劉知幾](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E7%9F%A5%E5%B9%BE) — author of the *Shǐtōng*; the Táng historian whose career inside the *Shǐguǎn* 史館 produced the first Chinese theoretical work on history-writing and the analytical vocabulary used in the division thereafter.
- [浦起龍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%B5%A6%E8%B5%B7%E9%BE%8D) — eighteenth-century editor whose annotated *Shǐtōng tōngshì* (1750) made the *Shǐtōng* readable for late-imperial scholars and remains the basis of every modern edition.
- [范祖禹](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8C%83%E7%A5%96%E7%A6%B9) — Sòng historian, deputy on the *Tōngjiàn* project, author of the model "mirror" treatise *Tángjiàn*; the figure who set the template for the dynasty-by-dynasty critical mirror.
- [朱熹](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E7%86%B9) — through the *Zīzhì tōngjiàn gāngmù*, the historian who reshaped the popular reception of all Chinese history and supplied the doctrine of *zhèngtǒng* 正統 that organises every later Gāngmù-style work in the division.
- [金履祥](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%87%91%E5%B1%A5%E7%A5%A5) — Yuán historian-philosopher and Zhū Xī school transmitter whose *Tōngjiàn qián biān* extends the *Gāngmù* back before 403 BCE.

### Topics

- *Zhí bǐ* 直筆 — the historian's duty of straight recording, free of patron pressure or moral euphemism. Liú Zhījǐ's foundational demand; reaffirmed in modified form by Zhāng Xuéchéng under the heading *shǐdé* 史德 (the historian's virtue) and contested across the *Gāngmù* tradition's praise-and-blame practice.
- *Zhèngtǒng* 正統 — legitimate dynastic succession. Sīmǎ Guāng accepted Wèi as the Three Kingdoms successor; Zhū Xī overturned this in favour of Shǔ-Hàn, and the resulting *Gāngmù* doctrine governs every imperially-annotated work in the cluster. Wilkinson treats the topic at length (§ A.2.1–6).
- The Two Forms — *biānnián* 編年 (annalistic) versus *jìzhuàn* 紀傳 (composite annals-biography). Liú Zhījǐ's pair; Zhāng Xuéchéng's diagnosis of the *jìzhuàn* form's exhaustion is the late-imperial reopening of the same question.
- *Liù jīng jiē shǐ* 六經皆史 — the Classics-as-history thesis. The organising claim of the *Wénshǐ tōngyì*; antecedents in Wáng Yángmíng and Lǐ Zhì. In `KR2o` the thesis is what allows historical criticism to absorb classical hermeneutics and step out of its category.
- The *Gāngmù* 綱目 form — the *gāng* / *mù* (outline / detail) layout that Zhū Xī adapted from administrative documents and that became, by the late Míng, the default vehicle in which historical narrative was read. The whole imperial cluster [KR2o0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0020)–[KR2o0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0022) is `KR2o`'s record of the form.
- *Yùpī* 御批 — imperial top-of-page comments on a historical work. Practised at scale by the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng emperors, the *yùpī* turns historical criticism from a scholar's genre into a sovereign's.
- *Jīngyán* 經筵 historical lecture as a critical genre — the imperial-classroom lecture (*jiǎngyì* 講義) becoming a published work of historical criticism. Exemplified by [KR2o0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0008) and [KR2o0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2o/KR2o0011).
- Evidential method (*kǎojù* 考據) on received historical anecdote — Lǐ Xīnchuán's *Jiùwén zhèngwù* model, extended in the Míng by Zhū Mínghào's *Shǐjiū*.
- *Fāngzhì* 方志 as serious historical writing — a programmatic claim original to Zhāng Xuéchéng and the doctrinal underpinning of all later Chinese local historiography.

# 史部其他 (KR2p)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR2p 出土文獻 *Chūtǔ wénxiàn* — Histories — Excavated Manuscripts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

`KR2p` 出土文獻 (*Chūtǔ wénxiàn*, "Excavated Documents") is a Kanripo extension category that sits formally under `KR2` 史部 (Histories) but in practice lies outside the traditional Sìkù taxonomy: the Sìkù subdivisions of 史部 stop at `KR2o` 史評類 and have no place for texts recovered by archaeology in the 20th and 21st centuries. The works collected here are pre-imperial or early-imperial manuscripts retrieved from tombs — silk rolls and bamboo strips of the late Wǎrring States (late 4th c. BCE) and early Western Hàn (sealed 168 BCE) — and they are heterogeneous in genre: a Mǎwángduī 馬王堆 bedchamber-arts silk text alongside two Guōdiàn 郭店 Confucian philosophical bamboo manuscripts. They are filed under 史部 because, from a transmission-history point of view, they are primarily *documents* (sources for the intellectual and material history of the period) rather than works of any one of the Four Categories — none of the three is part of the received canon, none has a continuous transmission history, and each survives in exactly one physical witness.

The relevant scholarly tradition is therefore not classical exegesis but modern Chinese palaeography and the philosophy-of-history reading of excavated texts. Wilkinson, *Chinese History: A New Manual*, treats this corpus in §59.7 (Excavated Documents — bamboo and silk manuscripts) and in the bibliographic chapters surrounding it (the *Lǎozǐ* Guōdiàn finds at §6 of the excavated-texts bibliography, the Mǎwángduī medical and philosophical caches in the Hàn manuscript sections); the field has its own *editiones principes* (the 1985 Wénwù chūbǎnshè reconstruction of the Mǎwángduī silks; the 1998 Wénwù *Guōdiàn Chǔmù zhújiǎn* volume), its own running critical apparatus (Liú Zhāo's 《郭店楚簡校釋》, Lǐ Líng's *Jiào dú jì*, Qiú Xīguī's 2014 *Chángshā Mǎwángduī Hànmù jiǎnbó jíchéng*), and its own meta-debates about strip ordering, modern editorial titles, and the relationship of the manuscripts to the transmitted canon. A reader approaching `KR2p` must therefore keep in mind that the *titles* under which these works appear are modern editorial assignments (from the opening graphs of the first strip, or by analogy with a transmitted text of the same name), and that the *texts* themselves are reconstructed from physically broken manuscripts whose strip order is, in places, still contested.

### Important texts and text clusters

The division currently holds three texts. They divide into two physical-archaeological clusters:

**Mǎwángduī 馬王堆 silk-manuscript cluster (Hàn tomb M3, sealed 168 BCE).** From the medical-technical silk cache, one text is at present catalogued in `KR2p`:

- *Hé yīnyáng* 合陰陽 [KR2p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0015) — short anonymous treatise on heterosexual technique within an early-Hàn medical-cosmological framework; the locus classicus for the "Ten Movements / Ten Postures / Eight Movements" catalogue of *fángzhōng* 房中 practice and for the ejaculation-restraint scheme later reused in the *Sùnǚ jīng* tradition.

**Guōdiàn 郭店 bamboo-manuscript cluster (Chǔ tomb 1, Jǐngmén, sealed c. 300 BCE).** From the Guōdiàn Confucian-text group, two texts are catalogued here:

- *Wǔxíng* 五行 [KR2p0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0021) — short Confucian treatise defining *rényìlǐzhìshèng* 仁義禮智聖 as inner virtues "formed within" (*xíng yú nèi* 形於內), structured around *shèn dú* 慎獨; the principal physical evidence for Páng Pú's identification of the so-called Sī-Mèng 思孟 school attacked in *Xúnzǐ* 荀子 *Fēi shí'èr zǐ* 非十二子, and the earliest witness of a *Wǔxíng* text whose Mǎwángduī counterpart adds a *shuō* 說 commentary layer.
- *Chéng zhī wén zhī* 成之聞之 [KR2p0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0024) — short Confucian discourse on rulership by personal exemplification (*shēn* 身), arguing that *jūnzǐ* governance requires *qiú zhū jǐ* 求諸己; thematically adjacent to *Lǐjì* 禮記 *Zī yī* 緇衣 and *Dàxué* 大學, and central to the Guōdiàn editorial debate over strip division (Lǐ Líng's redivision under the title 教 *Jiào* + 天常 *Tiān cháng*).

A natural further cluster — the Mǎwángduī companion *fángzhōng* texts (e.g. *Tiānxià zhìdào tán* 天下至道談, *Shíwèn* 十問) cited in [KR2p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0015)'s Abstract, and the wider Guōdiàn Confucian set (*Zī yī*, *Liù dé*, *Xìng zì mìng chū*, *Zūn dé yì*, *Tángyú zhī dào*) cited in [KR2p0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0024)'s Abstract — is at present only partially represented in the division. As further excavated texts are added to the Kanripo corpus, the cluster structure of `KR2p` will deepen along the lines laid out in these two abstracts.

### Important persons

All three works in the division are **anonymous excavated manuscripts** without attributable authors, and consequently their per-text frontmatter `persons:` lists are empty. The persons whose work has shaped this division are therefore modern: the *Mǎwángduī Hànmù bóshū zhěnglǐ xiǎozǔ* 馬王堆漢墓帛書整理小組 (the original collation team), the Jīngmén Municipal Museum 荊門市博物館 (Guōdiàn *editio princeps* team), and individual scholars — Páng Pú 龐樸 (Sī-Mèng-school identification of *Wǔxíng*), Lǐ Líng 李零 (palaeographic redivisions of the Guōdiàn Confucian cluster and of *Chéng zhī wén zhī*), Qiú Xīguī 裘錫圭 (lead editor of both the 1998 Guōdiàn volume's annotations and the 2014 *Chángshā Mǎwángduī Hànmù jiǎnbó jíchéng*), Liú Zhāo 劉釗 (current standard Chinese critical apparatus), and Donald Harper (standard English critical edition of the Mǎwángduī medical silks). These figures are named in the Abstracts of the individual texts ([KR2p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0015), [KR2p0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0021), [KR2p0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0024)); they are not catalogued as authors and have no Person notes in `kb/Persons/`.

### Topics

Three intertwined topics run through the division.

**Excavation, reconstruction, and editorial title.** Every text in `KR2p` is a physical artefact — broken silk, scattered bamboo strips — whose modern *form* (numbered sections, running order, even title) is an editorial reconstruction. *Hé yīnyáng* is named from its opening *fán jiāng hé yīnyáng zhī fāng* 凡將合陰陽之方; *Chéng zhī wén zhī* takes its title from the opening words of what is itself a contested strip-ordering; *Wǔxíng* alone has a title attested in the transmitted record (in *Xúnzǐ* *Fēi shí'èr zǐ*). Any use of these texts must therefore engage with the editorial apparatus, not just the words on the strip.

**Pre-Qín / early-Hàn Confucian moral psychology.** The two Guōdiàn texts ([KR2p0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0021), [KR2p0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0024)) supply the missing-link evidence between the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ* on the inner-versus-outer reading of virtue. *Wǔxíng*'s interiority criterion (*xíng yú nèi* / *xíng yú wài*) and *Chéng zhī wén zhī*'s *qiú zhū jǐ* programme have together reshaped the post-1993 scholarly account of how 仁-義-禮-智-聖 and the doctrine of *shèn dú* 慎獨 developed before being codified in the *Zhōngyōng* and *Dàxué*.

**Early Chinese medical and *yǎngshēng* technique.** Distinct from but contemporary with the Confucian moralisation of virtue, the Mǎwángduī medical silks ([KR2p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0015) and its M3 companions) show a parallel pre-religious idiom of bodily regulation: intercourse as controlled exchange of *qì*, ejaculation timing as a longevity technique, the Huáng Lǎo "live as long as Heaven and Earth" closing formula. The division as it currently stands therefore juxtaposes the two great strands of late-Wǎrring-States / early-Hàn elite self-cultivation — Confucian moral training and *fángzhōng* / *yǎngshēng* technical training — as physically contemporary documents.

A fourth running issue — the **status of the Sī-Mèng 思孟 school** and the long Qīng-era dispute over what *wǔxíng* meant in *Xúnzǐ Fēi shí'èr zǐ* — is decisively addressed by the Guōdiàn evidence in [KR2p0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0021) and remains the single most-cited contribution of this corpus to Confucian intellectual history.

### Timeline

- c. 350–300 BCE — *Wǔxíng* 五行 [KR2p0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0021) — earliest witness of the text; physical strips from a tomb sealed c. 300 BCE, composition placed in the second half of the 4th c. BCE.
- c. 350–300 BCE — *Chéng zhī wén zhī* 成之聞之 [KR2p0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0024) — same Guōdiàn cache; pre-Mèngzǐ Confucian discourse on rulership by self-cultivation.
- c. 300 BCE – 168 BCE — *Hé yīnyáng* 合陰陽 [KR2p0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2p/KR2p0015) — Mǎwángduī silk roll, sealed in M3 in 168 BCE; on palaeographic grounds composed late Wǎrring States to very early Western Hàn; here placed at the date of the received silk recension consistent with the project's dating policy.
