# 儒家類 (KR3a)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3a 儒家類 *Rújiā lèi* — Masters — Confucian Writers](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3a sits at the head of the *Sìkù* Masters Branch (子部) and gathers the works that the Qīng editors classed as *Rújiā* 儒家 — Confucian thinkers and statecraft writers whose books do not belong to the canonical *jīng* corpus in `KR1`. Following Wilkinson (§73.2.2; cf. *Box 284* and §28.7.3), the *Rújiā* category is the oldest of the fourfold *zǐbù* divisions, traceable to the *Hànshū yìwén zhì* "Confucian writers" rubric (53 titles) and re-anchored under the *Sìkù* as the leading subdivision of the Masters Branch on the strength of its post-Sòng *Lǐxué* expansion. The works collected here therefore form a single, continuous tradition reaching from the late Warring States *zǐ*-books that survived the early imperial canon-formation (only *Xúnzǐ* [KR3a0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0002) is pre-Hàn) through Hàn ministerial writings, Wèi-Jìn *zhūzǐ*, Suí-Táng *jiāxùn* / imperial-instructional works, and — overwhelmingly — the Sòng-Yuán-Míng-Qīng *Lǐxué* corpus that became the orthodoxy of late-imperial scholarship and education.

The chronological span runs from c. 280 BCE (the working life of Xún Kuàng) to the mid-eighteenth century (the Qiánlóng-era imperial readings, e.g. *Rì zhī huì shuō* [KR3a0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0104), and Lǐ Guāngdì's *Róngcūn yǔlù* [KR3a0114](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0114)). The principal transmissional traditions a reader must keep in mind are three: (1) the textual reconstruction of pre-Tāng *zǐ*-books from quotation-fragments in *lèishū* and commentary, of which `[KR3a0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0119)`–`[KR3a0158](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0158)` are *jíyì* reconstructions from CHANT 漢籍電子文獻; (2) the editorial canon-formation of Northern Sòng *daoxué* in Zhū Xī's editorial workshop (the *Yíshū* / *Wàishū* / *Cuìyán* of the Chéng brothers, the *Jìnsī lù* with Lǚ Zǔqiān, and the posthumous *Zhūzǐ yǔlèi*) — see Wilkinson §28.7.3; and (3) the late-imperial *Yǎnyì* tradition of *Dàxué*-based imperial pedagogy launched by Zhēn Déxiù (*Dàxué yǎnyì* [KR3a0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0058)) and continued by Qiū Jùn, the Yǒnglè court, and the Kāng-Qián throne. The Sòng-Yuán-Míng *xué'àn* genre noted by Wilkinson (§28.7.3, Box 162) — Huáng Zōngxī's *Sòng-Yuán xué'àn* and *Míngrú xué'àn* — provides the standard biographical-doctrinal map across most of the persons gathered here.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The Hàn–Wèi *zǐ*-books.** The pre-Sòng layer is dominated by the *Xúnzǐ* [KR3a0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0002) — the only Warring-States survival, in Yáng Liàng's 818 recension — together with the Hàn ministerial writings: *Xīnyǔ* [KR3a0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0004) (Lù Jiǎ, on the lessons of Qín's collapse), *Xīnshū* [KR3a0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0005) (Jiǎ Yì), *Yántiě lùn* [KR3a0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0006) (Huán Kuān's record of the 81 BCE court debate on the salt-and-iron monopolies), *Shuōyuàn* [KR3a0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0007) and *Xīnxù* [KR3a0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0008) (Liú Xiàng's didactic anthologies), *Yángzǐ Fǎ yán* [KR3a0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0009) (Yáng Xióng's *Lúnyǔ*-modelled re-canonisation), *Qiánfū lùn* [KR3a0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0010) (Wáng Fú's late-Hàn statecraft), *Shēn jiàn* [KR3a0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0011) (Xún Yuè), and *Zhōng lùn* [KR3a0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0012) (Xú Gàn). The *Kǒngzǐ jiāyǔ* [KR3a0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0001) is the most disputed work of the entire division — almost certainly Wáng Sù's mid-third-century reconstruction, designed to provide canonical ammunition against Zhèng Xuán, though revisionist scholarship since the 1980s has recovered authentic pre-Wèi strata. *Kǒng cóngzǐ* [KR3a0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0003) is the comparable pseudepigraphic problem from the Hàn-Wèi transition.

**The Suí–Táng transitional cluster.** *Fùzǐ* [KR3a0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0013) (Fù Xuán, Jìn), *Zhōng shuō* [KR3a0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0014) (Wáng Tōng's posthumously compiled Suí-Táng dialogues modelled on the *Lúnyǔ*), and the Táng-period *Dì fàn* [KR3a0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0016) of Tàizōng provide the bridge between Hàn *zǐ* and Sòng *Lǐxué*. *Xù Mèngzǐ* [KR3a0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0017) and *Shēnméngzǐ* [KR3a0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0018) by Lín Shènsī, and *Sùlǚzǐ* [KR3a0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0019) by Zhāng Hú, document the late-Táng Confucian revival that Wilkinson (§28.7.3) traces to Hán Yù, Lǐ Áo, and Liǔ Zōngyuán.

**The Northern Sòng *daoxué* founding corpus.** This is the doctrinal core of the division. Zhāng Zǎi's writings — *Zhāngzǐ quánshū* [KR3a0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0026) and *Zhāngzǐ yǔlù* [KR3a0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0027) — together with the *Zhèng méng* and its Míng-Qīng commentaries *Zhù jiě Zhèng méng* [KR3a0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0028) (Lǐ Guāngdì) and *Zhèng méng chū yì* [KR3a0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0029) (Wáng Zhí) record the *qì*-monist branch. The Chéng brothers' sayings, edited by Zhū Xī in 1168, form the foundational *Èr Chéng yíshū* [KR3a0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0030), *Èr Chéng wàishū* [KR3a0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0031), and Yáng Shí's *Èr Chéng cuìyán* [KR3a0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0032). Zhōu Dūnyí's two foundational pieces — the *Tàijí tú shuō* and the *Xī míng* (the latter Zhāng Zǎi's, conventionally paired with Zhōu's) — survive in this division only through commentaries: Cáo Duān's Ming-period *Tàijí tú shuō shùjiě* [KR3a0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0023), *Xīmíng shùjiě* [KR3a0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0024), and *Tōngshū shùjiě* [KR3a0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0025); and the Ming "*chāo shì*" 抄釋 set by Lǚ Nán — *Zhōuzǐ chāo shì* [KR3a0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0089), *Zhāngzǐ chāo shì* [KR3a0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0090), *Èr-Chéngzǐ chāo shì* [KR3a0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0091), *Zhūzǐ chāo shì* [KR3a0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0092).

**The Zhū Xī corpus and its editorial canon.** This is the largest single cluster. The *Zhūzǐ yǔlèi* [KR3a0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0047) (Lí Jìngdé's integrated 1270 recension of the disciples' *yǔlù*) is the principal source for Zhū's mature thought. The *Jìnsī lù* [KR3a0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0042) (1175, Zhū Xī and Lǚ Zǔqiān) is the canonical Northern-Sòng *daoxué* anthology; it accumulated two Qīng *jízhù* — Máo Xīnglái's [KR3a0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0043) and Jiāng Yǒng's [KR3a0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0044). Zhū Xī's other writings in the division include the *Yánpíng dá wèn* [KR3a0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0041) (correspondence with his teacher Lǐ Tóng), *Zá xué biàn* [KR3a0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0045) (polemic against Buddhist-Daoist syncretism), *Yùdìng Xiǎoxué jízhù* [KR3a0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0046) (with Chén Xuǎn's commentary), and the editorial *Jīngjì wén héng* [KR3a0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0057). The Sòng editorial workshop's wider reach is represented by Liú Qīngzhī's *Jiè zǐ tōng lù* [KR3a0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0048) and Zhāng Hóng / Qí Xī's *Zhūzǐ dúshū fǎ* [KR3a0070](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0070). The Kāngxī court's *Yù zuǎn Zhūzǐ quán shū* [KR3a0108](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0108) (1713–15, by Lǐ Guāngdì and Xióng Cìlǚ) made the Zhū corpus the official Qīng *Lǐxué* canon.

**The Lǚ Zǔqiān and Hú Hóng cluster.** *Lìzé lùn shuō jí lù* [KR3a0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0052) preserves Lǚ Zǔqiān's lectures at his Lìzé Academy; *Shào yí wài zhuàn* [KR3a0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0051) supplements the *Lǐjì* "Shào yí" with classical exemplars. Hú Hóng's *Zhī yán* [KR3a0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0049) is the *Hú-Xiāng* school's foundational text, methodologically distinct from the Cheng-Zhu mainstream.

**The Zhēn Déxiù / Qiū Jùn imperial-pedagogical *Yǎnyì* tradition.** *Dàxué yǎnyì* [KR3a0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0058) (1229–34) is the most influential Southern-Sòng imperial-instructional work; the structurally complementary *Xīshān dúshū jì* [KR3a0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0059), *Xīn jīng* [KR3a0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0060), and *Zhèng jīng* [KR3a0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0061) complete the Zhēn corpus. Qiū Jùn's *Dàxué yǎnyì bǔ* [KR3a0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0080) (1488, 160 *juǎn*) supplied the *zhì guó* and *píng tiānxià* outer-*tiáomù* treatment Zhēn had deliberately omitted. The pair became the canonical late-imperial imperial-instructional dyad, with parallel reception in Chosŏn Korea and Tokugawa Japan. Xià Liángshèng's *Zhōng yōng yǎn yì* [KR3a0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0093) and the Qīng *Yù dìng xiào jīng yǎn yì* [KR3a0105](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0105) extend the *Yǎnyì* genre to the *Zhōngyōng* and *Xiàojīng*.

**Sòng glossaries, commonplaces, and reading-records.** *Běixī zì yì* [KR3a0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0065) (Chén Chún, 1216–23) is the standard Northern-Sòng *Lǐxué* technical glossary; *Huángshì rì chāo* [KR3a0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0064) (Huáng Zhèn) is one of the most-cited reading-records of the entire tradition; *Xìnglǐ qúnshū jùjiě* [KR3a0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0067) (Xióng Jié and Xióng Gāngdà) anthologises the doctrinal corpus.

**The Yǒnglè *Xìnglǐ dàquán* and the Míng Cheng-Zhu mainstream.** *Xìnglǐ dà quán shū* [KR3a0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0078) (1414–15) is the foundational Míng *Lǐxué* compendium, the imperial textbook of *Lǐxué* in the *Guózǐjiàn* and provincial *guānxué* system. The early- and mid-Ming Cheng-Zhu mainstream is represented by Xuē Xuān's *Dú shū lù* [KR3a0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0079), Hú Jūrén's *Jū yè lù* [KR3a0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0081), Cáo Duān's foundational commentaries on the Northern Sòng masters ([KR3a0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0023)–[KR3a0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0025)), Lǚ Nán's *Jīngyězǐ nèi piān* [KR3a0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0087) and *chāo shì* set, Zhāng Jiǔsháo's *Lǐxué lèi biān* [KR3a0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0077), and Luó Qīnshùn's *Kùnzhī jì* [KR3a0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0084) — the most influential Míng *qì*-monist response to Wáng Yángmíng's *Xīnxué*.

**Late-Ming *shèndú* and Donglin-adjacent moral pedagogy.** *Liúzǐ yíshū* [KR3a0097](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0097) and *Rén pǔ* [KR3a0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0098) of Liú Zōngzhōu are the canonical late-Ming *shèndú* texts, foundational for the early-Qīng Huáng Zōngxī / Chén Què / Zhāng Lǚxiáng tradition. Huáng Dàozhōu's *Róng tán wèn yè* [KR3a0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0099) and Lǚ Kūn's *Shēn yín yǔ zhāi* [KR3a0096](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0096) sit in the same late-Ming moral-cultivation register.

**Domestic-instruction and *jiāxùn* texts.** *Jiā fàn* [KR3a0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0020) (Sīmǎ Guāng), *Yuánshì shì fàn* [KR3a0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0040) (Yuán Cǎi), *Nèi xùn* [KR3a0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0076) (Empress Xú of the Yǒnglè court), *Wēnshì mǔ xùn* [KR3a0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0100), *Xiàngshì jiā shuō* [KR3a0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0062), and the Yuán *Chéngshì jiāshú dúshū fēnnián rìchéng* [KR3a0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0033) (Chéng Duānlǐ) are the principal *Rújiā*-classed household-instruction texts.

**The Qīng imperial-Confucian canon.** *Yù dìng zī zhèng yào lǎn* [KR3a0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0101) (Shùnzhì), *Shèng yù guǎng xùn* [KR3a0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0102) (Yōngzhèng's 1724 amplification of Kāngxī's sixteen maxims, read monthly at *xiāng yuē* convocations throughout the empire), *Shèngzǔ Rénhuángdì tíngxùn gé yán* [KR3a0103](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0103), *Rì zhī huì shuō* [KR3a0104](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0104) (Qiánlóng), *Yù dìng nèizé yǎn yì* [KR3a0106](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0106), *Yù zuǎn xìnglǐ jīng yì* [KR3a0107](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0107) (Kāngxī, 1714–15, by Lǐ Guāngdì — the deliberate abridgment of the Yǒnglè *Dàquán*), *Qīn dìng zhí zhōng chéng xiàn* [KR3a0109](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0109), and *Yù lǎn jīngshǐ jiǎng yì* [KR3a0110](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0110) constitute the official Qīng *Lǐxué* corpus.

**Early- and mid-Qīng scholar-officials.** *Sī biàn lù jí yào* [KR3a0111](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0111) (Lù Shìyí, edited by Zhāng Bóxíng), *Dú Zhū suí bǐ* [KR3a0115](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0115), *Sānyútáng shèng yán* [KR3a0116](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0116), and *Sōngyáng chāo cún* [KR3a0117](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0117) (Lù Lǒngqí), and *Róngcūn yǔlù* [KR3a0114](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0114) (Lǐ Guāngdì) are the principal early-Qīng Cheng-Zhu-loyalist sources outside the imperial commissions.

**The CHANT *jíyì* fragments (`[KR3a0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0119)`–`[KR3a0158](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0158)`).** This second layer — added to the division from sources outside the WYG *Sìkù* — comprises forty *jíyì* reconstructions of Three-Kingdoms / Jìn / Nán-Běi-Cháo *zhūzǐ* whose full texts were lost between the Táng and the Sòng but quotation-fragments of which survive in *lèishū* (*Yìlín*, *Yìwén lèijù*, *Tàipíng yùlǎn*, etc.). The cluster includes *Zhōushēngzǐ yàolùn* [KR3a0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0119), the two *Zhènglùn* by Wáng Sù [KR3a0129](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0129) and Yuán Zhǔn [KR3a0130](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0130), *Qiáozǐ fǎxùn* [KR3a0123](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0123) of Qiáo Zhōu of Shǔ, Yuán Zhǔn's *Yuánzǐ zhèngshū* [KR3a0124](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0124), Gàn Bǎo's *Gānzǐ* [KR3a0154](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0154) (the same Gàn Bǎo as the *Sōu shén jì* compiler), and the rare Wú-period texts *Tōngyǔ* [KR3a0122](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0122), *Lùzǐ* [KR3a0137](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0137), *Tángzǐ* [KR3a0135](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0135), and *Zhūgězǐ* [KR3a0146](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0146) (Zhūgě Kè, son of Zhūgě Jǐn).

### Important persons

- [荀況](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8D%80%E6%B3%81) — Warring-States master, the only pre-Hàn author in the division; *Xúnzǐ* [KR3a0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0002) grounds the *Rújiā* category historically.
- [揚雄](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%8F%9A%E9%9B%84) — Hàn philosopher and lexicographer, author of *Yángzǐ Fǎ yán* [KR3a0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0009) and the pivotal early model of a *Lúnyǔ*-style re-canonisation.
- [劉向](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E5%90%91) — Hàn imperial-archive editor and compiler of *Shuōyuàn* [KR3a0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0007) and *Xīnxù* [KR3a0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0008); foundational to the early-imperial *Rújiā* anthology tradition.
- [王肅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E8%82%85) — Wèi-period commentator whose contested *Kǒngzǐ jiāyǔ* [KR3a0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0001), *Wángzǐ zhènglùn* [KR3a0129](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0129) and *Wáng Shǐ xīnshū* [KR3a0121](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0121) are the principal anti-Zhèng-Xuán Confucian works in the division.
- [王通](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E9%80%9A) — Suí Confucian who, through his posthumously compiled *Zhōng shuō* [KR3a0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0014), became one of the announced precursors of the Sòng Confucian revival.
- [張載](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E8%BC%89) — Northern-Sòng founder, the principal *qì*-monist source; *Zhāngzǐ quánshū* [KR3a0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0026), *Zhāngzǐ yǔlù* [KR3a0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0027), and (in commentary) *Zhèng méng* dominate the Zhāng cluster.
- [程顥](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%A8%8B%E9%A1%A5) and [程頤](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%A8%8B%E9%A0%A4) — Northern-Sòng founders of *Luòxué*; the *Èr Chéng yíshū* / *wàishū* / *cuìyán* [KR3a0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0030)–[KR3a0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0032) is the most-cited source-text of the entire Sòng-Yuán-Míng *Lǐxué* corpus.

### Topics

The principal interpretive problems running through the division are these:

1. **Cheng-Zhu *Lǐxué* versus *Xīnxué*.** The orthodox *daotong* line — Zhōu Dūnyí → Zhāng Zǎi → the two Chéngs → Zhū Xī — is the dominant trajectory in this *zǐbù* category. The Lù Jiǔyuán / Wáng Yángmíng line of *Xīnxué* is largely classified in `KR3` elsewhere, but the division registers the dispute directly through Luó Qīnshùn's *Kùnzhī jì* [KR3a0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0084) and indirectly through the Wàn-lì-period writings of Lǚ Kūn, Liú Zōngzhōu, and the early-Qīng Cheng-Zhu loyalists Lù Lǒngqí and Lǐ Guāngdì.

2. **The *daotong* and the late-Táng / Northern-Sòng revival.** Wilkinson (§28.7.3) traces the *Lǐxué* origin to the late-Táng revival of Hán Yù, Lǐ Áo, and Liǔ Zōngyuán; the division registers the immediate consequences in Lín Shènsī, Zhāng Hú, Sīmǎ Guāng (*Jiā fàn* [KR3a0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0020)), Fàn Zǔyǔ (*Dì xué* [KR3a0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0021)), and Wáng Kāizǔ (*Rú zhì biān* [KR3a0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0022)).

3. **Statecraft and imperial pedagogy.** The *Yǎnyì* / *Yǎnyì bǔ* / *Zhōng yōng yǎn yì* tradition, together with the Qīng *Yù dìng / Yù zuǎn* corpus and the *Shèng yù guǎng xùn* [KR3a0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0102), constitutes the Confucian statecraft strand classified here rather than in `KR3i` 政書 — works that are doctrinally Confucian rather than administratively documentary.

4. **Cultivation, *shèn dú*, and moral self-examination.** The Liú Zōngzhōu line of *Rén pǔ* / *Jì guò gé* moral-bookkeeping is the apex of this strand within KR3a; the earlier *Jiè zǐ tōng lù* [KR3a0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0048), *Xīn jīng* [KR3a0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0060), *Jiā fàn* [KR3a0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0020), and *Yuánshì shì fàn* [KR3a0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0040) provide the longer pedagogical-tradition background.

5. **Reconstruction of lost *zhūzǐ*.** The forty CHANT *jíyì* entries (`[KR3a0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0119)`–`[KR3a0158](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0158)`) raise problems of fragment-attribution, *lèishū*-citation reliability, and the relationship between the lost Six-Dynasties *zhūzǐ* and the Sòng catalogue tradition.

6. **The pseudepigraphic problem.** *Kǒngzǐ jiāyǔ* [KR3a0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0001) and *Kǒng cóngzǐ* [KR3a0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0003) are the canonical cases — Wáng-Sù-era reconstructions that nevertheless preserve genuine pre-Wèi material recovered from excavated manuscripts since the 1970s.

7. **The dialectic between Yǒnglè *Dàquán* and Kāngxī *Jīng yì*.** The Qīng court's deliberate replacement of the Yǒnglè *Xìnglǐ dà quán shū* [KR3a0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0078) by Lǐ Guāngdì's abridged *Yù zuǎn xìnglǐ jīng yì* [KR3a0107](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3a/KR3a0107) is the most explicit late-imperial canon-formation moment in the division and is reflected in the SKQS *tíyào*'s consistently dismissive treatment of the Yǒnglè compendia.

# 兵家類 (KR3b)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3b 兵家類 *Bīngjiā lèi* — Masters — Military Experts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3b is the *bīngjiā* 兵家 ("military experts") subdivision of the Masters branch (*zǐbù* 子部) in the Sìkù fourfold classification. Wilkinson (§26.5) treats this as a single coherent corpus running from the foundational Warring-States manuals (*Sūnzǐ*, *Wúzǐ*, *Sīmǎ fǎ*, *Wèi Liáozǐ*) through the Hàn aphoristic and apocryphal layer (*Sān lüè*, *Liù tāo*) to the Sòng-period synthesis. The decisive moment in the formation of this division is the canonisation of the *Wǔ jīng qī shū* 武經七書 ("Seven Military Classics") in c. 1078–1080 under Sòng Shénzōng as the curriculum for the military examinations; six pre-Hàn / Hàn texts plus the Táng-Sòng *Lǐ Wèigōng wèn duì* were thereby fixed as the authoritative canon of the genre, and remained so until the end of the empire (Wilkinson §26.5.3).

Inside KR3b, the division therefore stratifies cleanly into three transmissional layers: (1) the Warring-States and Hàn nucleus of the *Wǔ jīng qī shū*, much of it now controlled by the Yínquèshān 銀雀山 bamboo-strip find of 1972 (*Sūnzǐ*, *Sūn Bìn bīngfǎ*, *Wèi Liáozǐ*, etc.); (2) the Sòng compilation and pseudepigraphical efflorescence (the *Wǔ jīng zǒng yào*, the *Hǔ qián jīng*, the *Lǐ Wèigōng wèn duì* itself, the *Wòjī jīng*, the *Sù shū*), a period in which the genre was both standardised (canon, examinations) and saturated by retroactively-attributed material; and (3) the Late-Míng training-and-defence corpus of Qī Jìguāng 戚繼光 and his contemporaries, written in direct response to the *wōkòu* 倭寇 crisis on the Lower-Yangzi and Zhè-Mǐn coasts. The Wènyuāngé Sìkù preserves twenty principal works; three further entries ([KR3b0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0021)–0023) are *jíyì* fragments and pseudepigrapha included in the broader Kanripo digitisation.

### Important texts and text clusters

The *Wǔ jīng qī shū* canon (six of the seven are inside KR3b; the seventh, *Sūn Bìn bīngfǎ*, was already lost by the Sòng):
- *Sūnzǐ* 孫子 [KR3b0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0003) — the foundational Chinese military classic, c. late 4th–early 3rd c. BCE; the unbroken commentary tradition from Cáo Cāo onward is the spine of the entire division.
- *Wúzǐ* 吳子 [KR3b0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0004) — second of the Seven; received in 6 *piān*, sharply reduced from the 48 *piān* recorded in the *Hànshū yìwén zhì*.
- *Sīmǎ fǎ* 司馬法 [KR3b0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0005) — third of the Seven; Warring-States redaction in Qí of materials traceable to the Spring-and-Autumn general Sīmǎ Rángjū.
- *Wèi Liáozǐ* 尉繚子 [KR3b0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0006) — fourth of the Seven; Yínquèshān fragments confirm a pre-Hàn nucleus.
- *Liù tāo* 六韜 [KR3b0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0002) — pseudepigraphically ascribed to *Tàigōng* 太公 (Lǚ Wàng); one of the Seven; covers civil-government (*Wén tāo*) alongside strictly military materials.
- *Huángshí gōng sān lüè* 黃石公三畧 [KR3b0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0007) — Hàn-period aphoristic work, one of the Seven.

### Topics

- **Canonisation and the examination curriculum.** The single most important fact about KR3b is that the genre was fixed by the c. 1078–1080 selection of seven works as the *Wǔ jīng qī shū* — the curriculum for the Sòng military examinations and, with adjustments, for every later military examination system. The Sìkù *Bīngjiā lèi* organisation reflects this canon directly (Wilkinson §26.5.3).
- **Pseudepigraphy and the retro-attribution layer.** A high proportion of the works in the division are demonstrably or probably pseudepigraphic: the *Liù tāo* (ascribed to Lǚ Wàng), the *Sān lüè* and *Sù shū* (ascribed to Huángshí gōng), the *Lǐ Wèigōng wèn duì* (post-Táng, pre-1080), the *Wòjī jīng* (Sòng, ascribed to the Hàn), the *Xīnshū* (Sòng, ascribed to Zhūgě Liàng). The pattern is structural to the genre: military authority required ancient names. The dating policy in this knowledgebase places these works at the date of the received recension, not at the attributed author's lifetime.
- **The commentary tradition on the *Sūnzǐ*.** From Cáo Cāo through the Sòng *Shíyī jiā* compilation by Jí Tiānbǎo, the *Sūnzǐ* commentary tradition is the longest continuous textual project in the genre. The Mèngshì stratum [KR3b0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0022) is one of the eleven; the others (Cáo Cāo, Lǐ Quán, Du Mu, Méi Yáochén, Wáng Xī, Hé Yánxī, Zhāng Yù, Jiǎ Lín, Du You, Chén Hào) are not separately extant in the SKQS *Bīngjiā lèi*, only in the eleven-commentary edition.
- **Yínquèshān 銀雀山 (1972) and 20th-c. critical scholarship.** The Hàn-tomb find recovered late-Western-Hàn versions of the *Sūnzǐ*, *Sūn Bìn bīngfǎ*, *Wèi Liáozǐ* and other military texts, decisively reshaping modern philological work on the corpus (Wilkinson §26.5.1.1, §26.5.3). Although the bamboo strips themselves lie outside the SKQS, every modern critical edition of the relevant KR3b texts uses them as principal collation source.
- **Civil-military separation under the Sòng.** The Sòng deliberate downgrading of the military profession (Wilkinson §26.6) is the political background against which the Sòng compilation programme — *Wǔ jīng zǒng yào*, *Hǔ qián jīng*, *Lǐ Wèigōng wèn duì*, the canonisation of the Seven — must be read: a state attempt to codify and control military expertise at exactly the moment when general-officer prestige was being squeezed out of the elite culture.
- **Late-Míng *wōkòu* defence and military reform.** The Late-Míng cluster ([KR3b0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0016)–[KR3b0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3b/KR3b0020)) is unified by the *wōkòu* crisis on the Lower-Yangzi and Zhè-Mǐn coasts. Qī Jìguāng's *Jì xiào xīn shū* is the central work; Táng Shùnzhī's *Wǔ biān* and Zhèng Ruòzēng's *Jiāngnán jīng lüè* are the encyclopedic and regional-defence companions; Hé Liángchén's *Zhèn jì* is the tactical formal reference.
- **Siege warfare and the technical layer.** From Chén Guī's *Shǒu chéng lù* through the relevant chapters of the *Wǔ jīng zǒng yào* and the *Hǔ qián jīng* to Qī Jìguāng's training manuals, the division contains the principal pre-modern Chinese textual record of siege technology, fortifications, weapons and unit drill — a layer that is conceptually separable from the strategic-philosophical layer of the *Sūnzǐ* tradition.

# 法家類 (KR3c)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3c 法家類 *Fǎ-jiā lèi* — Masters — Legalists](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3c 法家類 (*Fǎjiā lèi*) sits within KR3 子部 (*Zǐbù*, Masters) and corresponds to the Sìkù quánshū *Zǐbù — Fǎjiā lèi*. The label is older and broader than its modern translation "Legalists" suggests: the Sìkù editors used 法家 as a bibliographic basket holding both the classical Warring States theorists of *fǎ* 法 (codified law), *shù* 術 (administrative technique), and *shì* 勢 (positional power), and the later judicial-casebook tradition concerned with the practical application of law in case adjudication. The division is therefore split internally into two distinct textual clusters connected only by the SKQS classifiers' decision to treat 法 as a single rubric.

The first cluster is the canonical pre-Qín statist literature — the *Guǎnzǐ*, *Shāngjūn shū*, *Hán Fēizǐ*, and the *Míngjiā*-adjacent *Dèng Xīzǐ* — composed or compiled in the Warring States and surviving in received recensions whose dating runs from the late Zhōu into the early Hàn. Wilkinson §58.6.3.2 catalogues these as the principal Warring States *zǐ*-texts on government, with the *Shāngjūn shū* singled out as the only extant pre-Hàn work describing the economic and social reforms of a pre-imperial polity. The *Hàn shū yìwén zhì* assigns the *Guǎnzǐ* to the Daoists and the *Shāngjūn shū* and *Hán Fēizǐ* to the *Fǎjiā* proper, of which it lists only ten titles; the SKQS reclassification pulls the *Guǎnzǐ* into 法家 on the strength of its *qīngzhòng* 輕重 (light-and-heavy) economic chapters and statist orientation. The second cluster is the Wǔ-dài-to-Sòng *yí yù* 疑獄 (difficult cases) genre — the *Yí yù jí*, *Zhé yù guī jiàn*, and *Táng yīn bǐ shì*. Wilkinson treats these at §25.3.2 (Sòng penal-law sources) and §137 (Five Legal Casebooks); they are forensic-pedagogical anthologies of judicial decisions, not works of political philosophy, but in the SKQS taxonomy they share the rubric of 法.

### Important texts and text clusters

**Classical Legalist *zǐ*-texts.** Four canonical Warring-States compilations form the core of the division:

- *Guǎnzǐ* 管子 [KR3c0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0001) — 24-juan, 76-篇 Warring States compilation attributed to the Spring-and-Autumn chancellor of Qí, foundational for Chinese economic, administrative, and political thought, with the *qīngzhòng* chapters among the earliest pre-modern treatments of price-currency theory and state monopoly.
- *Hán Fēizǐ* 韓非子 [KR3c0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0005) — the synthesising classical Legalist text by Hán Fēi, integrating Shēn Bùhài's *shù*, Shèn Dào's *shì*, and Shāng Yāng's *fǎ* into a coherent statist programme; the principal theoretical source for the Legalist tradition.
- *Shāngzǐ* 商子 [KR3c0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0004) (= *Shāngjūn shū* 商君書) — the only extant pre-Hàn work documenting a concrete legal-administrative reform programme, namely Shāng Yāng's reforms in Qín; doctrinally the most radical of the cluster, with its agriculture-and-warfare (*nóngzhàn* 農戰) doctrine and suppression of the *liù shī* 六蝨.
- *Dèng Xīzǐ* 鄧析子 [KR3c0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0003) — a brief 2-篇 pseudepigraphic text preserving *Míngjiā* (School of Names) technical terminology under a Spring-and-Autumn attribution, of late Warring States or early Hàn actual composition.

**Míng-period commentary.** A single commentarial work belongs to the classical cluster:

- *Guǎnzǐ bǔ zhù* 管子補注 [KR3c0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0002) — Liú Jì's 1490 supplementary commentary to the *Guǎnzǐ*, complementing Fáng Xuánlíng's Táng commentary; the standard Mid-Míng layer.

**The *yí yù* casebook tradition.** Three works form a tight Wǔ-dài-to-Sòng triad of judicial-decision anthologies:

- *Yí yù jí* 疑獄集 [KR3c0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0006) — Hé Níng and his son Hé Mèng's foundational casebook of difficult judicial cases, late Wǔdài / early Sòng; the seed text of the genre.
- *Zhé yù guī jiàn* 折獄龜鑑 [KR3c0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0007) — Zhèng Kè's mid-Southern-Sòng expansion of the *Yí yù jí*, the standard pre-Yuán reference work for case adjudication.
- *Táng yīn bǐ shì* 棠陰比事 [KR3c0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0008) — Guì Wànróng's 1196 casebook, distinguished by its mnemonic four-character couplet pairings of cases; the most popularly circulated of the three and the only Chinese pre-modern legal work with a major early Western Sinological translation (van Gulik 1956).

### Important persons

- [房玄齡](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%88%BF%E7%8E%84%E9%BD%A1) — Fáng Xuánlíng (578–648), the early-Táng statesman; provided the standard premodern commentary to the *Guǎnzǐ* preserved in the SKQS edition.
- [鄧析](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%84%A7%E6%9E%90) — Dèng Xī (ca. 545–501 BCE), legendary *Míngjiā* thinker; nominal author of the *Dèng Xīzǐ*.
- [商鞅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%95%86%E9%9E%85) — Shāng Yāng (ca. 390–338 BCE), the architect of the Qín legal reforms; nominal author of the *Shāngjūn shū* / *Shāngzǐ*, though the received text is a posthumous compilation by his successors.
- [韓非](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%9F%93%E9%9D%9E) — Hán Fēi (ca. 280–233 BCE), Hán prince-scholar executed in Qín; the synthesising philosopher of the pre-Qín Legalist tradition and author of most of the *Hán Fēizǐ*.
- [何犿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BD%95%E7%8A%BF) — Hé Fán (Yuán), commentator on the *Hán Fēizǐ* in the SKQS edition.
- [劉績](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E7%B8%BE) — Liú Jì (b. 1468), Mid-Míng scholar; author of the *Guǎnzǐ bǔ zhù*, the principal Míng-period commentary on the *Guǎnzǐ*.
- [和凝](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%92%8C%E5%87%9D) — Hé Níng (898–955), Wǔdài statesman who served under successive northern dynasties; founder of the *yí yù* casebook genre with the *Yí yù jí*.
- [和㠓](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%92%8C%E3%A0%93) — Hé Mèng (956–1000), son of Hé Níng; supplemented his father's casebook.
- [鄭克](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%84%AD%E5%85%8B) — Zhèng Kè (12th c.), Southern Sòng compiler whose *Zhé yù guī jiàn* became the standard Sòng-period casebook.
- [桂萬榮](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%A1%82%E8%90%AC%E6%A6%AE) — Guì Wànróng (Sòng), author of the *Táng yīn bǐ shì* in 1196.
- [吳訥](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%90%B3%E8%A8%A5) — Wú Nè (1372–1457), early Míng official who produced the cut-and-supplemented Míng recension of the *Táng yīn bǐ shì* transmitted in the SKQS.

### Topics

- **The triad *fǎ — shù — shì*.** The classical-Legalist conceptual core, drawn from Shāng Yāng, Shēn Bùhài, and Shèn Dào respectively, and integrated by Hán Fēi. *Fǎ* (law as the universal, impersonal mechanism of governance) is the doctrine most closely associated with the *Shāngjūn shū* ([KR3c0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0004)); *shù* (the ruler's technique for managing officials) and *shì* (the positional advantage of the throne) are theorised most explicitly in the *Hán Fēizǐ* ([KR3c0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0005)).
- **State power vs. Rú-Mò moral persuasion.** All four classical texts engage, polemically, with Confucian and Mohist programmes of virtue-based government; the *Wǔ dù* 五蠹 of the *Hán Fēizǐ* and the *liù shī* 六蝨 doctrine of the *Shāngjūn shū* are the canonical loci. The division is the principal home of the anti-Rú polemic in the Sìkù.
- **Agriculture-and-warfare (*nóngzhàn* 農戰).** The *Shāngjūn shū*'s programme of harnessing the peasantry as the dual fiscal and military base of the state; the most influential single doctrine in actual Warring-States and early-imperial statecraft.
- **Pseudepigraphy and recompilation.** Three of the four classical texts (*Guǎnzǐ*, *Dèng Xīzǐ*, *Shāngjūn shū*) carry attributions to figures who could not have written the received works. Dating policy for the division consequently brackets the received recensions, not the lifedates of the attributed authors — a recurrent issue across the entries.
- **The *Míngjiā* trace.** The *Dèng Xīzǐ* ([KR3c0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0003)) is the only text in the division attached to the School of Names rather than to *Fǎjiā* proper; its classification here reflects the SKQS editors' decision to absorb the small, fragmentary *Míngjiā* corpus into the adjoining bibliographic categories.
- **The judicial casebook as a genre.** The Wǔ-dài-to-Sòng *yí yù* tradition ([KR3c0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0006) → [KR3c0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0007) → [KR3c0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3c/KR3c0008)) is forensic-pedagogical: cases are presented as exemplars in which the judicial determination required exceptional reasoning, with the *Táng yīn bǐ shì* refining the form to mnemonic four-character couplets for memorisation by serving officials. The genre is distinct from the legal codes proper (which are catalogued elsewhere) and from forensic medicine (Sòng Cí's *Xǐ yuān jí lù*).
- **Inner-court Legalism, outer-court Confucianism.** Wilkinson §66 captures the political-cultural commonplace that the bifurcation of practical (Legalist) and ideological (Confucian) modes of governance is structural to the Chinese imperial system from the Hàn onward. The KR3c texts are the canonical pre-imperial sources for the inner-court half of that bifurcation.

# 農家類 (KR3d)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3d 農家類 *Nóngjiā lèi* — Masters — Agricultural Treatises](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3d 農家類 (*Nóngjiā lèi*) is the agricultural-treatises subdivision of the 子部 (Masters), gathering the comprehensive *nóng shū* 農書 — practical handbooks and imperially sponsored encyclopedias covering grain and rice cultivation, sericulture, horticulture, animal husbandry, water-control, agricultural implements, food preservation, and famine-relief botany. The classification has a continuous bibliographic history: from the Hàn 漢志 the genre was placed in section nine (*nóngshū*) of the Masters branch; by the Qīng *Sìkù quánshū* it sat in section four of the *zǐbù*, and the present KR3d retains that placement (Wilkinson, *Chinese History: A New Manual* §35.4).

The chronological span of the works actually collected here runs from the Northern Wèi *Qí mín yào shù* of the 530s — the first complete extant agricultural encyclopedia — through the Sòng-Yuán southern-rice and imperial-handbook traditions, the Míng famine-botany and Jesuit-influenced hydraulic literature, and culminates in the Qīng imperial *Qīn dìng shòu shí tōng kǎo* of 1742. Wilkinson (§35.4) notes that some 260 such treatises survive out of about 650 known titles, and characterises the genre as combining (i) quotation from earlier and now-lost agricultural works, (ii) hands-on experience by retired officials, magistrates, and estate-holders, and (iii) imperially commissioned popularisation. KR3d's 10 entries are a curated SKQS selection drawn precisely from these three streams.

### Important texts and text clusters

The ten works fall into four readily recognisable clusters.

**Foundational pre-Sòng treatise.**
- *Qí mín yào shù* 齊民要術 [KR3d0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0001) — Jiǎ Sīxié's Northern Wèi (533–544) encyclopedia, the first complete extant *nóng shū* and the cornerstone of the entire later tradition; about a third of every subsequent comprehensive treatise quotes from it.

**Sòng–Yuán southern-rice and imperial-handbook cluster.** The four medieval comprehensive treatises that together canonised the genre's two registers — private/regional and imperial/administrative.
- *Nóng shū* 農書 (Chén Fū) [KR3d0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0002) — the 3-juan 1149 Southern Sòng manual focused on Lower-Yangzi wet-rice cultivation, the first major treatise written from a southern-Chinese viewpoint.
- *Nóngsāng jí yào* 農桑輯要 [KR3d0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0003) — the 1273/1286 *Sīnóngsī* compilation under Khubilai, the earliest surviving officially sponsored agricultural treatise, distributed empire-wide to local magistrates.
- *Nóngsāng yīshí cuō yào* 農桑衣食撮要 [KR3d0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0004) — Lǔ Míngshàn's 1314 calendar-organised handbook for magistrates acting as agricultural instructors, distinguished by being written by a Uyghur Yuán official.
- *Nóng shū* 農書 (Wáng Zhēn) [KR3d0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0005) — the 22-juan Yuán encyclopedia (preface 1313), whose third part *Nóng qì tú pǔ* 農器圖譜 is the most extensive pre-modern Chinese illustrated technical catalogue of agricultural implements, and whose printing history is famous for the earliest detailed description of wooden movable-type technology.

**Late-Míng famine-relief and Jesuit-encounter cluster.** Four Míng works marking the genre's two great Late-Míng innovations: famine-relief edible-plants botany, and the integration of European agricultural and hydraulic technology.
- *Jiù huāng běn cǎo* 救荒本草 [KR3d0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0006) — Zhū Sù's 1406 famine-botany pharmacopoeia, methodologically pioneering for shifting from medicinal to emergency-edibility classification.
- *Nóng zhèng quán shū* 農政全書 [KR3d0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0007) — Xú Guāngqǐ's 60-juan synthesis (published posthumously 1639), the largest comprehensive Míng agricultural encyclopedia, incorporating both the entire prior tradition and Jesuit-introduced European material.
- *Tàixī shuǐ fǎ* 泰西水法 [KR3d0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0008) — the 1612 Xú Guāngqǐ–Sabatino de Ursis hydraulic-engineering translation (the SKQS catalog title 秦西水法 is a typographical slip for 泰西), introducing European water-lifting devices, pumps, and aqueduct construction.
- *Yě cài bó lù* 野菜博錄 [KR3d0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0009) — Bào Shān's ca. 1622 wild-vegetables reference, extending the Zhū Sù famine-botany tradition.

**Qīng imperial synthesis.**
- *Qīn dìng shòu shí tōng kǎo* 欽定授時通考 [KR3d0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0010) — the 78-juan Qiánlóng-commissioned encyclopedia (1737–1742) under È'ěrtài and Zhāng Tíngyù, the culmination of the pre-modern Chinese agricultural-administrative tradition, drawn almost entirely from the earlier works listed above.

### Important persons

- [賈思勰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B3%88%E6%80%9D%E5%8B%B0) (Jiǎ Sīxié, late-5th–6th c.) — Northern Wèi *Tàishǒu* of Gāoyángjùn whose private experience and reading of prior (now-lost) treatises produced the foundational text of the entire later genre.
- [陳旉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E6%97%89) (Chén Fū, 1076–1154) — Southern Sòng private author whose treatise gave the genre its first explicit wet-rice southern register.
- [魯明善](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%AD%AF%E6%98%8E%E5%96%84) (Lǔ Míngshàn, fl. 1314–1330) — the Uyghur Yuán magistrate whose handbook fixed the *agricultural-calendar* form for the magistrate-as-instructor.
- [王禎](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E7%A6%8E) (Wáng Zhēn, fl. 1295–1313) — Yuán county magistrate whose illustrated *Nóng qì tú pǔ* is the principal pre-modern Chinese visual record of agricultural implements, and whose own printing of his treatise occasioned the first detailed description of wooden movable-type technology.
- [朱橚](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E6%A9%9A) (Zhū Sù, Prince of Zhōu, 1361–1425) — fifth son of Míng Tàizǔ, founder of the famine-botany sub-tradition through his court-sponsored *Jiù huāng běn cǎo*.
- [徐光啟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BE%90%E5%85%89%E5%95%9F) (Xú Guāngqǐ, 1562–1633) — the central Late-Míng figure of the division, author or co-author of two KR3d entries ([KR3d0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0007), [KR3d0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0008)) and the principal mediator between the Chinese agricultural tradition and Jesuit-introduced European technical material.
- [西洋熊三拔](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A5%BF%E6%B4%8B%E7%86%8A%E4%B8%89%E6%8B%94) (Sabatino de Ursis, 1575–1620) — the Italian Jesuit whose collaboration with Xú Guāngqǐ produced the *Tàixī shuǐ fǎ*, one of the principal works of Late-Míng Chinese-Western technical encounter.
- [鄂爾泰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%84%82%E7%88%BE%E6%B3%B0) (È'ěrtài, 1677–1745) and [張廷玉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E5%BB%B7%E7%8E%89) (Zhāng Tíngyù, 1672–1755) — the senior Yōngzhèng-Qiánlóng ministers who directed the imperial synthesis [KR3d0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0010) that closes the SKQS *Nóngjiā* selection.

### Topics

- **Northern dry-field vs. southern wet-rice agriculture.** The single most persistent fault-line in the genre: *Qí mín yào shù* anchors the dry-land tradition of Guānzhōng and Shāndōng; Chén Fū's *Nóng shū* establishes the Lower-Yangzi wet-rice counter-tradition; Wáng Zhēn explicitly attempts to bridge the two. Wilkinson (§35.4) treats this north-south split as the structuring axis of the entire genre.
- **Private treatise vs. imperially sponsored manual (*quànnóng* 勸農).** Two registers coexist throughout: Jiǎ Sīxié, Chén Fū, and Wáng Zhēn write as informed private observers, while *Nóngsāng jí yào*, *Nóngsāng yīshí cuō yào*, and *Shòu shí tōng kǎo* are official handbooks distributed through the magistrate network. The genre is one of the clearest Chinese cases of a continuous bureaucratic-pedagogical literature.
- **Compilation, quotation, and lost-text recovery.** Much of every comprehensive treatise is verbatim quotation from earlier (and frequently now-lost) works; the genre's transmission is consequently also a major preservation channel for pre-Hàn through Táng technical literature. About a third of *Nóngsāng jí yào* is verbatim from *Qí mín yào shù*; *Shòu shí tōng kǎo* is "almost entirely culled" from *Nóng zhèng quán shū* (Wilkinson §35.4.9).
- **The agricultural calendar (*shí lìng* 時令 / *yuè lìng* 月令).** Many treatises organise material by lunar month, inheriting from the *Yuè lìng* of the *Lǐjì* and Cuī Shí's *Sì mín yuè lìng*; Lǔ Míngshàn's [KR3d0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0004) is the cleanest exemplar of this organisational principle inside KR3d.
- **Illustrated technology.** Wáng Zhēn's *Nóng qì tú pǔ* and the related *Gēng zhī tú* 耕織圖 tradition mark the genre's distinctive use of technical illustration; many of the implements depicted were still in use in early-20th-century rural China (Wilkinson §35.4.7 citing Hommel 1937).
- **Famine relief and applied botany.** Beginning with Zhū Sù's [KR3d0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0006) and continued by Bào Shān's [KR3d0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0009), the Míng adds a famine-emergency edibility register that is methodologically distinct from the older *běn cǎo* medical-pharmacognosy tradition.
- **The Late-Míng Jesuit encounter.** *Tàixī shuǐ fǎ* and the European-derived material in *Nóng zhèng quán shū* mark the only point in the pre-modern Chinese agricultural literature where European technical knowledge enters the canon — a localised episode, but a historically conspicuous one.

### Timeline

- 533–544 — *Qí mín yào shù* 齊民要術 [KR3d0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0001) — the foundational comprehensive treatise; every later entry in the division quotes from it.
- 1149 — *Nóng shū* 農書 (Chén Fū) 陳旉《農書》[KR3d0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0002) — the first Southern Sòng wet-rice treatise.

- 1406 — *Jiù huāng běn cǎo* 救荒本草 [KR3d0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0006) — the foundational famine-botany work.
- 1612 — *Tàixī shuǐ fǎ* 泰西水法 [KR3d0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0008) — the Jesuit-Xú Guāngqǐ hydraulic translation.
- 1622 — *Yě cài bó lù* 野菜博錄 [KR3d0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0009) — Bào Shān's Late-Míng extension of the Zhū Sù famine-botany tradition.
- 1620–1639 — *Nóng zhèng quán shū* 農政全書 [KR3d0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0007) — Xú Guāngqǐ's Late-Míng synthesis, published posthumously in 1639.
- 1737–1742 — *Qīn dìng shòu shí tōng kǎo* 欽定授時通考 [KR3d0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3d/KR3d0010) — the Qiánlóng-commissioned imperial culmination of the genre.

# 醫家類 (KR3e)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3e 醫家類 *Yī jiā lèi* — Masters — Medicine](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

`KR3e` 醫家類 (*Yī jiā lèi*, Masters — Medicine) collects the canonical and quasi-canonical works of the Chinese medical tradition under the Masters branch (子部) of the four-branch (四部) bibliographic system. The Hàn imperial bibliography (《漢書·藝文志》) had given medicine its own sixth-branch placement (醫經, 經方, 房中, 神仙); from the Suí-Táng standard-history bibliographies onward it was subsumed into 子部, where it has remained. The division as preserved in the Wényuāngé *Sìkù quánshū* and supplementary editions in this corpus runs from the late-Hàn clinical canon of Zhāng Jī to the mid-Qīng critical writings of Xú Dàchūn (《醫學源流論》, 1757) and the Qiánlóng imperial compilation 《御纂醫宗金鑑》 (1742) — covering roughly fifteen centuries of writing on aetiology, drug therapy, acumoxa, gynaecology, paediatrics, external medicine, materia medica, and pulse diagnosis. The principal commentarial and transmissional traditions a reader must keep in mind are: (i) the early-imperial medical *Classics* (《素問》《靈樞》《難經》《傷寒》《金匱》《甲乙經》《脈經》), repeatedly re-edited by the Northern-Sòng Bureau for Editing Medical Books (校正醫書局); (ii) the great Suí-Táng systematisers Cháo Yuánfāng, Sūn Sīmiǎo, Wáng Tāo; (iii) the Sòng state-sponsored materia medica and formularies (《證類本草》《聖濟總錄》《太平惠民和劑局方》); (iv) the four Jīn-Yuán masters (金元四大家); and (v) the late-Míng to mid-Qīng critical syntheses culminating in Lǐ Shízhēn, Zhāng Jièbīn, and Xú Dàchūn. Endymion Wilkinson's *Chinese History: A New Manual* devotes Section 41 to medicine, treating most of the works in this division as the principal Western-language entry points; that section structures the present overview.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The medical Classics (醫經).** Five works are foundational and define the *zhōngyī* curriculum down to the present.
- *Huángdì nèijīng Sùwèn* 黃帝內經素問 [KR3e0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0001) — the dialogic cosmological-physiological canon, transmitted in Wáng Bīng's 762 recension and Lín Yì's 1057–1067 校正 edition.
- *Língshūjīng* 靈樞經 [KR3e0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0002) — the second half of the *Nèijīng* corpus, focused on acupuncture meridians, re-edited by Shǐ Sōng in 1155 after the Wáng Bīng recension was lost.
- *Wáng Hànlín jízhù Huángdì bāshíyī Nánjīng* 王翰林集註黃帝八十一難經 [KR3e0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0003) and *Nánjīng běnyì* 難經本義 [KR3e0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0004) — the *Nánjīng*, attributed to Qín Yuèrén (Biǎn Què), preserved here in the Míng compiled commentary of Wáng Jiǔsī and in Huá Shòu's authoritative Yuán *běnyì*.
- *Jīnguì yàoluè lùnzhù* 金匱要略論註 [KR3e0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0006) and *Xīnbiān Jīnguì yàoluè fānglùn* 新編金匱要略方論 [KR3e0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0007) — Zhāng Jī's miscellaneous-disease canon, with Xú Bīn's 1671 Qīng commentary and the Sòng校正 1066 imperial recension respectively.
- *Shānghán lùn zhùshì* 傷寒論注釋 [KR3e0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0008) — Zhāng Jī's cold-damage classic in Chéng Wúyǐ's first complete line-by-line commentary (preface 1144), the recension on which all subsequent *Shānghán* scholarship builds.

**Suí–Táng systematisations.** *Zhēnjiǔ jiǎyǐ jīng* 鍼灸甲乙經 [KR3e0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0005) (Huángfǔ Mì, 256–282) is the earliest systematic acumoxa classic; *Xīnkān Wángshì màijīng* 新刊王氏脈經 [KR3e0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0009) (Wáng Shūhé, c. 280–300) is the first book-length pulse manual; *Zhǒuhòu bèijí fāng* 肘後備急方 [KR3e0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0010) (Gě Hóng, c. 280–343, supplemented by Táo Hóngjǐng) is the prototype of the "emergency at-the-elbow" formulary; *Cháoshì zhūbìng yuánhòu zǒnglùn* 巢氏諸病源候總論 [KR3e0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0012) (Cháo Yuánfāng, 605–615) is the great Suí imperial encyclopaedia of disease aetiology; the *Bèijí qiānjīn yàofāng* 備急千金要方 [KR3e0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0013) (Sūn Sīmiǎo, 650s) and *Wàitái mìyào fāng* 外臺秘要方 [KR3e0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0015) (Wáng Tāo, 752) together constitute the great Táng synthesis of Hàn–Suí clinical knowledge.

**Sòng state compilations and the 校正醫書局.** The Northern-Sòng court invested heavily in editing and printing medical literature. Among the results in this division: the imperial pharmacopoeia *Zhènglèi běncǎo* 證類本草 [KR3e0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0028) (Táng Shènwēi, 1108–1116) and its Dàquán revision *Zhòngxiū Zhènghé jīngshǐ zhènglèi bèiyòng běncǎo* 重修政和經史證類備用本草 [KR3e0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0029) (1204), the basis of all later 本草 down to Lǐ Shízhēn; the Huīzōng court compendium *Shèngjì zǒnglù zuǎnyào* 聖濟總錄纂要 [KR3e0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0027) (1111–1117); the standardised dispensatory *Tàipíng huìmín héjì jú fāng* 太平惠民和劑局方 [KR3e0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0033) (issued and revised 1107–1252); the materia-medica-based prescription manual *Sū-Shěn liángfāng* 蘇沈良方 [KR3e0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0020) (Sū Shì and Shěn Kuò), and the foundational gynaecological work *Fùrén dàquán liángfāng* 婦人大全良方 [KR3e0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0038) (Chén Zìmíng, 1237). Chén Yán's *Sānyīn jíyī bìngzhèng fānglùn* 三因極一病證方論 [KR3e0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0041) (1174) systematised the three-causes (內因 / 外因 / 不內外因) aetiology that becomes a Sòng doctrinal commonplace.

**The four Jīn-Yuán masters (金元四大家).** This division contains the principal works of all four.
- *Liú Wánsù* (劉河間) — 《素問玄機原病式》 [KR3e0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0047), 《宣明方論》 [KR3e0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0048), 《傷寒直格方》 [KR3e0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0049): the "cooling-cold" (寒涼) school grounded in the *Sùwèn*'s 五運六氣 doctrine.
- *Zhāng Cóngzhèng* (張子和) — 《儒門事親》 [KR3e0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0051): the "attacking-purging" (攻邪) school, advocating sweat–vomit–purge therapy.
- *Lǐ Gǎo* (李東垣) — 《內外傷辯惑論》 [KR3e0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0052), 《脾胃論》 [KR3e0053](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0053), 《蘭室祕藏》 [KR3e0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0054): the "spleen-stomach" (補土) school of internal damage. Continued in this division by his disciples Wáng Hǎogǔ (《此事難知》 [KR3e0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0055), 《醫壘元戎》 [KR3e0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0056), 《湯液本章》 [KR3e0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0057)) and Luó Tiānyì (in 《保命集》 [KR3e0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0050), a Zhāng Yuánsù compilation transmitted by him).
- *Zhū Zhènhēng* (朱丹溪) — 《格致餘論》 [KR3e0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0060), 《局方發揮》 [KR3e0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0061), 《金匱鈎玄》 [KR3e0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0062): the "nourishing-yīn" (滋陰) school, polemically opposed to the now-formulaic *Júfāng* prescribing of the Sòng pharmacy bureaus.

**Late-Yuán to Míng synthesis.** Wáng Lǚ's *Yījīng sùhuí jí* 醫經溯洄集 [KR3e0066](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0066) (c. 1360–1380) and Huá Shòu's *Nánjīng běnyì* [KR3e0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0004) inaugurate a movement of doctrinal return to the *Nèijīng*. The imperial Míng compendium *Pǔjì fāng* 普濟方 [KR3e0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0067) (Zhū Sù, 1390–1406) — the largest pre-modern Chinese formulary at 168 juan — preserves vast quantities of Sòng-Yuán prescription literature now otherwise lost. Xú Yòngchéng's *Yùjī wēiyì* 玉機微義 [KR3e0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0068) (1380–1410) is a key reorganisation of Zhū Zhènhēng's clinical doctrine.

**Míng materia medica and *Nèijīng* exegesis.** Lǐ Shízhēn's *Běncǎo gāngmù* 本草綱目 [KR3e0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0079) (1552–1590; printed 1603) is the canonical Chinese pharmacopoeia and one of the most influential natural-history works in any culture before the modern era; his *Qíjīng bāmài kǎo* 奇經八脉攷 [KR3e0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0080) and *Bīnhú màixué* 瀕湖脉學 [KR3e0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0081) complete his pulse-and-vessel programme. Zhāng Jièbīn's *Lèijīng* 類經 [KR3e0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0085) (1624) is the most systematic Míng topical rearrangement of the *Nèijīng*, and his *Jǐngyuè quánshū* 景岳全書 [KR3e0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0086) (1624–1640) is the principal Míng monument of the "warming-and-tonifying" (溫補) school that opposes Liú Wánsù's *hánliáng*. Miào Xīyōng's *Shénnóng běncǎo jīng shū* 神農本草經疏 [KR3e0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0084) (1620–1625) inaugurates the Míng-Qīng critical *běncǎojīng* recovery scholarship. Wú Yǒuxìng's *Wēnyì lùn* 瘟疫論 [KR3e0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0087) (1642) is the formative text of warm-pathogen / epidemic-febrile-disease theory, a precursor to the full Qīng 溫病學派.

**Qīng critical schools.** Yú Chāng's *Shànglùn piān* 尚論篇 [KR3e0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0091) (1648) and *Yīmén fǎlǜ* 醫門法律 [KR3e0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0092) (1658) re-edit and re-think the *Shānghán* and clinical practice; his disciples produce 《傷寒舌鑑》 [KR3e0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0093) and 《傷寒兼證析義》 [KR3e0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0094). Xú Dàchūn's quartet — 《蘭臺軌範》 [KR3e0097](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0097), 《神農本草經百種錄》 [KR3e0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0098), 《傷寒類方》 [KR3e0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0099), 《醫學源流論》 [KR3e0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0100) (1736–1764) — argues programmatically for return to the *Nèijīng*–*Nánjīng*–*Shānghán* line and against the Sòng-Yuán doctrinal schools. The imperial *Yùzuǎn Yīzōng jīnjiàn* 御纂醫宗金鑑 [KR3e0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0090) (Wú Qiān, 1742–1749) is the Qiánlóng-court standard-curriculum compendium that defined the imperial medical examinations.

### Important persons

- [張機](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E6%A9%9F) (Zhāng Jī, *zì* Zhòngjǐng, fl. 196–220) — author of the *Shānghán zábìng lùn* whose Sòng-recovered halves became 《傷寒論》 and 《金匱要略》, the twin pillars of clinical medicine in this division.
- [華佗](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%8F%AF%E4%BD%97) is absent as an author from this division (his works are lost), but [皇甫謐](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%9A%87%E7%94%AB%E8%AC%90) (Huángfǔ Mì, 215–282) supplies the foundation of acupuncture scholarship through 《針灸甲乙經》 [KR3e0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0005).
- [王叔和](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%8F%94%E5%92%8C) (Wáng Shūhé, c. 210–285) — Jìn editor of Zhāng Jī's corpus and author of 《脈經》 [KR3e0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0009), the first systematic pulse manual.
- [葛洪](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%91%9B%E6%B4%AA) (Gě Hóng, 283–343) — Eastern-Jìn Daoist physician whose 《肘後備急方》 [KR3e0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0010) is the prototype emergency formulary.
- [陶弘景](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B6%E5%BC%98%E6%99%AF) (Táo Hóngjǐng, 456–536) — Liáng polymath whose《本草經集注》 and 《名醫別錄》 (transmitted in *Zhènglèi běncǎo*) reshaped the 本草 tradition.
- [巢元方](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%B7%A2%E5%85%83%E6%96%B9) (Cháo Yuánfāng, fl. 605–615) — Suí imperial physician, lead compiler of 《諸病源候論》 [KR3e0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0012).
- [孫思邈](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AD%AB%E6%80%9D%E9%82%88) (Sūn Sīmiǎo, c. 581–682) — author of the *Qiānjīn* corpus [KR3e0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0013) and traditional attributee of the ophthalmological 《銀海精微》 [KR3e0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0014); the most influential single Táng clinician.
- [王燾](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E7%87%BE) (Wáng Tāo, c. 670–755) — author of 《外臺秘要方》 [KR3e0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0015), the great Táng compendium that preserves quotations from now-lost early formularies.
- [王冰](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%86%B0) (Wáng Bīng, fl. 762) — Táng recensionist whose 762 *Sùwèn* edition is the foundation of all later *Nèijīng* study; commented and re-edited in [KR3e0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0001).
- [林億](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9E%97%E5%84%84) (Lín Yì, fl. 1057–1067) — head of the Northern-Sòng 校正醫書局 (Bureau for Editing Medical Books); under his editorship the *Sùwèn*, *Nánjīng*, *Shānghán*, *Jīnguì*, *Màijīng*, *Jiǎyǐ jīng*, and *Qiānjīn* were re-edited and printed in the recensions still in use ([KR3e0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0001) [KR3e0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0005) [KR3e0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0009) [KR3e0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0013)).
- [唐慎微](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%94%90%E6%85%8E%E5%BE%AE) (Táng Shènwēi, fl. 1080s–1108) — Sòng pharmacist-author of 《經史證類備急本草》 [KR3e0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0028), the *běncǎo* on which all later materia medica down to Lǐ Shízhēn build.
- [陳言](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E8%A8%80) (Chén Yán, 1131–1189) — formulator of the three-causes aetiology in 《三因極一病證方論》 [KR3e0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0041).
- [許叔微](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%A8%B1%E5%8F%94%E5%BE%AE) (Xǔ Shūwēi, 1080–1154) — Sòng *Shānghán* expositor and author of 《類證普濟本事方》 [KR3e0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0032).
- [陳自明](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%99%B3%E8%87%AA%E6%98%8E) (Chén Zìmíng, c. 1190–1270) — Sòng gynaecologist, author of 《婦人大全良方》 [KR3e0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0038), the foundational systematic gynaecology of the imperial era.
- [劉完素](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E5%AE%8C%E7%B4%A0) (Liú Wánsù, c. 1110–1200) — founder of the *Héjiān* school of cooling-cold therapy and of the *Nèijīng*–五運六氣 revival ([KR3e0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0047)–[KR3e0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0049)).
- [張從正](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E5%BE%9E%E6%AD%A3) (Zhāng Cóngzhèng, 1156–1228) — *Zǐhé*, the attacking-purging master, author of 《儒門事親》 [KR3e0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0051).
- [李杲](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E6%9D%B2) (Lǐ Gǎo, 1180–1251) — *Dōngyuán*, founder of the *Píwèi* school ([KR3e0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0052)–[KR3e0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0054)), arguably the most influential single doctor of the Jīn-Yuán era.
- [朱震亨](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E9%9C%87%E4%BA%A8) (Zhū Zhènhēng, 1281–1358) — *Dānxī*, founder of the yīn-nourishing school and trenchant critic of the Sòng *Júfāng* ([KR3e0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0060)–[KR3e0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0062)).
- [滑壽](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%BB%91%E5%A3%BD) (Huá Shòu, c. 1304–1386) — late-Yuán scholar-physician whose 《難經本義》 [KR3e0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0004) is the standard *Nánjīng* commentary.
- [王履](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%B1%A5) (Wáng Lǚ, 1332–1391) — author of 《醫經溯洄集》 [KR3e0066](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0066), programmatic call to return from Sòng-Yuán doctrine to the *Nèijīng*–*Shānghán* line.
- [李時珍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E6%99%82%E7%8F%8D) (Lǐ Shízhēn, 1518–1593) — author of 《本草綱目》 [KR3e0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0079); the central figure in Míng natural history and pharmacology.
- [張介賓](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E4%BB%8B%E8%B3%93) (Zhāng Jièbīn, 1563–1640) — *Jǐngyuè*, the principal Míng *wēnbǔ* (warming-and-tonifying) thinker and author of 《類經》 and 《景岳全書》 ([KR3e0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0085)–[KR3e0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0086)).
- [繆希雍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%B9%86%E5%B8%8C%E9%9B%8D) (Miào Xīyōng, 1546–1627) — Míng critical pharmacologist, author of 《神農本草經疏》 [KR3e0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0084).
- [喻昌](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%BB%E6%98%8C) (Yú Chāng, 1585–1664) — Qīng *Shānghán* reformer of Jiāngxī, author of 《尚論篇》 and 《醫門法律》 ([KR3e0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0091)–[KR3e0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0092)).
- [徐大椿](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BE%90%E5%A4%A7%E6%A4%BF) (Xú Dàchūn, 1693–1771) — the central mid-Qīng critic, author of four foundational works in this division ([KR3e0097](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0097)–[KR3e0100](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0100)) calling for return to the medical Classics.
- [吳謙](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%90%B3%E8%AC%99) (Wú Qiān, c. 1689–1748) — chief editor of the imperial 《醫宗金鑑》 [KR3e0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0090), the standard Qīng curriculum.

### Topics

The division is organised around a number of overlapping debates and genres.

**The medical *Classics* (醫經) versus prescription literature (經方).** The Hàn imperial bibliography drew the line; the *Nèijīng*–*Nánjīng*–*Shānghán*–*Jīnguì* canon is the doctrinal pole, while the *fāng*-books (formularies — *Qiānjīn*, *Wàitái*, *Héjì jú fāng*, *Pǔjì fāng*) are the practical pole. Every major thinker in the division (Wáng Lǚ, Zhāng Jièbīn, Xú Dàchūn) is positioned somewhere along that axis.

**The four Jīn-Yuán masters and doctrinal schools.** The greatest single doctrinal innovation of the imperial era. *Hánliáng* (Liú Wánsù) versus *gōngxié* (Zhāng Cóngzhèng) versus *bǔtǔ* (Lǐ Gǎo) versus *zīyīn* (Zhū Zhènhēng) define the principal therapeutic styles of the next five hundred years, and the Míng-Qīng *wēnbǔ* school of Xuē Jǐ and Zhāng Jièbīn is in part a backlash against Zhū Dānxī's yīn-nourishing extremism.

**Cold damage (傷寒) versus warm pathogen (溫病).** *Shānghán* exegesis runs unbroken from Chéng Wúyǐ ([KR3e0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0008)) through Hán Zhīhé ([KR3e0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0025)), Páng Ānshí ([KR3e0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0026)), Fāng Yǒuzhí ([KR3e0082](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0082)), Yú Chāng ([KR3e0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0091)), Zhāng Dēng ([KR3e0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0093)), Zhāng Zhuō ([KR3e0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0094)), and Xú Dàchūn ([KR3e0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0099)). Wú Yǒuxìng's *Wēnyì lùn* [KR3e0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0087) marks the late-Míng break with the *Shānghán* model and the start of the Qīng 溫病 school — although the full Wú-Yè-Xuē-Wáng Wēnbìng canon of the eighteenth century is not in this division.

**Materia medica (本草).** A continuous lineage runs from the lost *Shénnóng běncǎo jīng* through Táo Hóngjǐng, Sū Jìng's Táng 《新修本草》, the Sòng *Zhènglèi běncǎo* [KR3e0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0028)–[KR3e0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0029), to Lǐ Shízhēn's *Gāngmù* [KR3e0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0079) and the Qīng critical recoveries of Miào Xīyōng [KR3e0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0084) and Xú Dàchūn [KR3e0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0098). The shift from accretive compilation to critical reconstruction of the *Shénnóng jīng* itself is the principal late-Míng to Qīng historiographical move.

**Acupuncture and moxibustion (鍼灸).** From Huángfǔ Mì [KR3e0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0005) through the Sòng *Tóngrén* tradition [KR3e0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0017), the *Míngtáng* moxibustion charts [KR3e0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0018), Wáng Zhízhōng's *Zhēnjiǔ zīshēng jīng* [KR3e0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0037), Wáng Guóruì's *Biǎnquè shényìng Yùlóng jīng* [KR3e0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0063), Dòu Hànqīng's *Zhēnjīng zhǐnán* [KR3e0107](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0107), down to Wāng Jī's late-Míng critical *Zhēnjiǔ wènduì* [KR3e0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0072).

**Specialised genres.** Gynaecology (Chén Zìmíng [KR3e0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0038), Chén Shīshèng [KR3e0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0040), the anonymous Sòng 《產寶諸寶》 [KR3e0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0044)); paediatrics (《顱顖經》 [KR3e0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0016), 《小兒衛生總散論方》 [KR3e0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0031), the smallpox-and-measles work 《仁端錄》 [KR3e0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0069)); external medicine and abscesses (Lǐ Xùn 《集驗背疽方》 [KR3e0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0042), Qí Dézhī 《外科精義》 [KR3e0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0064), Wāng Jī 《外科理例》 [KR3e0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0073)); geriatric care (Chén Zhí 《壽親養老新書》 [KR3e0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0021)); medical anecdota and case literature (Zhāng Gǎo 《醫說》 [KR3e0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0036), Jiāng Guàn 《名醫類案》 [KR3e0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0075), Wèi Zhīxiù 《續名醫類案》 [KR3e0096](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0096)); and the Sòng medical-examination *Tàiyī jú zhūkē chéngwén gé* [KR3e0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0039), which preserves the form of the imperial medical-examination essays.

**Five-Cycles, Six-Qi (五運六氣).** The cosmological-epidemiological doctrine grounded in the *Sùwèn*'s "Seven Great Treatises" supplied by Wáng Bīng. Liú Wēnshū's *Sùwèn rùshì yùnqì lùnào* [KR3e0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0024) (1099) is the principal Sòng systematic treatment and the gateway to the Liú Wánsù school.

**Pulse diagnosis (脈學).** From Wáng Shūhé [KR3e0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0009) through Dài Qǐzōng's *Màijué kānwù* [KR3e0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0065) (Yuán) to Lǐ Shízhēn's *Bīnhú màixué* [KR3e0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0081) and 《奇經八脉攷》 [KR3e0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3e/KR3e0080) — the central diagnostic art of the tradition.
