# 天文算法類 (KR3f)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3f 天文算法類 *Tiānwén suànfǎ lèi* — Masters — Astronomy and Mathematics](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

`KR3f` 天文算法類 is the sixth category of the *Sìkù quánshū* 子部, gathering works on observational and computational astronomy, calendrical mathematics (*lìfǎ* 曆法), instrumentation, and pure mathematics (*suànshù* 算術). Following the Sui-Tang library convention, the *Sìkù* editors kept astronomy and mathematics together as a single division on the principle that calendar-making was the practical end of mathematics: Wilkinson (§37.1) notes that astronomy and mathematics formed two of the four main scientific traditions of pre-modern China, each with its own paradigm, classical text(s) and learned community, and that astronomy before the telescope was "largely computational" — hence inseparable from arithmetic, geometry and algebra. Within KR3 子部, the division sits between medicine (`KR3e`) and the mantic arts (`KR3g`), reflecting its status as a useful, government-regulated technical knowledge.

Chronologically the division spans more than two thousand years, from the *Hàn* mathematical classics (the *Zhōubì* 周髀 and *Jiǔzhāng* 九章 traditions, Wilkinson §38.17.2) through the medieval *Suànjīng shíshū* 算經十書 corpus, the Sòng-Yuán algebraic peak, the dramatic late-Míng / early-Qīng absorption of Jesuit science, and the Kāngxī–Qiánlóng court compilations that synthesized the Western and Chinese traditions. Two organizing principles structure the corpus: in mathematics, the *Suànjīng shíshū* tradition recovered by Dài Zhèn 戴震 from the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn* 永樂大典 (eight of the ten were entered into the *Sìkù*); in astronomy, the cycle of dynastic calendar reforms (*Dàtǒng lì* 大統曆, *Shíxiàn lì* 時憲曆) and the cosmological debate between the *gàitiān* 蓋天, *húntiān* 渾天 and *xuānyè* 宣夜 theories (Wilkinson §39.1.1).

### Important texts and text clusters

- **The Ten Mathematical Classics (算經十書).** The Sui-Tang state curriculum at the *Suànxué guǎn* 算學館, recovered for the *Sìkù* by Dài Zhèn from the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn*: *Zhōubì suànjīng* 周髀算經 [KR3f0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0001), *Jiǔzhāng suànshù* 九章算術 [KR3f0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0032), *Sūnzǐ suànjīng* 孫子算經 [KR3f0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0033), *Hǎidǎo suànjīng* 海島算經 [KR3f0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0035), *Wǔcáo suànjīng* 五曹算經 [KR3f0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0036), *Wǔjīng suànshù* 五經算術 [KR3f0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0037), *Xiàhóu Yáng suànjīng* 夏侯陽算經 [KR3f0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0038), *Zhāng Qiūjiàn suànjīng* 張邱建算經 [KR3f0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0039), *Jígǔ suànjīng* 緝古算經 [KR3f0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0040), and the auxiliary *Shùshù jìyí* 數術記遺 [KR3f0034](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0034). The *Jiǔzhāng* with Liú Huī's 劉徽 commentary remains the most influential Chinese mathematical work in history; the *Zhōubì* is also the principal source for *gàitiān* cosmology (Wilkinson §38.17.2, §39.1.1).
- **Sòng-Yuán algebra.** The high-water mark of indigenous Chinese mathematics, centered on the *tiānyuán shù* 天元術 (counting-rod algebra). Qín Jiǔsháo's 秦九韶 *Shùxué jiǔzhāng* 數學九章 [KR3f0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0041) (1247) gives the first explicit statement of the Chinese Remainder Theorem; Lǐ Yě's 李冶 *Cèyuán hǎijìng* 測圓海鏡 [KR3f0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0042) (1248) and *Yìgǔ yǎnduàn* 益古演段 [KR3f0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0044) (1259) develop the *tiānyuán* method systematically; Gù Yìngxiáng's 顧應祥 *Cèyuán hǎijìng fēnlèi shìshù* 測圓海鏡分類釋術 [KR3f0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0043) is the Míng restatement (without rod-algebra).
- **Sòng instrument and classical-astronomy texts.** Sū Sòng's 蘇頌 *Xīn yíxiàng fǎyào* 新儀象法要 [KR3f0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0002) (1094), the illustrated treatise on the great water-powered armillary clock-tower at Kāifēng, and Wáng Yīnglín's 王應麟 *Liùjīng tiānwén biān* 六經天文編 [KR3f0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0003), an early-philological compendium of celestial references in the Classics.
- **Yuán cosmological synthesis.** Zhào Yǒuqīn's 趙友欽 *Géxiàng xīnshū* 革象新書 [KR3f0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0005) (with Wáng Yī's 王禕 Míng abridgement [KR3f0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0004)) consolidates *húntiān* cosmology with quantitative methods.
- **Míng calendar crisis and reform.** Zhū Zǎiyù's 朱載堉 *Shèngshòu wànnián lì* 聖壽萬年曆 [KR3f0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0007) (1595) and Xíng Yúnlù's 邢雲路 *Gǔjīn lǜlì kǎo* 古今律歷考 [KR3f0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0008) (1596–1611) attempt to restore the failing *Dàtǒng* calendar; Bèi Lín's 貝琳 *Qīzhèng tuībù* 七政推步 [KR3f0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0006) (1477) transmits the Islamic *Huíhuí lì* 回回曆 for planetary computation.
- **The Jesuit corpus (1607–1640s).** The first wave of European mathematics and astronomy in Chinese: *Jǐhé yuánběn* 幾何原本 [KR3f0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0047) (Euclid's first six books, Ricci–Xú Guāngqǐ 1607), *Tóngwén suànzhǐ* 同文算指 [KR3f0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0046) (European arithmetic, Ricci–Lǐ Zhīzǎo 1614), *Cèliáng fǎyì* 測量法義 [KR3f0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0014) (practical geometry), *Qiánkūn tǐyì* 乾坤體義 [KR3f0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0009) (cosmology), *Yuánróng jiàoyì* 圜容較義 [KR3f0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0016) (isoperimetric problems), *Húngài tōngxiàn túshuō* 渾蓋通憲圖說 [KR3f0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0015) (astrolabe), *Biǎo dù shuō* 表度說 [KR3f0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0010) and *Jiǎnpíng yí shuō* 簡平儀說 [KR3f0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0011) (Xióng Sānbá / Sabatino de Ursis), *Tiānwèn lüè* 天問畧 [KR3f0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0012) (Manuel Dias on telescopic astronomy), and culminating in the *Xīnfǎ suànshū* 新法算書 [KR3f0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0013) — the recompiled *Chóngzhēn lìshū* 崇禎曆書, the technical foundation of the *Shíxiàn* calendar.
- **The Kāngxī–Qiánlóng imperial compendia.** The four pillars of Qīng court mathematical-astronomical scholarship, all part of the *Lǜlì yuānyuán* 律曆淵源 project and its sequels: *Yùzhì lìxiàng kǎochéng* 御製歷象考成 [KR3f0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0018), its *Hòubiān* 後編 [KR3f0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0019) (incorporating Keplerian elliptical orbits), *Qīndìng yíxiàng kǎochéng* 欽定儀象考成 [KR3f0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0020) (the great star catalog), and *Yùzhì Shùlǐ jīngyùn* 御製數理精蘊 [KR3f0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0048) (the encyclopedic mathematical companion).
- **The Méi Wéndǐng school.** Méi Wéndǐng 梅文鼎 (1633–1721), the dominant Qīng mathematician-astronomer, is represented by his collected *Lìsuàn quánshū* 歷算全書 [KR3f0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0026), the catalog *Wù'ān lìsuàn shūjì* 勿菴歷算書記 [KR3f0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0028), and *Dàtǒng lìzhì* 大統歷志 [KR3f0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0027); his younger brother Méi Wénmì 梅文鼏 contributes *Zhōng-Xī jīngxīng tóngyì kǎo* 中西經星同異考 [KR3f0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0029). Allied works include Wáng Xīchǎn's 王錫闡 independent *Xiǎo'ān xīnfǎ* 曉菴新法 [KR3f0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0021) (1663), Jiāng Yǒng's 江永 *Shùxué* 數學 [KR3f0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0031), and the secondary tradition of Dù Zhīgēng's 杜知耕 *Shùxué yào* 數學鑰 [KR3f0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0050), Chén Xū's 陳訏 *Gōugǔ yǐnméng* 句股引蒙 [KR3f0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0052), Chén Shìrén's 陳世仁 *Shǎoguǎng bǔyí* 少廣補遺 [KR3f0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0054), Zhuāng Hēngyáng's 莊亨陽 *Zhuāngshì suànxué* 莊氏算學 [KR3f0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0055), and Tú Wényī's 屠文漪 *Jiǔzhāng lùyào* 九章錄要 [KR3f0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0056).
- **Mukinge / Polish-Jesuit alternative.** Mù Níjié / Jan Mikołaj Smogulecki 穆尼閣 and Xuē Fèngzuò's 薛鳳祚 *Tiānbù zhēnyuán* 天步眞原 [KR3f0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0024) and *Tiānxué huìtōng* 天學會通 [KR3f0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0025) preserve a logarithmic and Copernican-leaning channel of Western astronomy independent of the Beijing Jesuit mission.
- **Japanese supplement.** *Fóguó lìxiàng biān* 佛國暦象編 [KR3f0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0057) (Enzū 圓通, c. 1810) is a late Edo Buddhist defense of Indian/Buddhist cosmology against Jesuit astronomy.
- **Pre-Táng cosmological fragments.** The Liùcháo fragmentary corpus collected under `KR3f` from `krp-titles` includes *Yùfú ruìtú* 玉符瑞圖 [KR3f0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0058) (auspicious-image fragments), Yáo Xìn's 姚信 *Xīntiān lùn* 昕天論 [KR3f0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0059), Xú Zhěng's 徐整 *Chánglì* 長曆 [KR3f0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0060), Dù Yù's 杜預 *Niánlì* 年曆 [KR3f0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0061), Yú Sǒng's 虞聳 *Qióngtiān lùn* 穹天論 [KR3f0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0062), Yú Xǐ's 虞喜 *Āntiān lùn* 安天論 [KR3f0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0063), and the *Lòukè jīng* 漏刻經 [KR3f0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0064) (clepsydra manual). These are the chief surviving evidence for the *xuānyè* and supplementary cosmologies displaced by *húntiān* orthodoxy.

### Important persons

- [劉徽](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8A%89%E5%BE%BD) — late-3rd-c. commentator on the *Jiǔzhāng suànshù*, author of the *Hǎidǎo suànjīng*, and the most original Chinese mathematician of the early-medieval period; his commentary defines the canonical reading of the *Jiǔzhāng*.
- [李淳風](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E6%B7%B3%E9%A2%A8) — Táng court astronomer; annotator and editor of the *Suànjīng shíshū* curriculum (commentaries on [KR3f0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0001), 0032, 0035, 0036, 0037, 0039), the single figure who fixed the canonical Táng form of the medieval mathematical classics.
- [甄鸞](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%94%84%E9%B8%9E) — Northern-Zhōu mathematician, author of *Wǔjīng suànshù* and annotator of multiple *Suànjīng* texts; the principal pre-Táng commentator.
- [王孝通](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%AD%9D%E9%80%9A) — early-Táng author of the *Jígǔ suànjīng*, containing the world's first solution of cubic equations.
- [蘇頌](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%98%87%E9%A0%8C) — Northern-Sòng minister and polymath; engineer of the Kāifēng water-clock and astronomical tower described in [KR3f0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0002).
- [秦九韶](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%A7%A6%E4%B9%9D%E9%9F%B6) — Southern-Sòng mathematician whose *Shùxué jiǔzhāng* (1247) [KR3f0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0041) presents the Chinese Remainder Theorem; one of the two leading representatives of Sòng-Yuán algebra.
- [李冶](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E5%86%B6) — Jīn-Yuán mathematician, author of [KR3f0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0042) and [KR3f0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0044); consolidator of the *tiānyuán* algebraic method.
- [趙友欽](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%B6%99%E5%8F%8B%E6%AC%BD) — late-Yuán cosmographer; *Géxiàng xīnshū* [KR3f0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0005) is the most thoroughly quantitative *húntiān* synthesis before the Jesuit arrival.
- [朱載堉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9C%B1%E8%BC%89%E5%A0%89) — Míng prince, mathematician of equal-temperament fame; *Shèngshòu wànnián lì* [KR3f0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0007) applies his rigorous numerical methods to the calendar.
- [邢雲路](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%82%A2%E9%9B%B2%E8%B7%AF) — late-Míng astronomer whose *Gǔjīn lǜlì kǎo* [KR3f0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0008) documented the *Dàtǒng* calendar's accumulating error and set the stage for reform.
- [利瑪竇](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%88%A9%E7%91%AA%E7%AB%87) — Matteo Ricci; with Xú Guāngqǐ and Lǐ Zhīzǎo, the founder of the Chinese mathematical-astronomical Jesuit corpus ([KR3f0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0009), [KR3f0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0046), [KR3f0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0047)).
- [徐光啟](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BE%90%E5%85%89%E5%95%9F) — co-translator of *Jǐhé yuánběn* and architect of the *Chóngzhēn lìshū* reform that became *Xīnfǎ suànshū* [KR3f0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0013).
- [李之藻](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9D%8E%E4%B9%8B%E8%97%BB) — Ricci's principal Chinese collaborator after Xú; translator/expounder of [KR3f0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0015), [KR3f0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0016), and [KR3f0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0046).

### Topics

- **The *Suànjīng shíshū* and the state curriculum.** The Táng *Guózǐ jiàn* set the canon (Wilkinson §38.17), and Dài Zhèn's recovery from the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn* in the 1770s — the immediate prelude to the *Sìkù* — is the textual scaffolding on which the entire mathematical half of `KR3f` is built. Most of the medieval titles in this division are essentially Dài Zhèn editions.
- **Counting-rod algebra (*tiānyuán shù* 天元術).** The Sòng-Yuán method of representing one unknown by its position on the counting board, peaking in Qín Jiǔsháo and Lǐ Yě. The technique was largely forgotten by mid-Míng (Gù Yìngxiáng could no longer follow Lǐ Yě's [KR3f0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0042) and had to "explicate" it in [KR3f0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0043)), and was only restored to Chinese mathematical consciousness when Jesuit-era and Qīng scholars (especially Méi Wéndǐng) began re-reading the Sòng-Yuán texts.
- **The three cosmologies: *gàitiān* 蓋天, *húntiān* 渾天, *xuānyè* 宣夜.** The *Zhōubì* [KR3f0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0001) is the locus classicus of *gàitiān*; the Sòng-Yuán-Míng tradition (Sū Sòng [KR3f0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0002), Zhào Yǒuqīn [KR3f0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0005)) is *húntiān*; the fragmentary *Xīntiān lùn* [KR3f0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0059), *Qióngtiān lùn* [KR3f0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0062) and *Āntiān lùn* [KR3f0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0063) are the principal evidence for *xuānyè* and its variants. The *húntiān* model became orthodox after the 6th century (Wilkinson §39.1.1).
- **Calendar reform as political crisis.** Every major dynastic transition in the division (Yuán→Míng, Míng→Qīng) coincides with a calendrical reform: the *Dàtǒng lì* inherits the *Shòushí lì* 授時曆 (1280); Xíng Yúnlù [KR3f0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0008) and Zhū Zǎiyù [KR3f0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0007) document its breakdown; the *Chóngzhēn lìshū* / *Xīnfǎ suànshū* [KR3f0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0013) is the Jesuit-led replacement, instituted as the *Shíxiàn lì* under the Qīng in 1645; the *Lìxiàng kǎochéng* and its sequel [KR3f0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0018), [KR3f0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0019) are its Kāngxī–Qiánlóng refinements.
- **The Jesuit transmission and its limits.** The corpus from [KR3f0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0009) through [KR3f0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0019) documents the Ricci-Xú-Lǐ collaboration (Euclid, arithmetic, geometry, astrolabe, telescope) and its institutional outcome in the Imperial Astronomical Bureau. Crucially, the Jesuits transmitted Ptolemaic and Tychonic, not Copernican, planetary models; full Keplerian astronomy enters only in [KR3f0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0019) (1742, by Kögler). The Smogulecki/Xuē Fèngzuò line [KR3f0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0024)–[KR3f0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0025) is a partial exception.
- **The *Lǜlì yuānyuán* programme.** The Kāngxī emperor's three-part synthesis ([KR3f0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0018) *Lìxiàng kǎochéng*; the lost *Lǜlǚ zhèngyì* on harmonics; [KR3f0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0048) *Shùlǐ jīngyùn* on mathematics) is the single most consequential state intervention in this division, producing the authoritative Qīng textbooks of astronomy and mathematics. Méi Wéndǐng's [KR3f0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0026) and the entire Méi-school corpus are in dialogue with it.
- **"Western methods are originally Chinese" (*Xīxué Zhōngyuán* 西學中源).** The Qīng accommodationist thesis, developed by Méi Wéndǐng and ratified by the Kāngxī court, that European mathematics and astronomy ultimately derive from the lost learning of the *Zhōubì* and the *Jiǔzhāng*. The thesis underpins the synthetic ambition of [KR3f0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0026) and [KR3f0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0048) and is the philosophical horizon against which most 17th–18th-c. texts in this division should be read.
- **Mathematical traditions outside the *Suànjīng* canon.** Practical computation manuals (Tú Wényī [KR3f0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0056), Chén Xū [KR3f0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0052)), specialist tracts on circle-arc geometry (Gù Yìngxiáng [KR3f0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0045)), the *shǎoguǎng* 少廣 root-extraction tradition (Chén Shìrén [KR3f0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0054)), and Méi-school surveying ([KR3f0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0031)).

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3g 術數類 *Shù-shù lèi* — Masters — Mantic Arts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3g sits inside the *Sìkù* Masters Branch (子部) as the *Shùshù lèi* 術數類 — the "Numerical-and-Mantic Arts" — and gathers the works the Qiánlóng editors classed as technical divination, cosmological numerology, geomancy, astrology, fate-calculation, physiognomy, and hemerology. Following Wilkinson (§29.3 on *fāngshù* 方術, §33.1 on fengshui, §39.16 on the Five Agents and the calendar, §56.5 on Sòng cosmology, §57.3 and §58.3.1 on divinatory writing and the oracle bones, §73.2.2 on the *sìbù* classification; cf. *Box 348* on the Masters Branch subdivisions), this is the oldest continuously catalogued non-canonical Chinese genre: the *Hànshū Yìwén zhì* "Shùshù lüè" 數術略 already articulated six subdivisions (*tiānwén* 天文, *lìpǔ* 曆譜, *wǔxíng* 五行, *shīguī* 蓍龜, *zázhàn* 雜占, *xíngfǎ* 形法), and the *Sìkù* *Shùshù lèi* preserves substantially the same six-fold map: 數學 (numerological cosmology) — 占候 (celestial-portent astrology) — 相宅相墓 (residence- and tomb-siting / fengshui) — 占卜 (divination proper) — 命書相書 (fate-calculation and physiognomy) — 陰陽五行 (yīnyáng five-phase divination and almanac-making). The 52 works collected here cover all six.

The chronological span runs from the late Western Hàn (Jiāo Yánshòu's *Yìlín* [KR3g0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0029) and Jīng Fáng's *Yìzhuàn* [KR3g0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0030) in the second half of the 1st century BCE, and Yáng Xióng's *Tàixuán jīng* [KR3g0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0001) c. 2–4 CE) to the high Qiánlóng court (*Qīndìng Xiéjì biànfāng shū* [KR3g0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0051), promulgated 1741, and Wáng Zhí's *Huángjí jīngshì shū jiě* [KR3g0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0010), 1721–67). Three transmissional traditions structure the reading. (1) **The *xiàngshù* 象數 *Yìjīng* lineage**, from the Hàn *guàqì* (hexagram-pneuma) school of Jiāo Yánshòu and Jīng Fáng through Yáng Xióng's alternative-cosmology *Tàixuán*, the Sòng cosmological systems of Shào Yōng (*Huángjí jīngshì*) and Sīmǎ Guāng (*Qiánxū* [KR3g0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0004)), and the *Shàoshì* school of Zhāng Xíngchéng [KR3g0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0006)–[KR3g0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0008) and Zhù Mì [KR3g0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0009). (2) **The geomantic / *kānyú* 堪輿 lineage**, which the *Sìkù* editors treat as Táng-period in its received textual form despite its pseudepigraphic attributions to the Yellow Emperor and Jìn-period Guō Pú, and which crystallises around the Táng-end / Five-Dynasties *xíngshì* 形勢 trilogy ascribed to Yáng Yúnsōng [KR3g0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0021), [KR3g0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0023), [KR3g0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0024). (3) **The late-imperial *xīngmìng* 星命 / *zǐpíng* 子平 fate-calculation tradition**, whose proximate Sòng-Yuán-Míng synthesis is consolidated in Wàn Mínyīng's twin compendia of 1578 — *Xīngxué dàchéng* [KR3g0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0041) and *Sānmìng tōnghuì* [KR3g0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0042) — and which Wilkinson (§39.16 and *Box 354*) singles out as the canonical late-imperial fate-calculation reference set. Across all three the editors' principal hermeneutic problem is the same: how to preserve a technically valuable but doctrinally peripheral body of work without endorsing its *fāngshì* 方士 pretensions, which the *tíyào* address case by case with a characteristic mixture of textual-critical scepticism and documentary respect.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The Hàn alternative-cosmology cluster.** Yáng Xióng's *Tàixuán jīng* 太玄經 [KR3g0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0001) (c. 2–4 CE, with Fàn Wàng's Jìn-period commentary) is the most ambitious systematic Hàn-period alternative to the *Yìjīng*'s 8-fold structure, organising cosmology on a 9-fold (3⁴) scheme keyed to the 729-day periodicity of the *Tàichū* calendar. Yè Zǐqí's *Tàixuán běnzhǐ* 太玄本旨 [KR3g0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0002) (Míng, 1368–90) is the principal late-imperial commentary. The North-Zhōu monk Wèi Yuánsōng's *Yuánbāo jīngzhuàn* 元包經傳 [KR3g0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0003) (c. 560–575, with Táng commentary by Sū Yuánmíng and Lǐ Jiāng and Sòng supplementary apparatus by Zhāng Xíngchéng) carries the alternative-*Yì* cosmology forward through the Suí-Táng transition. Sīmǎ Guāng's *Qiánxū* 潛虛 [KR3g0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0004) (c. 1080–86, with Zhāng Dūnshí's *Qiánxū fāwēi lùn* supplement) is the Sòng-imperial-historian's own *Tàixuán*-modelled cosmological-numerical treatise.

**The Shào Yōng cosmological-historical system and its school.** Shào Yōng's *Huángjí jīngshì shū* 皇極經世書 [KR3g0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0005) (c. 1050–77) is, by Wilkinson's measure (§56.5.4), the most ambitious systematic cosmological-historical synthesis in pre-modern Chinese intellectual history — a 129,600-year *yuánhuìyùnshì* 元會運世 nested temporal scheme combining hexagram-based history with the *guānwù* 觀物 ("observing-things") philosophical method, by one of the *Wǔzǐ* 五子 Founders of Northern-Sòng *Lǐxué*. The *Shàoshì* school is represented by Zhāng Xíngchéng's three works — *Huángjí jīngshì suǒyǐn* [KR3g0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0006), *Huángjí jīngshì guānwù wàipiān yǎnyì* [KR3g0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0007), and the massive 40-juan *Yì tōngbiàn* [KR3g0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0008) (all 1132–66); Zhù Mì's *Guānwù piān jiě* [KR3g0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0009) (1235–41) with its appended *Qǐshù jué*; and, on the Qīng side, Wáng Zhí's *Huángjí jīngshì shū jiě* [KR3g0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0010) (1721–67), the standard late-imperial Cheng-Zhu commentary. Wáng Shí's *Yìxué* [KR3g0011](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0011) (1127–60) is a related Southern-Sòng treatment.

**The Sòng-Yuán cosmological-numerical supplement.** Cài Shěn's *Hóngfàn huángjí nèipiān* 洪範皇極內篇 [KR3g0012](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0012) (1200–30) extends the *Hóngfàn* 洪範 / *Hétú* / *Luòshū* numerological tradition Wilkinson treats at §39.11; Bào Yúnlóng's *Tiānyuán fāwēi* [KR3g0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0013) (c. 1280–1310), Dīng Yìdōng's *Dàyǎn suǒyǐn* [KR3g0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0014) (c. 1280–1310) on the *dàyǎn* divinatory number, and Zhāng Lǐ's Yuán-period *Yìxiàng túshuō* [KR3g0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0015) (1300–40) round out this layer. Huáng Dàozhōu's late-Míng *Sānyì dòngjī* 三易洞璣 [KR3g0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0016) (1620–46) is the closing major contribution of the *xiàngshù* cluster, by a *Donglin*-adjacent statesman-scholar.

**The Táng celestial-portent corpus.** Yú Jìcái's *Língtái mìyuàn* 靈臺祕苑 [KR3g0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0017) (originally Běi-Zhōu, c. 560, re-edited by Wáng Ānlǐ for the Sòng court c. 1085) and Qútán Xīdá's *Táng Kāiyuán zhànjīng* 唐開元占經 [KR3g0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0018) (718–29) are the two principal pre-Sòng Chinese astral-divination encyclopaedias. The *Kāiyuán zhànjīng* is, in addition, the principal surviving compilation of Hàn-Wèi *chènwěi* 讖緯 quotation-fragments and the conduit for the first Indian *Navagraha*-calendar (*Jiǔzhí lì* 九執曆) reaching the Chinese imperial astronomical bureau — a transmission Wilkinson registers at §39.16.

**The *xiàngzhái xiàngmù* fengshui cluster.** Nine consecutive works form the *Sìkù*'s geomantic subdivision: the residence-siting *Zháijīng* 宅經 [KR3g0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0019) (pseudepigraphic *Huángdì*, Táng received form), the tomb-siting *Zàngshū* 葬書 [KR3g0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0020) (pseudepigraphic Guō Pú, in fact Sòng-period — translated by Zhang Juwen and identified by Wilkinson §33.1 as the key early text linking fengshui to Confucianism), and the Táng-Sòng *xíngshì* 形勢 ("form-and-configuration") trilogy ascribed to Yáng Yúnsōng — *Hànlóng jīng* 撼龍經 [KR3g0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0021), *Qīngnáng àoyǔ* 青囊奧語 [KR3g0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0023), and *Tiānyù jīng* 天玉經 [KR3g0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0024) — supplemented by Zēng Wénshàn's *Qīngnáng xù* 青囊序 [KR3g0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0022). The *lǐqì* 理氣 ("principle-and-pneuma") counterpart is supplied by Hé Pǔ's *Língchéng jīngyì* 靈城精義 [KR3g0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0025) (Five-Dynasties / Sòng-Yuán recension) and Lài Wénjùn's *Cuīguān piān* 催官篇 [KR3g0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0026) (Sòng, c. 1150–1250). Cài Yuándìng's *Fāwēi lùn* 發微論 [KR3g0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0027) (1170–98) — by the Sòng Cheng-Zhu master who is also the father of Cài Shěn — supplies the philosophically-rigorised Northern-Sòng Cheng-Zhu reading of geomancy. Together this is the canonical Chinese geomantic primary-source set, treated comprehensively in Paton's *Five Classics of Fengshui* (2013).

**The divination-method (*zhānbǔ*) cluster.** The *Língqí jīng* 靈棋經 [KR3g0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0028) (pseudepigraphic Dōngfāng Shuò, in fact Six-Dynasties received form; with Liú Jī's late-Yuán / early-Míng commentary) is the foundational text of *qíbǔ* counter-divination. Jiāo Yánshòu's *Yìlín* 焦氏易林 [KR3g0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0029) (c. 75–50 BCE) and Jīng Fáng's *Yìzhuàn* 京氏易傳 [KR3g0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0030) (c. 50–37 BCE) are the two foundational Western-Hàn *guàqì* *Yìjīng*-divinatory works: 4,096 four-character verses for every hexagram-pair in the first, and the *bāgōng guà* 八宮卦 (eight-palace hexagram) re-organisation of the *Yìjīng* in the second. The Míng *Liùrén dàquán* 六壬大全 [KR3g0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0031) is the principal late-imperial *Liùrén* 六壬 divinatory reference, and Hú Xù's *Bǔfǎ xiángkǎo* 卜法詳考 [KR3g0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0032) (early Qīng) is the principal Cheng-Zhu-loyalist textual-historical examination of plastromantic and shī-yarrow divination, which Wilkinson (§57.3, §58.3.1) treats as the deep historical origin of Chinese writing itself.

**The *xīngmìng* / *zǐpíng* fate-calculation cluster.** The principal pseudepigraphic foundational texts are *Lǐ Xūzhōng mìngshū* 李虛中命書 [KR3g0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0033) (in fact Sòng-period, attributed via Guǐgǔzǐ to the Táng *xīngmìng* practitioner whose practice Hán Yù records) and the *Yùzhào dìngzhēn jīng* [KR3g0034](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0034) (pseudepigraphic Guō Pú, Sòng received form). *Xīngmìng sùyuán* [KR3g0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0035) is the principal late-Míng anthology. Two Sòng-period commentaries on the foundational *Luòlùzǐ* divinatory verses occupy [KR3g0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0036) (Tánying, 1127) and [KR3g0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0037) (Xú Zǐpíng — *the* foundational figure of the *zǐpíng* 子平 / eight-character system, c. 950–1100). *Sānmìng zhǐmí fù* [KR3g0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0038) and the Liáo-attributed *Xīngmìng zǒngkuò* 星命總括 [KR3g0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0039) (Yēlǜ Chún) complete the early layer. *Yǎnqín tōngzuǎn* 演禽通纂 [KR3g0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0040) introduces the *qínxīng* 禽星 ("bird-star") sub-system. Wàn Mínyīng's two monumental compendia of 1578 — *Xīngxué dàchéng* 星學大成 in 30 juan [KR3g0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0041) and *Sānmìng tōnghuì* 三命通會 in 12 juan [KR3g0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0042) — are, as Wilkinson notes at §39.16, "the most important primary source on fate calculation compiled in the later empire" and the universally-consulted late-imperial popular-divination reference ("almost 'every house has it'", per the *tíyào*).

**The physiognomy (*xiàngshù*) cluster.** *Yuèbō dòngzhōng jì* [KR3g0043](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0043) (anonymous, Five-Dynasties / Sòng), *Yùguǎn zhàoshén jú* 玉管照神局 [KR3g0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0044) (attributed to the Southern-Tang minister Sòng Qíqiū, c. 940–1000), and *Tàiqīng shénjiàn* 太清神鑑 [KR3g0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0045) (Five-Dynasties / Sòng) form the early physiognomic layer. Zhāng Xíngjiǎn's Jīn-period *Rénlún dàtǒng fù* 人倫大統賦 [KR3g0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0046) (with Xuē Yánnián's Yuán-period annotation) is, as the *tíyào* notes, one of the few surviving substantive Jīn-Yuán-period authored works in the entire division.

**The *yīnyáng wǔxíng* / *Sānshì* / hemerological cluster.** Wáng Xīmíng's Táng-period *Tàiyǐ jīnjìng shìjīng* 太乙金鏡式經 [KR3g0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0047) (720–41) is the principal received reference for the *Tàiyǐ* 太乙 cosmographic divinatory system; Chéng Dàoshēng's late-Míng *Dùnjiǎ yǎnyì* 遁甲演義 [KR3g0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0048) is the principal received reference for the *Dùnjiǎ* 遁甲 system; with the *Liùrén dàquán* [KR3g0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0031) these three form the canonical *Sānshì* 三式 triplet. Chí Běnlǐ's *Qínxīng yìjiàn* 禽星易見 [KR3g0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0049) (late Míng) is the *qínxīng* extension. The two Qīng imperial *xuǎnzé* 選擇 (auspicious-day-selection) compilations close the division: the Kāngxī-era *Yùdìng Xīnglì kǎoyuán* 御定星歷考原 [KR3g0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0050) (1713, by Lǐ Guāngdì) in 6 juan, and the Qián-lóng-era 36-juan *Qīndìng Xiéjì biànfāng shū* 欽定協紀辨方書 [KR3g0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0051) (1739–41, by Yǔnlù), the comprehensive imperial *xuǎnzé* reference of the entire late-imperial period. As an inserted addition the division also holds Xiāo Jí's Suí-period *Wǔxíng dàyì* 五行大義 [KR3g0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0052) (c. 581–614) — preserved by Japanese transmission and the principal pre-Táng surviving compendium of *yīnyáng wǔxíng* correlative cosmology, edited by Marc Kalinowski (EFEO 1991).

### Important persons

- [揚雄](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%8F%9A%E9%9B%84) — Western-Hàn philosopher and lexicographer, author of *Tàixuán jīng* [KR3g0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0001); the originating figure of the alternative-cosmology lineage.
- [焦延壽](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%84%A6%E5%BB%B6%E5%A3%BD) — Western-Hàn *Yìjīng* diviner, author of *Yìlín* [KR3g0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0029); founder of the *guàqì* hexagram-pneuma divinatory tradition.
- [京房](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BA%AC%E6%88%BF) — Western-Hàn court astrologer-and-diviner, student of Jiāo Yánshòu, author of *Jīngshì Yìzhuàn* [KR3g0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0030); established the *bāgōng guà* eight-palace hexagram framework that organises later *xiàngshù* *Yìjīng* learning.
- [蕭吉](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%95%AD%E5%90%89) — Suí court *yīnyáng* technician (d. 614), author of *Wǔxíng dàyì* [KR3g0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0052); the principal pre-Táng synthesist of *yīnyáng wǔxíng* correlative cosmology and *chènwěi* fragments.
- [庾季才](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BA%BE%E5%AD%A3%E6%89%8D) — Běi-Zhōu astronomer-astrologer, original compiler of *Língtái mìyuàn* [KR3g0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0017); pivotal figure in the institutional continuity of Chinese state astrology across the Northern-Dynasties / Suí transition.
- [瞿曇悉達](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%9E%BF%E6%9B%87%E6%82%89%E9%81%94) — Táng court astronomer of Indian-Buddhist descent (Gautama Siddhārtha), compiler of *Táng Kāiyuán zhànjīng* [KR3g0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0018) (718–29); the conduit for the first systematic Indian astronomical transmission into the Chinese imperial astronomical bureau.
- [王希明](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%B8%8C%E6%98%8E) — Táng court astronomical-divinatory official, author of *Tàiyǐ jīnjìng shìjīng* [KR3g0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0047); principal received-text source for the *Tàiyǐ* divinatory system.
- [楊筠松](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%A5%8A%E7%AD%A0%E6%9D%BE) — late-Táng / Five-Dynasties geomancer ("Yáng who saves the poor"), traditional author of the *xíngshì* trilogy [KR3g0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0021), [KR3g0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0023), [KR3g0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0024); the canonical patriarch of the *xíngshì* (form-and-configuration) school of fengshui.
- [徐子平](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BE%90%E5%AD%90%E5%B9%B3) — Sòng *xīngmìng* technician (c. 950–1100), author of *Luòlùzǐ sānmìng xiāoxī fù zhù* [KR3g0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0037); the eponymous founder of the *zǐpíng* eight-character fate-calculation system that became standard in late-imperial popular practice.
- [邵雍](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%82%B5%E9%9B%8D) — Northern-Sòng cosmologist (1011–77), one of the *Wǔzǐ* 五子 founders of *Lǐxué*; author of *Huángjí jīngshì shū* [KR3g0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0005) and the originating figure of the *Shàoshì* cosmological-historical school.
- [司馬光](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%8F%B8%E9%A6%AC%E5%85%89) — Northern-Sòng historian and statesman (1019–86), author of *Qiánxū* [KR3g0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0004); the imperial-historian's own *Tàixuán*-modelled cosmological-numerical exercise, signalling the Northern-Sòng *xiàngshù* revival.

### Topics

The principal subjects, debates, and interpretive problems running through the division are these:

1. **The *xiàngshù* 象數 versus *yìlǐ* 義理 *Yìjīng* split.** The Hàn *xiàngshù* school — represented here by Jiāo Yánshòu, Jīng Fáng, and Yáng Xióng's alternative-cosmology *Tàixuán* — was the *Sìkù* editors' principal reason for classifying these texts in the *Shùshù lèi* rather than [KR1a](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/) *Yìlèi*. The Sòng cosmological-numerological revival under Shào Yōng and the *Shàoshì* school re-anchored *xiàngshù* within the *Lǐxué* synthesis, and the editors' placement of Shào Yōng's *Huángjí jīngshì* here rather than in the [KR1a](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/) *Yì* division is a deliberate judgement, justified in the *tíyào* by Shào Yōng's cosmological-temporal scheme being structurally distinct from canonical *Yìjīng* exegesis. See Smith, Bol, Adler, and Wyatt, *Sung Dynasty Uses of the I Ching* (1990).

2. **The Hàn *chènwěi* 讖緯 inheritance.** The Hàn apocryphal-classical corpus — extensively excerpted in *Tāng Kāiyuán zhànjīng* [KR3g0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0018) and *Wǔxíng dàyì* [KR3g0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0052) — is the deep substratum of the entire division. Many *wěi* texts survive only through such anthological citation, making these two works indispensable witnesses to a Hàn cosmological-political universe that the *Sìkù* editors themselves treat with explicit ambivalence.

3. **Pseudepigraphy and textual-criticism.** The *Sìkù* editors' systematic textual-critical scepticism is at its sharpest in this division: *Zháijīng* [KR3g0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0019) is unmasked as Táng, *Zàngshū* [KR3g0020](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0020) as Sòng despite its Jìn attribution, *Língqí jīng* [KR3g0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0028) as Six-Dynasties despite its Hàn attribution, *Lǐ Xūzhōng mìngshū* [KR3g0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0033) as Sòng despite its Táng attribution, and the *Hànlóng / Tiānyù / Qīngnáng* trilogy [KR3g0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0021)–[KR3g0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0024) is treated as Five-Dynasties / Sòng in received form despite Yáng Yúnsōng's late-Táng dating. The *tíyào* preserve a remarkably even-handed editorial position: the *fāngshì*' pseudepigraphic deification of their lineage-founders is regularly criticised, while the technical-and-historical value of the resulting texts is regularly affirmed.

4. **The *Sānshì* 三式 (Three-Form) divinatory typology.** The triplet *Tàiyǐ* [KR3g0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0047) — *Liùrén* [KR3g0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0031) — *Dùnjiǎ* [KR3g0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0048) constitutes the high-technical-cosmological apex of late-imperial Chinese divination, drawing on the *jiǔgōng* nine-palace cosmography of the *Yìwěi Qiánzáo dù* and ultimately on the *Hétú* / *Luòshū* magic-square tradition (cf. Swetz, *Legacy of the Luoshu*, 2002).

5. **Fengshui and the *xíngshì* / *lǐqì* divide.** The *xíngshì* 形勢 (form-and-configuration) school of Yáng Yúnsōng and the *lǐqì* 理氣 (principle-and-pneuma) school of Hé Pǔ and Lài Wénjùn are the two principal late-imperial fengshui schools, both fully represented in the division. Wilkinson (§33.1; cf. Brown, *Laws of the Land*, PUP 2023) treats fengshui as one of the longue-durée mantic practices most deeply embedded in late-imperial Chinese state and society, with documented legal-political consequences extending into Qīng case-law.

6. **The *zǐpíng* synthesis and popular fate-calculation.** Xú Zǐpíng's Sòng-period eight-character ([KR3g0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0037) commentary on *Luòlùzǐ*) consolidation of *xīngmìng* practice into the year-month-day-hour bāzì format — the basis of essentially all late-imperial popular fate-calculation — runs continuously to Wàn Mínyīng's monumental 1578 codification in [KR3g0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0042). Wilkinson (§39.16 and the discussion at *Sanming tonghui*) registers this as the canonical late-imperial reference set, and notes the appearance of detailed horoscopes — including a technically-correct example — in the *Jīn Píng Méi*.

7. **Imperial rationalisation of mantic practice.** The Qīng imperial *xuǎnzé* corpus — *Yùdìng Xīnglì kǎoyuán* [KR3g0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0050) and *Qīndìng Xiéjì biànfāng shū* [KR3g0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0051) — represents the deliberate state-cosmological project of removing later-accreted *fāngshì* superstitions while preserving the core *yīnyáng wǔxíng* technical apparatus, presented as a state-administrative reference rather than as folk-divination. The Qiánlóng preface to [KR3g0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0051) ironically acknowledges that what folk custom has long followed cannot be entirely removed: the imperial project rationalises rather than abolishes.

8. **Japanese transmission and global circulation.** *Wǔxíng dàyì* [KR3g0052](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/KR3g0052) survives only because the Japanese *Onmyōryō* 陰陽寮 preserved and re-transmitted it; Smith ("The transnational travels of geomancy in premodern East Asia", 2019) treats the longue-durée transmission of geomancy from China to the rest of East Asia. The division therefore registers an East-Asian cosmological-technical exchange running in both directions across the *kànyú* / *onmyōdō* boundary.

# 藝術類 (KR3h)

## Division note (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君): [KR3h 藝術類 *Yì-shù lèi* — Masters — Arts](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/)

### Scope and scholarly tradition

KR3h sits inside the *Sìkù quánshū* Masters Branch (子部) as the *Yìshù lèi* 藝術類 — the "Arts" — and gathers the works the Qiánlóng editors classed as the practice and connoisseurship of the literati arts: calligraphy 書 and painting 畫 (which together account for roughly three-quarters of the division), antiquarian *jīnshí xué* 金石學, music for the *qín* zither, chess and Go, seal-script and seal-cutting, and one major treatise on garden design. Following Wilkinson (§2.9 on calligraphy as a fine art, §2.10–§2.12 on stone inscriptions, inscribed landscapes, and seals, §32 on painting and especially §32.3 on the literati theoretical tradition and §32.11 on collection catalogs, §33.4 on imperial parks and private gardens, and §34.2 on ancient music), the division is the single best-documented Chinese genre-cluster for what the Western tradition would call the "fine arts" — and the editorial point of the *Sìkù* *Yìshù lèi* is the consolidation, under one heading, of what earlier *sìbù* schemes had distributed across *záyì* 雜藝, separate calligraphy- and painting-catalogs, and the *qín* and *qí* subdivisions of the Masters Branch.

The chronological span runs from the Wèi-Jìn games-anthology *Yì jīng* 藝經 [KR3h0099](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0099) (c. 200–221, Hándān Chún) and Cáo Pī's *Tánqí jīng* 彈碁經 [KR3h0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0102) (c. 220–226) — the earliest received Chinese writings on parlour-arts — through to the high Qiánlóng court, where the imperial *Shíqú bǎojí* [KR3h0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0063) (1744–45) catalogs over ten thousand secular calligraphies and paintings in the inner-palace collection and the *Xīqīng gǔjiàn* [KR3h0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0089) (1749–55) catalogs 1,529 antique bronzes. Three transmissional traditions structure the reading. (1) **The calligraphy tradition**, from the Wèi-Jìn *Cǎoshū zhuàng* [KR3h0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0091) of Suǒ Jìng and the *Sìtǐ shūshì* [KR3h0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0092) of Wèi Héng through the Liáng *pǐn*-criticism of Yǔ Jiānwú [KR3h0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0002), the Táng theoretical canon of Sūn Guòtíng [KR3h0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0005) and Zhāng Huáiguàn [KR3h0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0006) and Zhāng Yànyuǎn's encyclopaedic *Fǎshū yàolù* [KR3h0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0008), the Northern Sòng connoisseurship of Mǐ Fú [KR3h0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0022)–[KR3h0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0024) and the imperial *Xuānhé shūpǔ* [KR3h0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0026), to the late-imperial syntheses of Yuán Zhèng Jiǎo's *Yǎnjí* [KR3h0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0038), Míng Xiàng Mù's *Shūfǎ yǎyán* [KR3h0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0050), and the 420-juan Qīng compendium *Liùyì zhī yī lù* [KR3h0070](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0070) by Ní Tāo. (2) **The painting tradition**, from Zōng Bǐng's foundational *Huà shānshuǐ xù* [KR3h0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0095) (c. 420–443) and Xiè Hè's *Liùfǎ* in *Gǔhuà pǐnlù* [KR3h0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0001) (c. 480–510) through the Táng art-historical synthesis of Zhāng Yànyuǎn's *Lìdài mínghuà jì* [KR3h0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0009) (847), the *yìpǐn* 逸品 elevation of Zhū Jǐngxuán [KR3h0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0010) and Huáng Xiūfù [KR3h0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0016), the Northern Sòng *xièyì* 寫意 / *qìyùn fēi shī* doctrines of Guō Ruòxū [KR3h0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0017) and Guō Xī [KR3h0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0018), the imperial *Xuānhé huàpǔ* [KR3h0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0025), and Mǐ Fú's *Huàshǐ* [KR3h0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0021), through the Yuán biographical-dictionaries of Tāng Hòu [KR3h0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0037) and Xià Wényàn [KR3h0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0041), the late-Míng connoisseurial compendia of Zhāng Chǒu [KR3h0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0055)–[KR3h0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0059) and Wāng Kěyù [KR3h0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0060), to the imperial Qīng catalogs *Pèiwénzhāi shūhuà pǔ* [KR3h0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0061), *Mìdiàn zhūlín* [KR3h0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0062), and *Shíqú bǎojí* [KR3h0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0063). (3) **The antiquarian *jīnshí* tradition**, from Liáng Táo Hóngjǐng's *Gǔjīn dāojiàn lù* [KR3h0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0083) and Chén Yú Lì's *Dǐng lù* [KR3h0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0084) through Lǚ Dàlín's *Kǎogǔ tú* [KR3h0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0086) — the founding work of empirical Chinese antiquarianism, c. 1092 — and the imperial *Chóngxiū Xuānhé bógǔ tú* [KR3h0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0087), to the high-Qīng *Xīqīng gǔjiàn* [KR3h0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0089). Smaller but established subclusters in the catalog cover *qín* zither (Zhū Chángwén's *Qínshǐ* [KR3h0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0073), Yán Chéng's *Sōngxián guǎn qínpǔ* [KR3h0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0074), etc.), Táng music (Nán Zhuó's *Jiégǔ lù* [KR3h0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0079), Duàn Ānjié's *Yuèfǔ zálù* [KR3h0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0080)), seal-script and seal-cutting (Wú Qiūyǎn's *Xuégǔ biān* [KR3h0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0077), Zhū Xiàngxián's *Yìn diǎn* [KR3h0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0078)), Go and chess (Yàn Tiānzhāng's *Qí jīng* [KR3h0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0081), Liú Zhòngfǔ's *Qí jué* [KR3h0082](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0082), and the Six-Dynasties anthological fragments [KR3h0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0098)–[KR3h0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0102)), and the unique Míng treatise on garden design, Jì Chéng's *Yuányě* [KR3h0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0090) (1631–34). Across all of these the editors' principal hermeneutic problem is the same: how to discipline a body of work composed largely of *pǐn*-grade aesthetic verdicts, eyewitness colophons, and connoisseurial anecdote into the evidential format the *Sìkù tíyào* demand — which they accomplish through the same regime of textual-critical scepticism they apply to [KR3g](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/) *Shùshù lèi*, treating pseudepigraphic Wèi-Jìn brush-treatises (*Bǐzhèn tú* [KR3h0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0093), *Bǐjīng* [KR3h0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0094)) and reassigned colophons (the *Shānhú mùnán* / *Tiěwǎng shānhú* doublet [KR3h0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0044)/[KR3h0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0045)) with the same documentary respect-with-scepticism the cosmological pseudepigrapha receive next door.

### Important texts and text clusters

**The Six-Dynasties theoretical foundation.** Three works compose the conceptual armature of Chinese painting criticism. Xiè Hè's *Gǔhuà pǐnlù* 古畫品錄 [KR3h0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0001) (c. 480–510) articulates the **Six Methods** (*huà liùfǎ* 畫六法) — *qìyùn shēngdòng*, *gǔfǎ yòngbǐ*, *yìngwù xiàngxíng*, *suílèi fùcǎi*, *jīngyíng wèizhì*, *chuánmó yíxiě* — that govern every subsequent Chinese pictorial criticism through the Qīng. Zōng Bǐng's *Huà shānshuǐ xù* 畫山水敘 [KR3h0095](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0095) (420–443) is the founding metaphysical statement of landscape painting, with the geometric-perspectival argument and the doctrine of *wò yóu* 臥遊 ("recumbent travel"). Yáo Zuì's *Xù huàpǐn* 續畫品 [KR3h0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0003) (540–552) is the second-oldest painting catalog and the principal correction of Xiè Hè's grade-assignments. Liáng *pǐn*-criticism trio: Yǔ Jiānwú's *Shūpǐn* 書品 [KR3h0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0002) (c. 530–551), Liǔ Yún's *Qípǐn* 棋品 [KR3h0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0101) (505–517), and Xiè Hè's *Gǔhuà pǐnlù* together form the late-Liáng *pǐn*-discourse triplet that anchors the aesthetic-critical vocabulary of all the *yìshù* fields (paralleling Zhōng Róng's *Shī pǐn* in poetry).

**The Wèi-Jìn calligraphic-foundational layer.** Suǒ Jìng's *Cǎoshū zhuàng* 草書狀 [KR3h0091](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0091) (270–303), Wèi Héng's *Sìtǐ shūshì* 四體書勢 [KR3h0092](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0092) (270–291), and the pseudepigraphic *Bǐzhèn tú* 筆陣圖 [KR3h0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0093) and *Bǐjīng* 筆經 [KR3h0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0094) (attributed to Wèi Shuò / Wáng Xīzhī, in fact 4th–8th-c. composite) furnish the earliest stratum of Chinese calligraphic theory and the source of the "battle-formation" stroke-imagery and the *wénfáng sìbǎo* (Four Treasures of the Studio) literature.

**The Táng systematic synthesis.** Sūn Guòtíng's *Shūpǔ* 書譜 [KR3h0005](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0005) (687) is the canonical Táng theoretical treatise on calligraphy and the principal organising statement of the field by script-genre (*zhēn / xíng / cǎo / lì*); Zhāng Huáiguàn's *Shūduàn* 書斷 [KR3h0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0006) (720–740) is the model for all later Chinese calligraphic biographical-rank treatises; Dòu Jì's *Shùshū fù* 述書賦 [KR3h0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0007) (754–758) with Dòu Méng's commentary anchors the *fù*-form treatment of calligraphy and the earliest collector's-seal documentation. The two great Táng art-historical syntheses are by Zhāng Yànyuǎn: *Fǎshū yàolù* 法書要錄 [KR3h0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0008) (847–855) — the single most important preserver of Six-Dynasties and early-Táng calligraphic theory — and *Lìdài mínghuà jì* 歷代名畫記 [KR3h0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0009) (847), the earliest fully extant systematic art history in any language and the model for every subsequent Chinese art-historical work. Zhū Jǐngxuán's *Tángcháo mínghuà lù* 唐朝名畫錄 [KR3h0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0010) (840–846) introduces the **untrammelled grade** (*yìpǐn* 逸品) — the conceptual move that, once Huáng Xiūfù [KR3h0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0016) elevates *yì* above *shénpǐn*, becomes the theoretical foundation of the literati-painting tradition.

**The Northern Sòng painter-biography tradition.** Liú Dàochún's *Wǔdài mínghuà bǔyí* 五代名畫補遺 [KR3h0014](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0014) (1059) and *Sòngcháo mínghuà píng* 宋朝名畫評 [KR3h0015](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0015) (1086–1100) are the earliest systematic records of Five-Dynasties and Northern Sòng painters, seeding the Jīng-Guān monumental-landscape genealogy. Huáng Xiūfù's *Yìzhōu mínghuà lù* 益州名畫錄 [KR3h0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0016) (1006) registers Shǔ-court painting and gives the theoretical elevation of *yìpǐn*. Guō Ruòxū's *Túhuà jiànwén zhì* 圖畫見聞誌 [KR3h0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0017) (1074–80) — translated by Soper as *Experiences in Painting* — supplies the *qìyùn fēi shī* 氣韻非師 ("vital-pneuma cannot be transmitted from a teacher") doctrine and the Northern / Southern landscape-lineage scheme that anchors literati art theory. Guō Xī (with Guō Sī's editing) in *Línquán gāozhì jí* 林泉高致集 [KR3h0018](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0018) (1117) articulates the *Sānyuǎn* 三遠 doctrine — *gāoyuǎn* 高遠 (high distance), *shēnyuǎn* 深遠 (deep distance), *píngyuǎn* 平遠 (level distance) — the standard typology for spatial recession in all subsequent Chinese landscape practice. Hán Zhuō's *Shānshuǐ chúnquán jí* 山水純全集 [KR3h0027](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0027) (1121) supplies the most-cited Northern Sòng source for the technical vocabulary of *cūnfǎ* (texture-stroke methods) and adds three further "distances" to Guō Xī's three. Dèng Chūn's *Huàjì* 畫繼 [KR3h0030](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0030) (1167) is the principal bridge text between the late-Huīzōng academy and the early Southern Sòng.

**Mǐ Fú and Sòng connoisseurship.** Mǐ Fú's three short connoisseurial works of 1086–1107 — *Bǎozhāng dàifǎng lù* 寶章待訪錄 [KR3h0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0023) (1086), *Huàshǐ* 畫史 [KR3h0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0021) and *Shūshǐ* 書史 [KR3h0022](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0022) (both c. 1100–07), and *Hǎiyuè míngyán* 海嶽名言 [KR3h0024](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0024) — are the foundation of Chinese connoisseurship literature: the earliest detailed first-person records of private collections, the earliest systematic descriptions of seals and mountings, and the canonical sceptical rejection of metaphor-laden criticism. Dǒng Yǒu's two paired colophon-collections *Guǎngchuān shūbá* 廣川書跋 [KR3h0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0028) and *Guǎngchuān huàbá* 廣川畫跋 [KR3h0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0029) (1115–27) found the colophon-essay form (*bá* 跋 / *tíbá* 題跋) that dominates Yuán-Míng-Qīng connoisseurial writing — and, on the calligraphic side, advance *jīnshí xué* into systematic connoisseurial appraisal.

**The Northern Sòng imperial catalogs.** *Xuānhé huàpǔ* 宣和畫譜 [KR3h0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0025) (1120) — translated by Ebrey 2008, with McNair 2023 arguing for the eunuch Liáng Shīchéng as actual editor — and *Xuānhé shūpǔ* 宣和書譜 [KR3h0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0026) (1120–23) are the foundational documents for the Huīzōng imperial collection, ten-fold subject-classified for painting (Wilkinson §32.11 reproduces the breakdown: 6,396 scrolls under 231 painters) and the canonical model for all subsequent imperial collection-catalogs. Zhū Chángwén's *Mòchí biān* 墨池編 [KR3h0019](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0019) (1066–80) is the great non-imperial calligraphic compendium of the period.

**The Southern Sòng anthological consolidation.** Jiāng Kuí's *Xù shūpǔ* 續書譜 [KR3h0031](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0031) (1200–08, translated alongside Sūn Guòtíng in Chang and Frankel 1995) is the principal Southern Sòng systematic calligraphic doctrine, organised by aesthetic category. Yuè Kē's *Bǎozhēnzhāi fǎshū zàn* 寶眞齋法書贊 [KR3h0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0032) is the largest family-collection catalog of the era and the only premodern source preserving the *Èguó chuánjiā tiè* of Yuè Fēi's correspondence. Chén Sī's *Shūyuàn jīnghuá* 書苑菁華 [KR3h0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0033) (1234–59) and *Shū xiǎoshǐ* 書小史 [KR3h0034](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0034) (1259–67) — 521 figures — together provide the systematic biographical reference set for calligraphers from antiquity through the Five Dynasties; Dǒng Gèng's *Shūlù* 書錄 [KR3h0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0035) is a rare prosopographic survey of Sòng-dynasty calligraphers, one of the few medieval Chinese calligraphic prosopographies systematically including women.

**The Sòng antiquarian / *jīnshí* cluster.** Lǚ Dàlín's *Kǎogǔ tú* 考古圖 [KR3h0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0086) (1092) is the founding work of empirical Chinese antiquarianism — Wilkinson (§2.10) treats it as the systematic point of departure of *jīnshí xué* — establishing the *yǒu yí zé quē* ("doubt-then-leave-blank") evidential principle. Wáng Fú's *Chóngxiū Xuānhé bógǔ tú* 重修宣和博古圖 [KR3h0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0087) (1107–23) is the imperial counterpart, in 30 *juàn* with over 800 vessels. Wáng Qiú's *Xiàotáng jígǔ lù* 嘯堂集古錄 [KR3h0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0085) (1130–70) supplies the *kuǎnshí*-with-gloss format that gives the earliest surviving Sòng readings for many Shāng-Zhōu inscriptions. Together with Ōuyáng Xiū's *Jígǔ lù* (in [KR2k](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR2/KR2k/) not here) and Zhào Míngchéng's *Jīnshí lù* (also outside KR3h), the *Kǎogǔ tú* / *Bógǔ tú* / *Xiàotáng* triplet is the canonical Sòng *jīnshí* primary-source set.

**The Yuán reference works.** Lǐ Kàn's *Zhúpǔ* 竹譜 [KR3h0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0036) (1300–19) is the only Chinese treatise combining a complete bamboo-painting manual with a systematic botanical catalog, foundation of *mòzhú* practice. Tāng Hòu's *Huàjiàn* 畫鑒 [KR3h0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0037) (1322–30) is the principal Yuán connoisseur's manual; Zhèng Jiǎo's *Yǎnjí* 衍極 [KR3h0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0038) (with Liú Yǒudìng's commentary, 1324–28) is the principal Yuán calligraphic-theoretical treatise; and Shèng Xīmíng's twin compendia — *Túhuà kǎo* 圖畫攷 [KR3h0039](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0039) and *Fǎshū kǎo* 法書考 [KR3h0040](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0040) (1330–49) — are the earliest topical (rather than chronological) systematic references on painting and calligraphy. Xià Wényàn's *Túhuì bǎojiàn* 圖繪寶鑑 [KR3h0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0041) (1365) becomes, after the dynastic transition, the standard biographical dictionary of Chinese painters and is reprinted through the Míng and Qīng.

**The late-Míng connoisseurial complex.** The richest sustained cluster of the division. Dū Mù's *Yùyì biān* 寓意編 [KR3h0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0042) (c. 1495–1525) and Zhū Cúnlǐ's *Shānhú mùnán* 珊瑚木難 [KR3h0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0044) (1495–1513) open the late-Wú connoisseurial mode. Yáng Shèn's *Mòchí suǒlù* 墨池璅錄 [KR3h0046](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0046) (1530–59) and Fēng Fāng's *Shūjué* 書訣 [KR3h0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0048) (1523–63) carry the calligraphic-theoretical thread through the mid-century Zhào Mèngfǔ revival. Xiàng Mù's *Shūfǎ yǎyán* 書法雅言 [KR3h0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0050) (1580–1600) supplies the explicit calligraphic recovery of the Wáng Xīzhī tradition — the calligraphic parallel to Dǒng Qíchāng's *Nánběi zōng* 南北宗 painting theory. The compilation *Tiěwǎng shānhú* 趙氏鐵綱珊瑚 [KR3h0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0045) (1600–20, attributed to Zhū Cúnlǐ but rejected by the *Sìkù tíyào*, with Zhào Qíměi as actual editor) and Sūn Kuàng's *Shūhuà bábá* 書畫跋跋 [KR3h0047](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0047) (1590–1613) extend the colophon-collection mode. Zhào Yíguāng's *Hánshān zhǒután* 寒山帚談 [KR3h0051](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0051) (1600–25) is the principal doctrinal statement of the late-Míng *cǎozhuàn* (cursive seal-script) innovators. The three terminal compendia — Zhāng Chǒu's *Qīnghé shūhuà fǎng* 清河書畫舫 [KR3h0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0055) (1615–16) with its tabular companions *Qīnghé shūhuà biǎo* [KR3h0057](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0057), *Shūhuà jiànwén biǎo* [KR3h0058](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0058), *Nányáng shūhuà jí* [KR3h0059](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0059), and the *Zhēnjī rìlù* [KR3h0056](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0056); Yù Féngqìng's *Shūhuà tíbá jì* 書畫題跋記 [KR3h0054](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0054) (1634–44); and Wāng Kěyù's monumental 48-*juàn* *Shānhú wǎng* 珊瑚網 [KR3h0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0060) (1643) — together form the terminal record of Jiāngnán connoisseurship before the dynastic collapse, alongside Táng Zhìqì's *Huìshì wēiyán* 繪事微言 [KR3h0049](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0049) (the principal late-Míng systematic landscape-painting compendium) and Zhū Móuyīn's *Huàshǐ huìyào* 畫史會要 [KR3h0053](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0053) (1631).

**The Qīng imperial-catalog programme.** Sūn Yuèbān's *Yùdìng Pèiwénzhāi shūhuà pǔ* 御定佩文齋書畫譜 [KR3h0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0061) (1708, 100 *juàn*, with 1,844 sources cited per-entry) is the principal single Qīng reference work on Chinese calligraphy and painting up to the late Kāngxī, and stands as the Qīng equivalent of the Sòng *Xuānhé* catalogs. The Qiánlóng-court imperial catalogs follow: *Mìdiàn zhūlín* 祕殿珠林 [KR3h0062](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0062) (1744, Buddhist and Daoist works in the inner-palace collection), *Shíqú bǎojí* 石渠寶笈 [KR3h0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0063) (1744–45, the more than ten thousand secular pieces — the most ambitious catalog of any premodern Chinese imperial art collection, and the principal modern provenance reference for surviving post-Sòng masterworks in Beijing and Taipei), and Liáng Shīzhèng / Jiǎng Pǔ's *Xīqīng gǔjiàn* 西清古鑑 [KR3h0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0089) (1749–55, 40 *juàn*, 1,529 antique bronzes — the closing imperial antiquarian compilation). Around them, Biàn Yǒngyù's 60-*juàn* *Shūhuà huìkǎo* 書畫彙考 [KR3h0068](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0068) (1682) is the largest single private compendium of calligraphy-and-painting records before the *Pèiwénzhāi*; Sūn Chéngzé's *Gēngzǐ xiāoxià jì* 庚子銷夏記 [KR3h0064](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0064) (1660), Gāo Shìqí's *Jiāngcūn xiāoxià lù* 江村銷夏錄 [KR3h0067](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0067) (1693), and Lì È's *Nán Sòng yuànhuà lù* 南宋院畫錄 [KR3h0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0069) (1721–45) are the principal scholar-connoisseurs' catalogs of the Kāngxī-Yōngzhèng-Qiánlóng cohort.

**The Qīng calligraphic-and-painting handbooks.** Féng Wǔ's *Shūfǎ zhèngchuán* 書法正傳 [KR3h0066](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0066) (1707) is the principal Qīng compilation of regular-script theory; Ní Tāo's *Liùyì zhī yī lù* 六藝之一錄 [KR3h0070](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0070) (1700–60, 420 *juàn*) is one of the longest single-author *kǎozhèng* compendia in the entire *Sìkù*, effectively a one-volume library of pre-Qīng calligraphy literature; Wáng Yùxián's *Huìshì bèikǎo* 繪事備考 [KR3h0065](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0065) (1691) is the standard Qīng painter-dictionary bridging Xià Wényàn and the *Pèiwénzhāi*; Jiǎng Jì's *Chuánshén mìyào* 傳神祕要 [KR3h0072](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0072) (1707–27) is the first and principal Chinese treatise on portraiture, elevating *xiězhēn* 寫真 from artisanal to *shìdàifū* status; and Zōu Yīguì's *Xiǎoshān huàpǔ* 小山畫譜 [KR3h0071](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0071) (1756) is the principal Qiánlóng-court theoretical handbook on flower painting in the *mòjīng* (boneless) tradition.

**The qín, seal, music, and games subclusters.** *Qínshǐ* 琴史 [KR3h0073](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0073) (Zhū Chángwén, c. 1080) is the first systematic history of the *qín* zither and the earliest substantial Chinese music-historical work; the *Sōngxián guǎn qínpǔ* [KR3h0074](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0074), *Sōngfēng gé qínpǔ* [KR3h0075](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0075), and the bilingual Chinese-Manchu *Qínpǔ hébì* [KR3h0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0076) are the major received Míng-Qīng tablature collections. Wú Qiūyǎn's *Xuégǔ biān* 學古編 [KR3h0077](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0077) (early Yuán) and Zhū Xiàngxián's *Yìn diǎn* 印典 [KR3h0078](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0078) (Qīng) are the principal pre-modern Chinese treatises on seal-cutting and seal-script; Wilkinson (§2.12 on seals) treats them as foundational to the late-imperial *zhuànkè* revival. Nán Zhuó's *Jiégǔ lù* 羯鼓錄 [KR3h0079](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0079) and Duàn Ānjié's *Yuèfǔ zálù* 樂府雜錄 [KR3h0080](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0080) are the two principal Táng records of court music and entertainment, indispensable for the Tang music section that Wilkinson treats at §34.2. Yàn Tiānzhāng's *Qí jīng* 棋經 [KR3h0081](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0081) and Liú Zhòngfǔ's *Qí jué* 棋訣 [KR3h0082](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0082) are the two principal Sòng received writings on Go. Together with the Six-Dynasties fragments [KR3h0098](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0098)–[KR3h0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0102) (Yóu Zhào's *Rúqí gé*, Hándān Chún's *Yì jīng*, the Five-Dynasties / Táng *Qíshǒu shì*, Liǔ Yún's *Qí pǐn*, and Cáo Pī's *Tánqí jīng*), these constitute the canonical *qí* primary-source set; Liǔ Yún's *Qí pǐn* [KR3h0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0101) in particular completes the late-Liáng *pǐn*-criticism quartet.

**Bronze-and-blade antiquaria.** Táo Hóngjǐng's *Gǔjīn dāojiàn lù* 古今刀劔錄 [KR3h0083](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0083) (502–536) is the standard premodern Chinese source on the historiography of blade-weapons; Yú Lì's *Dǐng lù* 鼎錄 [KR3h0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0084) (557–569) is the earliest surviving Chinese register of ritual tripods — predating Lǚ Dàlín by some five centuries. Lǚ Zhèn's *Xuāndé dǐngyí pǔ* 宣德鼎彝譜 [KR3h0088](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0088) (1428) is the principal document of the 1428 Xuāndé imperial bronze-recasting programme.

**Garden design.** Jì Chéng's *Yuányě* 園冶 [KR3h0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0090) (1631–34) is the foundation of Chinese garden theory and the single most influential premodern Chinese treatise on landscape-garden design, articulating the doctrines of *yīn* 因 (working with the site), *jiè* 借 (borrowed scenery), and *tǐyí* 體宜 (appropriate scale). The work is the only pre-modern Chinese architectural treatise to give a systematic poetics of practice; rediscovered by Edo-period Japanese architects and re-introduced to Chinese scholarship in the 1930s. Wilkinson (§33.4) treats it as the canonical theoretical reference for the Sūzhōu and Yángzhōu private-garden tradition.

### Topics

1. **The Six Methods (*huà liùfǎ* 畫六法).** Xiè Hè's six-fold framework — *qìyùn shēngdòng*, *gǔfǎ yòngbǐ*, *yìngwù xiàngxíng*, *suílèi fùcǎi*, *jīngyíng wèizhì*, *chuánmó yíxiě* — is the conceptual armature of every subsequent Chinese pictorial criticism through the Qīng. The principal interpretive problem the tradition negotiates is the supremacy and untranslatability of *qìyùn shēngdòng* and its relationship to teachability: Guō Ruòxū's *qìyùn fēi shī* doctrine [KR3h0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0017) is the canonical reply, asserting that the supreme aesthetic quality cannot be transmitted from a teacher and so must be cultivated through the painter's personal *xiūyǎng* (self-cultivation). See Acker (1954–74), Bush and Shih (1985), and Vinograd's "Classification, canon, and genre" essay in Powers and Tsiang's *Companion to Chinese Art* (2016).

2. **The *yìpǐn* 逸品 elevation.** The Táng grading-categories *shénpǐn* 神品 (spirit grade), *miàopǐn* 妙品 (subtle grade), *néngpǐn* 能品 (competent grade) are inherited from Xiè Hè's six-grade scheme. Zhū Jǐngxuán's *Tángcháo mínghuà lù* [KR3h0010](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0010) introduces *yìpǐn* (the untrammelled grade) outside the existing scale; Huáng Xiūfù's *Yìzhōu mínghuà lù* [KR3h0016](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0016) elevates *yìpǐn* to the top of the scale. This is the conceptual move that founds the literati-painting tradition's theoretical superiority over technically-trained court / academy painting.

3. **The *xièyì* 寫意 vs. *gōngbǐ* 工筆 polarity and the *Nánběi zōng* theory.** The principled distinction between the spontaneous-suggestive literati hand and the meticulous court / professional hand crystallises in Northern-Sòng colophon-criticism (Sū Shì, Mǐ Fú in [KR3h0021](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0021), Guō Ruòxū in [KR3h0017](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0017)) and culminates in Dǒng Qíchāng's late-Míng *Nánběi zōng* (Southern / Northern school) theory of painting lineages — paralleled on the calligraphic side by Xiàng Mù's *Shūfǎ yǎyán* [KR3h0050](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0050). The polarity is the principal organising distinction of late-imperial art-historical writing.

4. **Pseudepigraphy and textual-criticism in brush-treatises.** The *Sìkù tíyào* exhibit the same textual-critical scepticism here as in [KR3g](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3g/): the brush-treatises *Bǐzhèn tú* [KR3h0093](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0093) and *Bǐjīng* [KR3h0094](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0094) are exposed as pseudepigraphic notwithstanding their Wèi Shuò / Wáng Xīzhī attributions, the *Tiěwǎng shānhú* [KR3h0045](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0045) is rejected as a Wàn-lì-period editorial fabrication built on Zhū Cúnlǐ's [KR3h0044](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0044), and the *Tánqí jīng* [KR3h0102](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0102) is treated as a composite anthology rather than a single Cáo Pī work. The *tíyào* preserve a characteristic stance: the pseudepigraphic ascription is repudiated, the document's technical-and-historical value preserved.

5. ***Jīnshí xué* 金石學: from inscriptions to evidential history.** Wilkinson (§2.10 on stone inscriptions, §2.12 on seals) treats Sòng antiquarianism as the systematic origin of Chinese evidential / *kǎozhèng* method. The triplet *Kǎogǔ tú* [KR3h0086](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0086) / *Bógǔ tú* [KR3h0087](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0087) / *Xiàotáng jígǔ lù* [KR3h0085](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0085) — in conjunction with Ōuyáng Xiū's *Jígǔ lù* and Zhào Míngchéng's *Jīnshí lù* (both outside KR3h) — establishes empirical antiquarianism in Northern-Sòng China, with the *yǒu yí zé quē* principle. The Qing high-imperial *Xīqīng gǔjiàn* [KR3h0089](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0089) is the closing imperial expression of the same tradition; the gap between the two registers the lapsed-and-revived character of the *jīnshí* tradition Wilkinson treats at length.

6. **Imperial collecting and the catalog as state document.** The transformation of the painter's-eye record into the imperial-bureaucratic catalog runs from the Tang *Zhēnguān gōngsī huàshǐ* [KR3h0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0004) through *Xuānhé huàpǔ* / *Xuānhé shūpǔ* [KR3h0025](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0025)/[KR3h0026](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0026) (which Ebrey 2008 and McNair 2023 treat as cultural-political instruments) to the Qing *Pèiwénzhāi* [KR3h0061](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0061) and *Shíqú bǎojí* [KR3h0063](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0063). The imperial catalog is simultaneously inventory, legitimation, and aesthetic-canonical declaration — and its provenance information is the principal modern basis for authenticating surviving pre-Qing masterworks.

7. **The colophon (*tíbá* 題跋) as critical form.** Dǒng Yǒu's pair [KR3h0028](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0028)/[KR3h0029](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0029) founds the colophon-essay, which the Yuán-Míng-Qīng connoisseurial compendia ([KR3h0042](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0042) through [KR3h0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0060)) carry as their dominant form. The colophon is the calligraphic-pictorial equivalent of the *bǐjì* 筆記 form: episodic, dated, signed, frequently dialogic with prior colophons on the same piece — and structurally inseparable from the physical-object practices Wilkinson treats at §32.3 (the *shuāngkuǎn* signature-plus-dedication form, the *tíshī* picture-poem).

8. **The late-Liáng *pǐn*-criticism quartet.** Within a single generation (c. 505–552) the Liáng / Chén court produces Zhōng Róng's *Shī pǐn* (poetry, in [KR4d](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR4/KR4d/)), Yǔ Jiānwú's *Shūpǐn* [KR3h0002](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0002) (calligraphy), Xiè Hè's *Gǔhuà pǐnlù* [KR3h0001](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0001) (painting), and Liǔ Yún's *Qípǐn* [KR3h0101](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0101) (Go). This is the foundational moment of Chinese aesthetic-critical *pǐn*-discourse, in which the four major non-Confucian literati arts simultaneously acquire systematic ranked criticism.

9. **Forgery, authentication, and the social life of objects.** Late-Míng connoisseurship is acutely aware of forgery: Mǐ Fú's bipartite *mùdǔ* / *díwén* model [KR3h0023](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0023) is the canonical methodological response, and the late-Míng compendia of Zhāng Chǒu [KR3h0055](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0055) and Wāng Kěyù [KR3h0060](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0060) organise themselves around the eyewitness-record distinction. The notorious Fēng Fāng [KR3h0048](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0048) embodies the period's productive ambivalence around forgery: a substantial calligraphic theorist who was also one of the era's most famous forgers. Park (2025, on Zhāng Tàijiē's *Bǎohuì lù*) treats this strain in late-Míng connoisseurship; Wilkinson (§32.9) treats Chinese forgery historically.

10. **East-Asian circulation.** *Yuányě* [KR3h0090](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0090) survives because Edo-period Japanese architects collected and preserved a corpus the early Qīng allowed to fall into neglect; Japanese rediscovery in the late nineteenth century re-introduced the work to twentieth-century Chinese architectural scholarship. The bilingual *Qínpǔ hébì* [KR3h0076](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3h/KR3h0076) (Yáng Lún's Míng *qín*-manual with Hé Sù's Qīng Manchu translation) registers an interior East-Asian musical-cultural translation. Both works register the longue-durée cross-border circulation of Chinese art-knowledge that Wilkinson sketches at §34.2.5 on early musical interactions.
